about: Anoria: 150 more cards from real history, found only in packs (merged into the game on 2026-11-11: see `merged`; nothing in the game loads this file): 100 Figures, 20 Relics and 30 Deeds. cards: one object per card, with the fields of cards.js (key, n, t, f, c, m, reg, era, y, k, arr, insp, from) and of text.js (cap, ll, tx, fact, say, art; links holds the card's LINKS sentences as 'source>key'). A Relic or a Deed has `fx`, the card already in the game whose effect, cost and rules text it takes, and `fit`, one line on why the history suits that effect. src is the reference page for the card's dates, fact and links. Wikipedia could not be opened from the session that wrote the cards, so each card was checked through web search, which quotes Wikipedia and other pages; src2 is a second page the search quoted in support. sure is true when the search confirmed the card's dates, its fact and every link sentence, and false when it did not return one of them; check says what was not returned, or what the sources disagree about. Picture briefs (art) were written from memory and get the usual audit before any art is made. threads: named lines to collect, shaped like THREADS in cards.js. threadAdds: new cards that belong in a line cards.js already has. existing: links the new cards could give to cards already in the game (each needs a line in FROM or insp, and its sentence in LINKS). needsEngine: a few Relics and Deeds that are not among the 150, because each needs an effect the engine does not have. dropped: the cards that left the first draft, each with its reason. heldForGuides: five of those, kept whole, because a Guide's picture for each is on the working branch. merge: what the merge has to do that is not copying. Check with: node scripts/anoria/check-set.js

links.@library>euclid: Ancient writers place Euclid in Alexandria under the first Ptolemy, the king who began its Library.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: His Elements builds the whole of geometry, step by step, from a handful of plain starting points. It was copied, printed and taught from for more than two thousand years.
cards.art: Euclid about 300 BC in a shaded colonnade at Alexandria, teaching the first proposition of his Elements: a spare Greek man of about fifty with cropped gray hair and a short gray beard, in a plain wool cloak over a tunic, seated on a stone bench with a papyrus roll held open between his two hands, one hand on each rolled end, reading the next step aloud and glancing over the top of the roll. Beside him, close, a shallow wooden tray of smoothed sand, about as wide as a man's arm is long, stands on a waist-high stone table, and a pupil of sixteen bends over it: a short cord is pegged at one end in the sand, and with a pointed stick tied to the cord's other end he is scoring a circle. The figure in the sand is the first in the Elements: two circles of the same size, side by side, that overlap by half their width, so that the rim of the left circle runs exactly through the center of the right circle and the rim of the right circle runs exactly through the center of the left one, leaving a pointed almond shape where they overlap. A small peg stands at each of the two centers, on the two sides of the almond. Three straight lines make a triangle of three equal sides: one from peg to peg across the middle of the almond, and one from each peg up to the top tip of the almond. Both circles can be seen whole, and there is nothing else drawn in the sand. Two more pupils lean in, one a grown bearded man holding a wax tablet, one a boy: three pupils in all. The bright harbor shows between the columns, with two small sailing ships and no lighthouse (the Pharos is not built yet). Seen from above the near edge of the sand tray, looking down into it and across it at Euclid, so that the tray with its whole figure fills the middle of the picture from a third to half of the way down, and Euclid's face and the roll are just above it, a little right of center, his head a fifth to a third of the way down the picture, with a wide band of column and sky above his head. Nobody knows his face, so he is an ordinary Greek scholar of his day: no long white beard, no metal compasses with a hinge, no bound books, nobody kneeling on the ground. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with Euclid's head, the roll, the pupils' heads and the whole sand tray with its two circles all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the legs of the table and the paving. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only column and shadow there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The search did not return that he worked in Alexandria under the first Ptolemy, or how long the Elements was taught from. Both are standard, written from memory. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written. The link sentence now says only what the ancient writers say.

cards.cap: Cyrene and Alexandria, c. 276 to c. 194 BC
cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: He measured the Earth from a noon shadow in Alexandria on midsummer's day, when the Sun stood straight above a town far to the south. His answer was close to the truth.
cards.art: Eratosthenes at noon on midsummer's day about 240 BC, measuring the Earth from a courtyard in Alexandria: a Greek scholar of about thirty-five, clean-shaven, with short dark curly hair, in a light linen tunic with a cloak over one arm, standing bent over a bronze sundial bowl set on a stone pillar at chest height. The bowl is a hollow half-sphere about as wide as his forearm is long, open to the sky, its inside scored with a few fine curved lines, and one thin upright bronze pin rises from the very bottom of the bowl to the level of its rim. The sun is almost straight overhead, so the pin's shadow is very short, a small dark dash on the bottom of the bowl beside the foot of the pin, and every shadow in the white courtyard is small and sharp. He touches the tip of that shadow with the point of a thin reed held in his right hand, squinting against the glare, and his left hand shades his eyes. A boy of twelve beside him holds a hinged wooden wax tablet and a bronze stylus, ready to write. Seen from the far side of the bowl, low, so that we look into the bowl and up at him, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his head. Ptolemaic Alexandria: no telescope, no globe, no glass lenses, no inkpot, nobody kneeling, no obelisk. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with his head, both his hands, the boy's head and the whole bowl with its pin all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the pillar and the white paving. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only bare sunlit wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: He and his school taught that illness has natural causes, and that a doctor should watch the patient closely and note what happens day by day. Many new doctors still take an oath that carries his name.
cards.art: Hippocrates on the island of Kos about 400 BC, examining a patient in the open air: an old man with a bald crown and a short white beard, as the ancient busts named for him show, in a plain cloak that leaves one shoulder bare, bending with his ear laid flat against the bare back of a fisherman who sits on a stool, listening to the man's breathing with his eyes shut and one hand raised for quiet. Two students stand by, one a youth with a hinged wax tablet and stylus ready, the other an older bearded man holding a bowl and a sponge. They are in the dappled shade of a huge plane tree in a small harbor town. Seen from the side, from the waist up, the old doctor's head right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above it. Classical Greece: no serpent staff, no white coat, no surgery or blood, no listening tube. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with the doctor's head against the patient's back, the patient's head and the two students' heads and hands all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the stool, legs and the ground. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only leaves and sky there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. cards.fact: In 132 he showed the Han court a bronze urn ringed with eight dragons, each holding a ball above an open-mouthed toad. When the ground shook far away a ball dropped, said to mark an earthquake days before riders brought the news.
cards.art: Zhang Heng, court astronomer of the Han dynasty, in AD 138, at the moment his earthquake vessel proves itself: a slender scholar of sixty with a thin gray beard, in a long dark robe with wide sleeves, a sash and the stiff black cap of a Han official, standing with one hand raised and his head turned sharply toward a great bronze vessel shaped like a covered wine jar with a domed lid, as wide across as a man is tall and standing higher than his head, its sides cast with mountains, birds and beasts in low relief. Eight bronze dragons are set evenly around its shoulder, each head down with its body running up the side of the jar, and the vessel is turned so that exactly four of them face us across its front, two near the middle and two near the edges; the other four are round the back and cannot be seen. On the floor around the foot of the vessel squat eight bronze toads, one directly under each dragon, each toad facing in toward the vessel and looking up at its dragon with its mouth wide open, so that exactly four toads can be seen, one under each of the four dragons, the nearest ones from behind. Three of the four dragons in view each hold a bronze ball the size of a plum in their jaws; the jaws of the fourth, one of the middle two, are open and empty, and its one ball is in mid-air, half way down to the open mouth of the toad below it: one falling ball only, drawn once, with no second ball and no trail. One junior official, a young man, has dropped his bundle of bamboo slips and stares. A timber hall with red pillars. Seen from across the vessel, Zhang Heng's face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his cap. Eastern Han China: writing on bamboo slips and silk, no paper books, no chairs, no dragon breathing fire, no writing on the vessel. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with the whole vessel from lid to foot, the four dragons, the falling ball, the four toads on the floor and Zhang Heng's whole figure all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only bare floor tiles and the dropped bamboo slips, so the vessel is drawn standing well back from us. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only dark roof beams there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: An official of the Han court, he reported to the emperor in 105 a way of making paper from bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets. Rougher paper was older, but his was cheap and good to write on, and it spread across China.
cards.art: Cai Lun, an official of the imperial workshops of Han China, in AD 105: a beardless man of about fifty with a smooth full face, as a palace eunuch was, his hair in a topknot under a small cloth cap, in a plain belted robe with the sleeves tied back, standing in a workshop yard at a low wooden vat of gray pulp and lifting out with both hands a four-sided bamboo frame about as wide as his chest, stretched with coarse cloth, water streaming from it and a thin even sheet of wet gray paper lying on the cloth. He tilts it to the light to judge it. Behind him an old worker and a young one pound bark and rags in a stone mortar with long wooden pestles, and three earlier sheets are drying in the sun, each still on its own cloth frame, the frames leaned against a rammed-earth wall. Seen from across the vat, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his head, and the dripping frame at the center. Eastern Han China: no printed pages, no bound books, no writing on the sheets, no sheets hung over a line. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with his head, his two hands and the whole dripping frame, with the workers and the drying frames behind all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the side of the vat and the wet ground. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: His birth year is given as anything from 50 to 62, so the caption gives only his death.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: His book of 628 is the first we know that treats zero as a number like any other, with rules for adding, taking away and multiplying with it. It speaks of numbers below zero as debts, and numbers above it as fortunes.
cards.art: Brahmagupta at thirty, in AD 628, an astronomer of western India, timing the rising of the Moon from a flat stone roof at dusk: a lean man with his hair tied in a knot on top of his head and a short dark beard, bare to the waist with a cotton shawl over one shoulder and a wrapped lower cloth. He sits cross-legged on the roof in the right half of the picture, facing left, sighting with one eye past the edge of a plain straight wooden staff, about two thirds as long as a man is tall, which he holds upright in one fist with its foot on the roof floor, toward a huge moon just clearing the horizon at the left; nothing sticks out of the staff. His other hand is lifted, palm open, to give the signal. Across the picture behind him runs the roof's parapet: one single low, straight wall of dressed stone at the roof's edge, as high as his chest as he sits, with a flat top as wide as a forearm is long; one wall only, no separate blocks, no steps, and beyond it nothing but the open air, the dusk plain far below and the sky. Nobody is on the far side of the parapet. On the parapet's flat top, in the left half of the picture, stands a water clock: a small copper bowl with a tiny hole in its base, floating and slowly sinking in a larger basin of water. The basin is as wide as a forearm is long and stands wholly on the parapet's flat top, its whole base resting on the stone, well back from every edge, with nothing hanging over the side. A boy pupil of about ten, smaller than the man, kneels on the roof floor on the near side of the parapet, on the same side of the wall as the astronomer, his back partly to us and his face in profile, his forearms resting on the parapet's top beside the basin as he watches the bowl sink; he keeps the count with a short row of pebbles on the stone. A bundle of long narrow palm-leaf pages tied between two wooden boards lies by the astronomer's knee. Seen from close by on the roof, low: the astronomer's face is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, with clear space above his head, and his lifted hand does not reach into the top right corner. India of the seventh century: palm-leaf pages, no paper books, no telescope, no turban of later centuries. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with his head, the staff, the moon, the boy and the water clock on the parapet all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only his crossed legs, the palm-leaf book and the stone roof. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

links.brahmagupta>alkhwarizmi: Al-Khwarizmi's star tables follow the Sindhind, an Arabic version of Indian astronomy that is thought to come from Brahmagupta's book, and his own book on Indian numerals taught readers of Arabic to reckon with zero.

cards.tx: Your Deeds cost 1 less.
cards.fact: His book on solving equations, written in Baghdad about 820, gave algebra its name, from the Arabic word al-jabr in its title. The word algorithm comes from his own name.
cards.art: Al-Khwarizmi about AD 820, on a canal bank outside the round city of Baghdad, putting his new method to work: a scholar of about forty with a full dark beard, in a long plain robe and a neatly wound turban, standing on the raised earth bank with a small wooden board held against his chest in his left hand, a sheet fixed to it, and a reed pen in his right hand, looking up from his reckoning to call a figure to two surveyors, one stout and one thin, who are stretching a knotted measuring rope across a field between two stakes just behind him, so that they are drawn level with his shoulder and chest on the left side of the picture. A farmer and his younger brother stand beyond them at the field's edge, waiting for the answer that will divide their inheritance. Date palms, the canal, and far behind the long plain wall of the city. Seen from the bank, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his turban. Abbasid Iraq: no chalkboard of modern symbols, no x and y, no Ottoman dress, no domes with crescents. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with his head, the board and pen, the two surveyors with their rope and the two brothers all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the earth bank and reeds at his feet. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only pale sky there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: That the Sindhind comes from Brahmagupta's book is generally presumed, not proven; the link says so.

links.alkhwarizmi>fibonacci: Fibonacci learned the Indian numerals as a boy in North Africa, and his book draws on al-Khwarizmi and the Arab mathematicians who followed him.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, you gain 1 Spark.
cards.fact: His book of 1202 taught Europe's merchants to reckon with the Indian figures and zero instead of Roman numerals. Its puzzle of breeding rabbits gives the numbers that bear his name.
cards.art: Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci, about 1202, in a merchant's counting house in Pisa: a man of about thirty with dark hair cut straight across the brow and no beard, in a long belted tunic and a soft cap, standing at a sloping desk and writing a short column of small figures with a quill held in his right hand, quick and sure, the figures only fine marks too small to read. The older grey-bearded merchant stands at his left side, which is the right-hand side of the picture, still pushing round counters about on a lined counting board, and Fibonacci holds up his open left hand toward him to stop him. So from left to right the picture shows the written sheet and the quill in his right hand, then Fibonacci, then his raised left hand, then the merchant with the counting board. The older man stares at the finished sum. Sacks, a pair of hanging scales and bolts of cloth fill the room, and through the open arch behind stands the cathedral's new round bell tower of white marble, only three stories built and no more, so it is a short stump about as wide as it is tall, with exactly three rings counted from the ground: first one ring of tall blind arches on half-columns against the solid wall, then one open gallery of small arches, then a second open gallery of small arches, and nothing above that but a flat unfinished top with a few scaffolding poles. It already leans a little. The whole stump can be seen through the arch from its foot to its top. Seen from across the desk, from the waist up, Fibonacci's face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his cap. Pisa about 1200: no printed books, no eyeglasses, the tower unfinished. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with both men's heads, the quill and the written sheet, the counting board, and the tower in the arch all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the front of the desk and sacks on the floor. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only stone wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

links.press>gutenberg: Gutenberg built his press in Mainz about 1450 and printed his great Bible on it.
links.paper>gutenberg: Most copies of Gutenberg's Bible were printed on paper, which cost far less than calfskin.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: A goldsmith by training, he worked out how to cast metal letters by the thousand, all alike, in a small mold held in the hand. About 180 copies of his Bible were printed, and nearly fifty still exist.
cards.art: Johannes Gutenberg about 1450 in his workshop at Mainz, casting type: a man of about fifty in a plain dark gown with the sleeves rolled and a leather apron, a close cap on his head, clean-shaven with a lined face, standing by a small brick furnace on which an iron pot of molten metal sits with a small long-handled iron ladle in it. In his left hand, raised to the level of his chest, he holds the hand mold he has just opened: two halves, each a block of iron set in a wooden shell, small enough to sit in the palm, the two halves hinged apart like an opened fist. In his right hand, between finger and thumb, he holds up beside it to the firelight the single piece of type he has just cast: a thin bright square stick of metal as long as the top joint of his finger, with a little tail of spare metal still on its lower end, and he peers closely at its tip. On the bench stand a shallow tray of finished type packed on end, seen only as a fine texture of small metal squares, a file and a short steel punch. Deep in the room behind, dim, stands the wooden press: two thick upright posts joined by a crossbeam, a big wooden screw coming down through the beam with a bar through it for a handle, and a flat board under the screw. Firelight on his face and hands. Seen from the bench, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his cap. No portrait of him from life exists, so the face is an ordinary craftsman's: no long forked beard, no fur hat, no readable letters anywhere. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with his head, the piece of type in his right hand, the open mold in his left hand, and the press behind all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the bench with the tray of type, the file and punch, and the furnace. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only dark beams there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: He was the first to sail the Northwest Passage, in a small fishing boat, and spent two winters on the way learning from the Netsilik Inuit to dress in furs and drive dogs. In 1911 what they taught him took him first to the South Pole.
cards.art: The South Pole on 14 December 1911: Roald Amundsen and his four companions plant the Norwegian flag together, as Amundsen wrote: five weather-beaten, frost-bitten fists. Seen from low on the snow, close, looking up at the five men and the flag against a deep cobalt sky. The pole is one plain straight wooden pole about twice a man's height, pushed upright into the snow two fifths of the way across the picture. The five men stand in a tight half ring round it, each reaching in with one arm, so that there are exactly five hands on the pole, one above another, and each hand's arm leads plainly back to its own man's shoulder; every man's other hand hangs at his side. Amundsen, aged thirty-nine, stands right of the pole, his hand the highest: a tall, lean man with a long weathered face, a large hooked nose, a receding hairline of thin fair hair, a short fair moustache, a few days of fair stubble and pale eyes narrowed against the glare; he is not white-haired and not old. The other four, each a different man with his own face and build, their faces all at about the same height and the same size: Olav Bjaaland, broad-faced, with a heavy moustache; Helmer Hanssen, dark-haired with a short dark beard; Sverre Hassel, the youngest, round-faced and clean-shaven; Oscar Wisting, square-jawed with a short beard. All wear roomy hooded pullover blouses of grey-brown windproof cloth over thick wool, some hoods up, some down, with frost on their eyebrows and moustaches. At the top of the pole a new, whole flag of Norway streams out to the right in the wind: a red flag with a dark blue cross outlined in white, the upright of the cross set nearer the pole; it flies across the top middle of the picture, its top edge a ninth of the way down and its far end only two thirds of the way across, clear of both top corners. Far off on the flat white plain, small, one loaded sledge and three sledge dogs. Amundsen's face is three fifths of the way across the picture and three tenths of the way down, below the flag; all five heads, the hands and the flag are in the upper half of the picture. Historically accurate for 1911: no fur suits, no long full beards, no ice axes, no mountains, no tent, no Sun in the sky. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

Written from memory and not searched: the Gjøa with seven men in all, the two winters at Gjoa Haven (1903 to 1905) and the Pole on 14 December 1911 are standard. The observations with sextant and mercury tray are in his own book, The South Pole.

links.copernicus>kepler: Kepler's first book, printed in 1596, was a defense of Copernicus's Sun-centred system.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: From years of sightings of Mars he found that planets move in ovals, not circles, and go faster nearer the Sun. He also defended his mother against a charge of witchcraft, and won.
cards.art: Johannes Kepler in Prague in the spring of 1605, at the end of his long war with the planet Mars: a thin, slight man of thirty-three with dark hair, a high forehead, a moustache and a pointed dark beard, in a black doublet with a small white collar, bent very close over a large sheet of paper pinned to a sloping writing desk that tilts toward us, for his eyes were weak, drawing with a quill pen, his face only a hand's breadth above the sheet. On the sheet is the figure from his own book: a large circle, and inside it an oval only a little narrower than the circle and touching it at both ends, a small Sun drawn on the long axis well to one side of the center, and straight lines running from the Sun out to the oval. His free hand presses flat a stack of pages covered edge to edge with fine columns of marks too small to read, and more discarded pages cover the floor. The candles have burned down and gray dawn shows at a small leaded window; a brass quadrant hangs on the wall, a quarter of a circle with a scale along its curved edge and a plumb line hanging from its corner. Seen from across the table, low, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his head. Prague in 1605: he has no telescope yet, no globe of the planets, no wig, no spectacles. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with his head, his pen hand, the whole drawn figure on the sloping sheet, the quadrant on the wall and the window all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the front of the desk, the stack of pages, a burned-down candle and the littered floor. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. cards.fact: As the British ambassador's wife in Constantinople, she saw children guarded against smallpox by a scratch of matter from a mild case. She had her son treated in 1718, and pressed London's doubting doctors to try it.
cards.art: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu in Constantinople in March 1718, having her son protected against smallpox: an Englishwoman of twenty-eight with dark hair, her face lightly pitted by the smallpox she survived and her eyelashes gone, wearing the Turkish dress she adopted and was painted in, a long fitted coat of patterned silk over a fine white shift and loose trousers, and a small jewelled cap worn on one side of her head. She sits on a low cushioned sofa that runs along the wall, holding her small son, nearly five years old, firmly and high on her lap so that his head is just under her chin, his sleeve rolled to the shoulder, her eyes fixed on the work. An old Greek woman in a dark headscarf bends over the boy's bare upper arm with a thick sewing needle in her right hand and half a walnut shell held in her left. Behind them stands the embassy surgeon, a Scot of fifty in a dark coat and a plain short wig, watching closely. A window shows domes and cypress trees. Seen from close, Lady Mary's face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above her head. Ottoman Constantinople in 1718: no harem fantasy, no veils over faces, no syringe, no doctor's instruments of a later age, no plates or dishes on the wall. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with the heads of all four people, the boy's bare arm, the needle and the walnut shell all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only her skirts, the sofa and the carpet. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. links.newton>duchatelet: Émilie du Châtelet put Newton's Principia into French, and hers is still the standard French translation.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: She translated Newton's great book from Latin into French and added pages of her own to explain its mathematics. She finished the work in 1749, only days before she died.
cards.art: Émilie du Châtelet in the summer of 1749, working through the night to finish her translation of Newton: a tall woman of forty-two with a long, lively face, a strong nose and dark hair loosely dressed and unpowdered, in a loose silk morning gown with the sleeves pushed back, seated at a table crowded with candles. A thick Latin book stands open on a reading stand before her; she writes fast on a sheet with a quill in her right hand while her left hand holds a pair of brass dividers stepped across a drawn diagram of an oval orbit. Finished pages lie in a deep pile at her elbow, tied in bundles with ribbon, and a cold cup of coffee stands forgotten. A tall window is black with night. Seen from the side, so that she is in profile from the waist up against the black window, her head right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above it. France in the 1740s: no towering wig, no court hoops, no chalkboard, no readable writing. cards.fact: In 1796 he put cowpox from a milkmaid's sore into a boy, who then could not catch smallpox. Vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow, and in 1980 smallpox became the first disease wiped out.
cards.art: Edward Jenner in May 1796 in a Gloucestershire dairy, studying the hand of the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes: a country doctor about to turn forty-seven with a round, kindly face and his own brown hair tied back at the neck, dressed as his friends remembered him, in a blue coat with yellow metal buttons, a pale waistcoat, buckskin breeches and polished riding boots, holding the young woman's right hand in both of his and turning it to the light from the door to look at the three raised round blisters of cowpox on her hand and wrist. She stands in a cap and apron, patient and a little amused. Behind them a dark brown Gloucester cow with a white stripe along her back and a white tail turns her horned head in the stall, and a three-legged milking stool and a wooden pail stand in the straw. On a ledge of the stall at the height of his elbow lies his open leather pocket case holding exactly two small folding lancets, each a short leaf-shaped steel blade pinned between two tortoiseshell covers. Seen from inside the shed, from the waist up, Jenner's face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his head. cards.fact: For five years he explored South and Central America, measuring everything from the heat of the sea to the blue of the sky. In 1802 he climbed higher on the volcano Chimborazo than anyone on record had ever climbed.
cards.art: Alexander von Humboldt at one o'clock on 23 June 1802, high on the volcano Chimborazo in the Andes, at the ravine that stopped him: a slim man of thirty-two with windblown light brown hair, in the ordinary clothes of a gentleman of 1802, a dark tailcoat, waistcoat, neckcloth, long trousers and short boots soaked through, his hands scraped by the rock, his eyes bloodshot and a thread of blood at his lips from the thin air. He crouches low on a narrow ridge of crumbling black rock patched with old snow, at the lip of a deep ravine, and reads with fierce attention a mountain barometer set upright before him: a glass tube of mercury in a slim wooden case not quite as long as a man's leg, with a small brass scale near its top. His friend Aimé Bonpland, a stocky man of twenty-eight with dark hair, steadies the foot of the instrument, and young Carlos Montúfar, a slight dark-haired man of twenty-two in a short cloak, writes the figure in a notebook with numb fingers. Mist boils below them on both sides and for a moment the white dome of the summit hangs close above. Seen from just along the ridge, from the knees up, Humboldt's face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his head. No ropes, ice axes or climbing clothes of later times, no fur, no hats with feathers. cards.fact: She was twelve when she and her brother dug an ichthyosaur out of the sea cliffs near their home, and she went on to find the first complete plesiosaur. She sold fossils for a living, and the learned men who bought them seldom gave her the credit.
cards.art: Mary Anning in 1812, aged twelve, digging the first ichthyosaur skeleton out of the foot of the crumbling cliffs of Black Ven, between Lyme Regis and Charmouth, the year after her brother Joseph found its skull, at dusk with a storm coming in: a thin, determined working girl of twelve, a real child with a narrow wind-reddened face, in a heavy brown wool cloak blowing out behind her, a plain long dress hitched up and muddy, stout boots, and a cloth bonnet tied under her chin. The ichthyosaur lies in the face of a great fallen block of gray shale that stands upright like a wall at the left of the picture, taller than she is, and she kneels on a ledge against it, with a small iron hammer raised in her right hand and a short chisel in her left set against the bone. The skeleton is flat in the upright rock face like a pressed leaf, level across the block at the height of her face and shoulders: right beside her chisel the skull, a long narrow snout lined with small pointed teeth reaching away to the left, and a huge round eye socket ringed with a circle of small bony plates and as wide as her head; then, going left from the skull, a backbone of many disc-shaped bones, curved ribs, and one front flipper made of many small rounded bones packed like cobbles. The skull with its snout is nearly as long as she is tall. Her brother Joseph, a lanky boy of fifteen, taller than she is, in a coarse jacket and a cap, stands just behind her at the right holding up a lit horn lantern by its handle at the height of his shoulder, its orange light falling on the bones. Behind them, at the right, white surf breaks on the rocks under a wild cobalt storm sky, and the dark cliff rises behind the block. Seen from low on the beach, Mary from the knees up, her face three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down; Joseph's head is a little higher than hers and well below the top edge; Mary, Joseph, the lantern and the skull, ribs and flipper are all in the upper half of the picture. England in 1812: no dinosaur shown alive, no magnifying lens, no trousers on her, no dog, no second skull, no hind legs on the skeleton. cards.fact: A schoolboy who taught himself Coptic, the last form of Egyptian, he worked out in 1822 how to read hieroglyphs, which nobody had read for some 1,400 years.
cards.art: Jean-François Champollion at noon on 14 September 1822, in his attic study in Paris, at the instant he understands the hieroglyphs: a dark, curly-haired man of thirty-one with a full face and a swarthy skin, in shirtsleeves and an open waistcoat, half risen from his chair so suddenly that it is tipping over behind him. In his right hand he grips a sheet of paper copied from a temple wall, on which a single upright oval ring is drawn in ink with four picture signs inside it: a round sun disc at the top, under it a sign like three strokes tied together at the top, and under that two tall hooked signs side by side. His left hand is flat on the table among thick dictionaries and sheets of the same kind of picture signs set out in rows. His mouth is open in a shout. Sunlight from a small window falls across the papers. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his head. cards.art: Florence Nightingale in the winter of 1854 on her night round of the army hospital at Scutari: a slender woman of thirty-four with a calm, firm face and brown hair parted in the middle under a small white cap, in a plain black wool dress with a white collar and a short dark cape. In her left hand she carries the lamp she really used, a Turkish lantern: a short upright cylinder of pleated waxed cloth, folded like a small concertina, between a round metal base and a round metal top with a wire handle, a candle glowing inside it, held at the level of her chest so that its glow lights her face from below. She has stopped beside a low bed in a long stone corridor and stoops a little, drawing the blanket up over the shoulder of a sleeping soldier with her right hand. Two more beds can be made out beyond his, each with a different man in it, one bearded and awake, watching her, one with a bandaged head, and the rest of the corridor is lost in the dark: no rows of beds or of repeated figures. Seen from the foot of the bed, from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above her cap. links.jenner>pasteur: Pasteur gave his own method the name vaccination, in honor of Jenner's work with cowpox.

cards.tx: Steadfast: +2 Might when defending.
cards.fact: He showed that germs spoil food and cause disease, and that gentle heat kills them, which is why milk is pasteurised. In 1885 his new vaccine saved a nine-year-old boy who had been badly bitten by a rabid dog.
cards.art: Louis Pasteur on 6 July 1885 in his laboratory in Paris, on the evening the boy Joseph Meister is first treated: a grey-bearded man of sixty-two with a grave, anxious face and short gray hair, in a dark coat and a small round black skullcap, his left arm held a little stiffly at his side. He stands with his right hand resting on the shoulder of a nine-year-old boy in a short jacket who sits on a high stool, his head level with Pasteur's chest, one hand and one leg bandaged where the dog bit him, and he watches without blinking as, in the background, Doctor Grancher, a dark-bearded man of forty-two in a dark frock coat, draws liquid from a small glass into a little syringe with a glass barrel and metal ends. On a shelf beside them, at the height of Pasteur's shoulder, stand exactly two glass flasks of clear broth, each a round bulb whose long thin neck is drawn out sideways, dips down and rises again in a swan's-neck curve, open at the tip; and a tall glass jar stopped with cotton wool in which a short strip of dried tissue hangs from a thread above a few white lumps on the jar's bottom. Low daylight from a high window. Seen from the bench, from the waist up, Pasteur's face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his cap, the boy lower and to the left. France in the 1880s: no white coats, no microscope held to the eye, no electric light, no plates or dishes on the wall. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with Pasteur's head, the boy's head and bandaged hand, the doctor with the syringe, the two swan-necked flasks and the jar all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the boy's bandaged leg, the stool and the floor. cards.art: Nellie Bly in January 1890 on the last leg of her race around the world, crossing America by special train: a small, quick young woman of twenty-five with a fringe of dark hair, in the one dress she took, plain dark blue wool, under a long checked traveling coat, a small peaked cloth cap on her head. cards.tx: When you play this Figure, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: He designed the alternating-current motors and power system that still carry electricity to homes around the world. On the lecture stage he made glass lamps glow with no wire leading to them.
cards.art: Nikola Tesla in 1892, lecturing in a darkened hall: a very tall, very thin man of thirty-five with black hair parted in the middle and a neat dark moustache, in a black tailcoat and white tie, standing alone on the stage with his elbows bent and his two hands raised to the height of his shoulders. In each bare hand he holds one straight glass tube as long as his forearm, upright like a candle, the two tubes rising on either side of his head and no higher than the top of his hair, both well inside the picture and far from its side edges and top corners, with no wire leading to it, and both tubes are glowing with a cold white light that is the only light in the picture, throwing his face and shirt front into sharp relief. Behind him, half seen in the gloom, stand two tall flat metal sheets on insulated posts, and a table that carries his coil: a wooden box the size of a small trunk with two short dark pillars on its lid, each topped by a brass ball, and beside it two glass jars coated with tinfoil to the shoulder. Three listeners in the front row are dark shapes at the bottom edge, each different: a bald man, a woman in a hat, a man with a full beard. Seen from the stalls, from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his head. In his lectures of 1891 to 1893 he lit tubes both ways, held in his hands and hung between the sheets; this picture shows them in his hands. No lightning bolts leaping about the room, no tower, no goggles, no light bulbs with filaments. Correct anatomy, two hands, each holding one tube. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only darkness there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. One search summary said his lamps glowed in the field between two plates and were not held in his hands, so the fact now says only that they glowed with no wire, and the picture brief asks for a check. The link to Faraday is physics, not checked. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

cards.fact: He built the largest empire the world had yet seen, and let the peoples he conquered keep their own gods and customs. A clay cylinder found at Babylon records, in his name, that he sent exiled peoples home.
cards.art: Cyrus, king of Persia, entering Babylon on a day in late October of 539 BC, after the city had opened to his army without a fight: a man of about sixty with a full gray beard and gray hair to the nape, bare-headed but for a narrow band of gold around his brow, in the long robe of an Elamite king, as the one carving that stands at his own palace shows it: a straight ankle-length robe with short sleeves, not pleated, its edge finished with a fringe and a band of small rosettes that runs down the right side and around the hem. He walks on foot under the towering Ishtar Gate, whose blue-glazed brick is set with bulls and long-necked dragons in yellow and white brick, one animal above another (each dragon has a scaly body, a snake's head with one horn, a lion's forefeet, an eagle's hind claws and a long tail: not a deer, not a gazelle). He holds his right hand open at shoulder height in greeting, and his short sword stays sheathed at his belt. Four people of the city, each different in age and dress, an old man in a long fringed shawl and a tall rounded cap, a woman, a youth and a child, are laying green branches on the paving in front of his feet; they kneel in the foreground, nearer to us than he is. Behind him a groom leads his horse, which has a fringed saddle cloth, no saddle and no stirrups, and two spearmen follow in soft felt caps, belted tunics and trousers. Everyone is drawn at one scale: Cyrus is a man of ordinary height, not a giant among his men. The groom walks one pace behind his shoulder and is as tall as Cyrus is: the top of the groom's head is level with the top of Cyrus's head, and the two heads are nearly the same size. The two spearmen, three paces behind, are as tall as he is too, their heads at the height of his and only a little smaller for being farther off. The horse is taller than any of the men: its back is level with the groom's shoulder and its ears are above every man's head. Nobody else is shown: no crowd lining the way. Seen from the street in front of him, from the knees up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. The Persia of his own day: no tall crown, no pleated court robe of the later kings, no winged figure, no chariot. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. links.@wall>qinshihuang: Qin Shi Huang had the old border walls of the northern kingdoms joined into one long wall, the first Great Wall.

cards.tx: Guard: enemies here must clash with this Figure first.
cards.fact: At thirty-eight he became the first emperor of a united China, with one script, one coinage and one set of measures. Eight thousand life-size clay soldiers, each with its own face, guard his tomb.
cards.art: Qin Shi Huang in 221 BC, aged thirty-eight, in the year he made himself First Emperor of China, at the bronze foundry of his capital Xianyang, where the weapons taken from the six kingdoms he has conquered are being melted down, as the historian Sima Qian records: a heavy-set man with a high-bridged nose, a thin dark moustache and chin beard and a hard, searching stare, in long black silk robes with wide sleeves, black being the color of his dynasty, a tall black cap tied under the chin with cords, and a long straight bronze sword in its scabbard at his belt. He stands beside a heap of surrendered bronze weapons that is taller than he is: straight two-edged swords, spearheads, and dagger-axes, each a broad pointed blade set crosswise at the top of a long wooden shaft. He has lifted one sword from the heap and holds it level across his two open palms, looking along the blade before it goes to the fire. Behind him two foundrymen stripped to the waist, one old and lean and one young and broad, carry a glowing clay crucible slung from a pole between them towards a brick furnace that throws sparks and black smoke. Seen from low beside the heap, the emperor from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Qin China: no yellow dragon robe, no crown hung with strings of beads, no curved sabers, no plate armor, no paper, no stirrups. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dark smoke there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.caesar>augustus: Julius Caesar adopted Augustus, his great-nephew, in his will and left him his name.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, enemy Figures here miss their next turn.
cards.fact: Julius Caesar's adopted heir, he ended a century of civil wars and ruled Rome for more than forty years as its first emperor. The month of August is named after him.
cards.art: The shrine of Janus in the Roman Forum in 29 BC, the first time in two hundred years it was shut, seen from inside: we stand in the small dark bronze room of the shrine, low down beside the bronze statue of the god Janus, and look out through its doorway as Augustus, aged thirty-four, pushes its doors shut from outside, because Rome is at peace. The statue stands in deep shadow at the lower left: a bronze figure about one and a third times as tall as a man, and its one head has two bearded faces, one looking left and one looking right, joined back to back, with no back of the head; seen from the side we see both profiles at once, one nose pointing left and one pointing right, like the head on a Roman coin of Janus. The doorway is tall and narrow, with a pair of bronze doors that open inward: the left leaf is already shut, and the right leaf is swinging in toward us, leaving a narrowing upright gap of hard golden daylight between them. In the gap, framed by the light, stands Augustus, facing us, both palms flat against the edge of the right leaf, pushing it: a slight man, not tall, with a calm, clean-shaven face, a broad brow, a narrow chin, a small mouth, ears that stand out a little and short hair falling over his forehead in small curved locks, parted in a little fork over his left eye, as his statue from Prima Porta shows him, in a white woollen toga with a fold of it drawn up over the back of his head, as a Roman covers his head for a rite. Behind him, small in the sunlight, the columns and tiled roofs of the Forum and one old senator in a toga watching. The bronze walls inside are dark green and gold, lit only by the light through the gap. His face is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, in the gap; the gap of light, his face and his hands are in the upper half of the picture, and so are the statue's two faces. Rome in the first years of the emperors: no laurel wreath, no armor, no purple robe, no beard on Augustus, no torches, no lamps. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The naming of August was not returned.

links.press>franklin: Franklin was a printer by trade, and made his name with Poor Richard's Almanack.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: A printer who taught himself science, he flew a kite in a thunderstorm to show that lightning is electricity. As a diplomat in Paris he won France to the American side in 1778.
cards.art: Benjamin Franklin with long hair and round spectacles, coat flapping in a storm, flying a kite on a string with a key tied to it as lightning forks behind. He is seen from a low angle, from the chest up, his face lifted to the sky: balding on top, long gray hair to his collar, a broad plain face with small round wire spectacles, a dark blue coat with big buttons and a white neckcloth. His head is three fifths of the way across the picture and two fifths of the way down. His one raised arm reaches up to the left, and its fist, at the left of the picture a third of the way down, grips the kite string; his other arm is down out of the picture. Everything that matters is in the upper half of the picture: the kite, the string, the raised fist, the key and his face. Get the sizes right. The kite is high up and far away, so it is small: a plain diamond of silk on two crossed sticks with a short tail of knotted rag, no bigger in the picture than his raised fist, flying whole in the dark sky above and to the left of his fist, a fifth of the way down from the top edge and well inside the picture, not touching any edge. There is exactly one string: a single thin unbroken line from the kite straight down to his raised fist, and from the fist on down past his coat and out of the bottom of the picture. No other line or string anywhere. The key is an ordinary small iron door key, only as long as his forefinger and much smaller than his hand and his face: it is not near the kite, it hangs on the string just below his raised fist, a hand's breadth under it, tied by a short ribbon, dangling against the dark sky at the height of his forehead, with a small spark at its tip. One fork of lightning in the clouds at the right. No second kite, no second key, no giant key, no second string. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Written from the standard record (the kite experiment of 1752, the printing trade and Poor Richard's Almanack, the treaty of alliance with France in 1778). Not searched in this session.

links.cyrus>darius: Darius married Atossa, a daughter of Cyrus, and had it carved on the cliff at Behistun that he came of the same royal house.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, you gain 1 Spark.
cards.fact: His empire reached from Egypt to the Indus, tied together by a royal road about 1,700 miles long. Herodotus wrote that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor darkness stopped its mounted messengers.
cards.art: Darius, king of Persia, about 500 BC, crossing the half-built terrace of his new palace at Persepolis as a royal messenger reaches him, drawn after the carved reliefs of his own palace: a tall man of about fifty with a long squared beard curled in rows and hair bunched in curls at the nape, in a long pleated robe with wide hanging sleeves, belted at the waist, a tall straight-sided crown with a notched upper rim, and a long thin staff in his right hand. He has stopped in mid stride, seen in three-quarter profile, and looks down at the courier in front of him, a young man gray with dust in a knee-length belted tunic, trousers and a soft felt cap with flaps tied under the chin, who bows from the waist with one hand held before his mouth, as Persians greeted their king, and with the other hand holds out a small rolled letter of leather, tied and sealed with a lump of clay. Behind the king a beardless attendant holds a round fringed parasol on a long pole above the king's head. Behind the courier a groom holds a lathered horse, which is larger than the men and has a saddle cloth, no saddle and no stirrups. Further back two stonemasons, each different, work with mallet and chisel on a half-carved column capital shaped like the foreparts of two kneeling bulls set back to back. Bare brown mountain behind, hard morning light. Seen from low on the terrace, the king from the knees up, his head right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, the parasol above it. The Persia of his own day: no winged figure in the sky, no chariot, no Greek armor, no rows of guards. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only clear sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.art: Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1193, aged about seventy, gathering the ransom for her son King Richard, which was kept in chests in St Paul's in London under her seal: a tall, straight-backed old woman with a strong-boned face, her hair and throat covered by a white linen veil and a band of linen under the chin, under a narrow gold crown, in a long dark red gown with close sleeves, belted at the waist, and a mantle held by a cord across the breast, as her tomb effigy shows her. She stands at a table in a stone crypt and presses her seal, a pointed oval of bronze as long as her palm, into a lump of soft wax on the cords that tie down the lid of an iron-bound chest, bearing down hard with the heel of her hand. Beside her one clerk weighs silver cups, a chalice and small silver pennies on a great pair of hanging scales, and a second, older clerk cuts notches in a wooden tally stick with a knife. More sealed chests are stacked behind her. Candlelight. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. England in the 1190s: no tall pointed hat with a veil, no ruff, no paper ledgers, no gold coins. cards.fact: A grandson of Genghis Khan, he became emperor of all China and built his capital where Beijing stands today. Marco Polo was amazed to find that people in his empire paid for goods with money made of paper.
cards.art: Kublai Khan about 1275 in his palace at Khanbaliq, drawn after the portrait made by his own court painter: a big, heavy man of sixty with a broad, round, ruddy face, narrow eyes, a thin moustache that curves down past the corners of his mouth and a pointed beard on the chin, his hair looped in a braid behind each ear, wearing a white cap whose dark brim is turned up at the front and falls to a flap at the neck, and a wide plain white Mongol robe that crosses over the chest and fastens at his right side. He sits cross-legged on a low broad couch spread with a tiger skin and holds up between two fingers a sheet of dark gray paper money, a tall oblong about as long as his forearm, printed in black and stamped with two red seals, weighing it against a short string of round bronze coins with square holes that hangs from his other hand. A Chinese official in a black cap and long robe stands bowing beside the couch with a lacquer tray of more notes, and behind stand a Persian minister with a full beard and a white turban and a Mongol guard with a bow case at his belt. Everyone is drawn at one scale. Kublai is a big, heavy man, but a man and not a giant: the official bowing beside the couch is as near to us as Kublai is, so his head is the same size as Kublai's head and his hands are the same size as Kublai's hands. The minister and the guard stand two paces farther from us, and their heads are a little smaller than Kublai's only because they are farther away. Red lacquered pillars and a felt hanging. Seen from in front, from the waist up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Yuan dynasty China: no dragon robe of the Ming, no pigtail, no fur hat with horns. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Checked at the merge: Marco Polo's chapter on the Great Khan's paper money, in Yule's edition (archive.org, bookofsermarcopo00polo).

cards.fact: Four years shut in an Algerian castle gave him his book on why kingdoms rise, grow rich and fall, answered from how people live together. In 1401 he was lowered by rope from besieged Damascus to bargain with Timur.
cards.art: Ibn Khaldun in January 1401, aged sixty-eight, being lowered by rope down the outside of the city wall of Damascus to meet the conqueror Timur, as he tells it himself. The wall is one single flat, sheer wall of large squared stone blocks, seen side-on: it fills the left third of the picture from top to bottom like a cliff, its face perfectly vertical and unbroken, with a row of square battlements along its top edge and flat open ground at its foot. There is no second wall, no ledge, no tower, no corner and no lower wall anywhere. Ibn Khaldun hangs against the wall face about half way down: an old North African scholar with a white beard and a calm, shrewd face, in the hooded woollen cloak of the Maghreb with its hood thrown back, over a long robe, a large white turban on his head, seated in a sling made of one thick rope that passes under his thighs and up in front of him to the battlements; both his hands grip that rope above his head and his slippered feet are braced flat against the stone. He looks down past his shoulder. At the top of the wall two men, each different, lean out between the battlements holding the same rope, which runs straight and taut from their hands down to his sling. To the right of the wall the picture opens on a wide, empty plain in the cold first light of morning: far away, four or five round felt tents and a line of tethered horses, and one single thin thread of smoke rising straight up from one fire. On the ground at the foot of the wall, small because they are far below him, three riders wait on horseback, each different, in fur-edged caps and long belted coats, looking up. Seen from level with him in mid-air; his face is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, with pale sky to the right of him. Syria in 1401: no cannon, no Ottoman dress, no sword in his hand, no burning buildings, no rows of smoke plumes. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The four years at the castle and the meeting with Timur in 1401 were confirmed. Being lowered over the wall by ropes was found in one retelling only; it is from his own autobiography (W. J. Fischel, Ibn Khaldun and Tamerlane, 1952), not checked. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

cards.fact: As a boy he watched his father killed, and lived for years on the run before winning back his city of Texcoco. As king he was a poet, a lawgiver and an engineer, and built a long dike that kept salt water out of the Aztec capital's lake.
cards.art: Nezahualcoyotl, king of Texcoco, about 1450, on the great dike he designed across the lake of Mexico, in the dress that the painted book of his own family shows on the kings of Texcoco: a lean man of forty-eight with a thoughtful face, his black hair cut straight across at the jaw, with one lock at the crown bound in red ribbon from which two green feather tassels hang at the back of his head; a long cotton cloak of deep blue patterned all over with small pale squares and edged with a patterned border, tied at the throat and hanging open to the calves over his bare chest; a loincloth of the same blue with broad embroidered ends hanging in front; a collar of green stone beads, gold bands on his upper arms and below his knees, and sandals with heel guards. He stands on the half-built dike, holding a coil of knotted measuring cord in both hands with one end paid out along the ground, and looks along the dike's line to where it runs out across the water. The dike is two rows of upright timber stakes with stone and earth packed between them. It is a great work and he is an ordinary man standing on it, not a giant: the dike is four times as wide as he is tall, and each stake near him is a whole tree trunk as thick as his thigh, standing as high as his knee. Out on the lake, at least thirty paces behind him and off to the left, two dugout canoes heaped with rock are poled toward the dike by two men, each different, in plain white loincloths; because they are far behind him they are small in the picture, and each canoe is four times as long as its man is tall. Nobody and no boat is close beside him or near his feet. On the calm lake behind lie low garden plots edged with willows and the white temples of a far island city. Two snow-capped volcanoes of different shapes on the skyline. Seen from on the dike a few paces in front of him, from the height of his chest, from the knees up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Central Mexico before the Spanish: no feather war bonnet, no tall crown of feathers, no skulls, no horses, no metal tools. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played. Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: King of Korea, he gave his people an alphabet of twenty-eight letters, so simple that a scholar of his court wrote that a clever person could learn it in a morning. Koreans write with it to this day, and keep a holiday in its honor.
cards.art: Sejong, king of Korea, about 1445, perfecting his new alphabet at night with the young scholars of his Hall of Worthies: a broad, heavy man of forty-eight with a full face and a short black beard, in the red royal robe with a round gold dragon badge on the chest and one on each shoulder, and a black cap with a rounded crown in two steps and two small wings standing up at the back. He sits cross-legged on a floor cushion at a low table and holds two fingers to his own throat while he sounds a syllable aloud, his eyes narrowed with poor sight, and with his other hand he points to a sheet on which a young scholar has brushed three large plain shapes in black ink: a circle, a short level bar, and an angle made of a level stroke that turns straight down at its right end, like the top right corner of a square. Two more scholars lean in, one mouthing the same sound. The three scholars are different in age and face, in plain round-collared robes of blue or green with wide sleeves and black gauze caps with a low front, a higher back and a narrow flap at each side. Everyone is drawn at one scale. The king is a broad, heavy man, but no larger than his scholars: he sits on the far side of the low table, the farthest of the four from us, so his head is no bigger in the picture than the head of any scholar, and his hands are the same size as theirs. The scholars sit at the two ends and the near side of the table, nearer to us than he is, so they are drawn the same size as he is or a little larger, never smaller. A candle on a tall stand and a folding screen painted with mountains. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Early Joseon Korea: no wide-brimmed horsehair hats, no embroidered squares on the scholars' chests, no Chinese emperor's bead crown, no Japanese dress. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The scholar's remark that the letters can be learned in a morning (Jeong In-ji's postface to the Hunminjeongeum) was not returned.

links.@machu>pachacuti: Machu Picchu is thought to have been built as a royal estate for Pachacuti, about 1450.
links.@qhapaq>pachacuti: The great Inca road grew with the conquests that Pachacuti began, and it tied his new empire to Cusco.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, look at the top three Domains of your stack. You may lay one of them at your Gate or your Outpost, in place of the Domain there. The others go under your stack.
cards.fact: He made the kingdom of Cusco into the Inca Empire, and rebuilt its capital in stone cut so finely that no blade fits between the blocks. His name means “he who remakes the world”.
cards.art: Pachacuti, ruler of the Inca, about 1450, overseeing the rebuilding of Cusco in stone: a stern, broad-chested man of middle age with his hair cut short, wearing a knee-length sleeveless tunic woven all over in a grid of small bright squares, a plain cloak knotted at the shoulder, a braided band wound around his head from which a red wool fringe four fingers deep hangs across his forehead from temple to temple, two small black-and-white feathers standing up from the band above it, large round gold discs set in his ear lobes, and sandals. He stands with one hand on a huge many-sided block of gray stone, one and a half times as tall as a man, that four men in plain tunics, each different in age and build, are easing into place with ropes, an earth ramp and long wooden levers, and he bends a little to look along the joint where the block meets its neighbors, so close that no light shows. Everyone is drawn at one scale: Pachacuti is a man of ordinary height, the same size as his workmen, not a giant. A workman hauling on a rope right beside him, at the same distance from us, has a head the same size as his and stands as tall as he does. The workmen in the foreground, nearer to us than he is, are drawn larger than he is, never smaller. A finished wall of the same fitted many-sided blocks runs away behind, with thatched roofs above it and steep mountains beyond. Seen from the foot of the wall, from the knees up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. The Andes before the Spanish: no wheels, no iron tools, no feather war bonnet, no horses. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The estate at Machu Picchu and his reign were confirmed; the stonework of Cusco and the meaning of his name were not returned.

cards.fact: He ruled the Ottoman Empire for forty-six years, when it reached from Hungary to the Persian Gulf. Europeans called him the Magnificent, but his own people called him the Lawgiver, for the order he brought to the empire's laws.
cards.art: Suleiman, sultan of the Ottomans, about 1540, aged forty-five, having his cipher set at the head of a new law: a tall, thin, pale man with a long neck, a hooked nose and a short dark beard, as the envoys of Venice described him, wearing a very large white turban, egg-shaped and taller than his face, as his portraits show, with clear space above it in the picture, and a long robe of patterned silk over an inner robe, its outer sleeves hanging empty to the floor behind his arms. He sits on a low cushioned seat in a tiled room of the palace, leaning forward with his hands on his knees, and watches closely as a court scribe kneeling at a low desk draws with a reed pen, in gold and blue ink at the head of a long scroll, the sultan's great looping cipher: three tall upright strokes, and two wide loops that swing out to the left. A grey-bearded judge in a wide white turban stands by holding the rolled text of the law, and a casement shows cypress trees and the sea. Seen from beside the scribe, so that the sultan is seen from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. The Ottoman court of the sixteenth century: no fez, no curved sword in his hand, no harem scene. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only blue and white tiles there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. links.douglass>lincoln: Frederick Douglass went to the White House in 1863 to press Lincoln for equal pay for Black soldiers, and Lincoln heard him out.

cards.tx: +2 Might while you have more Figures here than the other player.
cards.fact: He held the United States together through its civil war and ended slavery there. His speech at Gettysburg took about two minutes.
cards.art: Abraham Lincoln at Gettysburg in November 1863, aged fifty-four: very tall and gaunt, a deeply lined, sad, kind face with a chin beard and no moustache, dark untidy hair, bareheaded, wearing a long black frock coat, a black waistcoat, a white shirt and a black bow tie. He stands on a plain wooden speakers' platform seen from a little below and in three-quarter profile, two small sheets of paper in one hand and the other hand open at his side, speaking quietly. His head is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Close behind him on the same planks, only one pace back, three men sit on plain wooden chairs, each one a different, particular man: a stout clean-shaven statesman of sixty with white hair, a thin man with a long gray beard, and an army officer in a dark blue coat with brass buttons. Get the scale right: Lincoln is a tall thin man, not a giant, and the seated men are full-sized men right beside him, drawn to exactly the same scale as he is. Each seated man's head is as big as Lincoln's own head. Because they sit and he stands, the top of each seated man's head comes level with Lincoln's chest, and their knees are level with his knees. Beside him stands one empty chair, its seat at the height of his knee and its back at the height of his waist, with his tall black stovepipe hat resting on the seat; the hat is the right size to fit his head. Below the platform, nearest to us, only four listeners are seen from behind, each different: a woman in a bonnet, a soldier in a cap, an old farmer, a boy. The rest of the crowd is not drawn as people at all, only a dark mass far off on a bare autumn hillside under a pale sky, with one flag hanging limp on a pole so that its stars cannot be counted. Dignified and plain: no wide gesture, no monument, no eagle, no writing on the papers. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Written from the standard record (the Gettysburg Address of November 1863, about two minutes; Douglass's White House meeting of 10 August 1863 about equal pay for Black soldiers, from his own Life and Times). Not searched in this session.

links.duchatelet>voltaire: Voltaire lived and worked for fifteen years at the country house of Émilie du Châtelet, whose mathematics helped him to write his book on Newton.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, you gain 1 Spark, or 2 if the other player holds this Place.
cards.fact: His plays, stories and letters mocked cruelty and unjust laws, and twice put him in the Bastille. As a young man he got rich by spotting a flaw in a state lottery and buying up the tickets.
cards.art: Voltaire about 1765, aged seventy, at home at Ferney near Geneva, dictating a letter, drawn after the sketches his friend Jean Huber made of him at home: a very thin old man with a long sharp nose, sunken cheeks, bright mocking eyes and a wide toothless grin, in a long fur-edged dressing gown that hangs open over a waistcoat and breeches, slippers, and a soft cloth cap pulled down over a short gray wig. He is on his feet in the middle of his study, bent a little forward in mid stride with his dressing gown swinging, shaking a sheet of paper that he holds out at arm's length at the height of his chest and laughing at what he has just said; at a small desk beside him his young secretary, a plain man of twenty-five in a brown coat, sits on a plain wooden chair and writes it down fast with a goose quill, not looking up. The desk top is at the height of Voltaire's hip, and the seated secretary's head is level with Voltaire's chest and the same size as Voltaire's head. Books lie open face down on the floor and on the desk. The secretary's chair is the only chair in the room: no armchair, stool or other furniture stands in the foreground, and nothing in the room is drawn at a smaller scale than the two men. A tall window behind, twice Voltaire's height, shows a garden and, far off, snow mountains. Seen from low in front of him, from the knees up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. France in the 1760s: no full court dress, no tall powdered wig, no guillotine or revolution. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

links.voltaire>catherine: Catherine exchanged letters with Voltaire for fifteen years, and bought his library after he died.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, the weakest enemy Figure here is pushed one step toward its Gate.
cards.fact: Arriving from Germany at fourteen, she learned Russian, took the throne from her husband in 1762 and ruled for thirty-four years. She wrote to France's great thinkers and bought their libraries.
cards.art: Catherine on the evening of 28 June 1762, aged thirty-three, the day she seized the throne of Russia, riding out of St Petersburg at the head of her Guards on the road to Peterhof, as Vigilius Eriksen later painted her: she rides astride her gray stallion Brilliant, in the borrowed uniform of an officer of the Preobrazhensky Guards, a dark green coat with red collar and cuffs and gold braid, a black three-cornered hat trimmed with a sprig of green oak leaves, the broad pale blue sash of the Order of St Andrew across her chest, her own long brown hair unpowdered and loose down her back, a drawn straight sword held upright in her right hand and the reins in her left. A woman of middle height with a high forehead, a long chin, a firm small mouth and bright blue eyes, her face flushed and exultant. It is a white night of the northern summer, near midnight but still light: a pale glowing sky of gold and teal. The horse is a big animal: its back is at the height of a standing man's shoulder, its head is as long as a man's forearm and hand together, and she sits high above the men on foot. She is much smaller than her horse: her body from saddle to hat is about as tall as the horse's front leg is long. The horse walks toward us at an angle, with exactly four legs, a long gray mane and tail; she rides with her feet in the stirrups. Two guardsmen on foot walk at the horse's shoulder, each different: a grizzled old sergeant with a musket on his shoulder looking up at her, and a young soldier waving his three-cornered hat in the air; their heads come up only to the horse's neck. Far off on the flat skyline, the thin gilded spire of the Admiralty. Seen from low on the road ahead of her, her face three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, the sword's point well below the top edge; she, the sword and the horse's head and neck are in the upper half of the picture, the horse's legs and the road in the lower half. Russia in 1762: no crown, no ermine, no powdered wig, no side-saddle. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Her arrival at 14, the coup of 28 June 1762, the 34 years and the purchase of Diderot's library were confirmed, and that she corresponded with Voltaire. The fifteen years of letters and the purchase of Voltaire's own library were not returned. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.
