cards.fact: Her book of 1792 argued that women seem less able than men only because they are given less schooling, and that girls and boys should be taught together. She wrote it in about six weeks.
cards.art: Mary Wollstonecraft in 1791 at one of her publisher's dinners in London, in the middle of an argument: a woman of thirty-two with auburn hair hanging loose about her shoulders and unpowdered, a direct gaze and a plain dark dress of coarse cloth with a white muslin kerchief crossed at the neck. She has pushed back her chair and leans forward with one hand flat on the tablecloth and the other raised, a forefinger marking her point, speaking straight across the table to three gentlemen in dark coats, each different in age and build, one of whom has his mouth open to interrupt and another of whom has put down his knife to listen. A plain meal of boiled fish and vegetables, wine glasses, candles. A framed print hangs on the wall. Seen from the men's side of the table, so that she faces us from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. London in the 1790s: no powdered wig, no wide court skirts, no bonnet. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.tx: Can't be moved. +1 Might for each round this Figure stays, up to +2.
cards.fact: Queen at eighteen, she reigned sixty-three years while steam and telegraph tied a quarter of the world into her empire. Her nine children married so widely that she was called the grandmother of Europe.
cards.art: Queen Victoria on 1 May 1851, aged thirty-one, opening the Great Exhibition in the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, standing on the raised dais under the soaring glass vault of the transept, moved almost to tears by the cheering and the music: a very small woman, not quite five feet tall, with a round face, rather prominent pale blue eyes, a small mouth and a short chin, her light brown hair parted in the middle and drawn smoothly down over her ears into a knot at the back, as her portraits of 1851 show her, in a gown of pink silk woven with silver, the broad dark blue ribbon of the Garter across her, and a small diamond tiara at the back of her head. She lifts her chin and looks up and out over the hall, her eyes bright. She is very much shorter than her husband: the top of her tiara is level with Prince Albert's chin. Prince Albert, tall and slim, with dark side whiskers and a moustache, in a dark field marshal's uniform, stands half a step behind her at the right, looking down at her. Her eldest son Bertie, a boy of nine in Highland dress with a short dark jacket and a kilt, holds her left hand at the left; the top of his head comes only to her chest. Behind them stands Osler's crystal fountain, a tall tiered fountain of clear, colourless cut glass, sparkling where the sun catches it and not pink, about four times a man's height and rising high above them, water falling from its tiers, and high above curves the great arched roof of the transept, slender iron ribs and glass panes all lined up in one perspective, over the green crown of a full-grown elm tree that stands inside the building. Sunlight pours down through the glass in long slanting shafts that fall across the queen. The crowds are out of the picture: only these three people. Seen from very low on the floor close in front of the dais, looking up, the queen from the knees up, her face three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down; the queen, the boy, the prince and the fountain are in the upper half of the picture. England in 1851: no crown, no widow's black, no old queen, no throne. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The morning of her accession was confirmed from her own journal; the 63 years and nine children were not returned.

links.@seneca>stanton: Elizabeth Cady Stanton lived in Seneca Falls, helped call the convention of 1848 and wrote most of its declaration.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: At a meeting she helped call in 1848, she declared that all men and women are created equal, and asked for the vote. She fought for it all her life, and American women won it eighteen years after she died.
cards.art: Elizabeth Cady Stanton at thirty-two, on Sunday 16 July 1848, drafting the declaration for the convention at a friend's parlor table: a short, plump, lively young woman of thirty-two, smooth-faced and fresh, with dark curls gathered at each side of her face, in a striped silk day dress with a lace collar, seated at a small round mahogany tea table. She writes with a steel pen, and with her left hand she holds flat a printed copy of the American Declaration of Independence, running her finger under a line as she changes its words. An older Quaker woman of forty-eight in a plain gray dress, a white kerchief and a plain close-fitting white cap without frills sits beside her, reading the last sheet, and a younger woman of twenty-seven leans over the back of the chair. An ink bottle, a tea tray pushed aside, summer light through muslin curtains. Seen from across the little table, from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. New York State in 1848: no sash, no placards, no white hair. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wallpaper there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.tx: +2 Might while outnumbered here.
cards.fact: He lived for two years in a cabin he built by Walden Pond, to find out how little a person needs. He spent a night in jail for refusing a tax to a government that allowed slavery, and his essay about it was read around the world.
cards.art: Henry David Thoreau at twenty-seven, in April of 1845, in the pine woods beside Walden Pond, hewing the timbers for the small house he is about to build there: a short, wiry man with a large nose, deep-set gray-blue eyes and rough brown hair, clean-shaven, in shirtsleeves rolled to the elbow, a waistcoat and patched trousers. He stands close beside a felled pine log that rests on two short cross-pieces and brings a borrowed axe down along its side, both hands on the straight wooden handle, the single narrow steel blade leading with its cutting edge towards the log. One side of the log is already hewn flat and pale, and big chips lie on the ground. Three squared timbers are stacked beside him, and against a tree lean a few gray second-hand boards and one old window sash. His coat hangs on a branch. Between the tall straight pines the pond shows below, with the last gray ice melting at its edge. Seen from low on the ground at the end of the log, from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. New England in 1845: no beard, no cabin yet and no cabin of round logs (it was a framed and boarded house), no rifle. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only pine branches there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: Not returned by the search. Walden, the night in jail in 1846 and the essay are standard, written from memory. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

links.stanton>anthony: Susan B. Anthony met Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1851, and the two worked side by side for women's rights for fifty years.

cards.tx: Steadfast: +2 Might when defending.
cards.fact: In 1872 she walked into a Rochester polling place and voted for president, which the law forbade a woman to do. She was arrested, tried and fined a hundred dollars, and never paid a cent.
cards.art: Susan B. Anthony on 5 November 1872, aged fifty-two, casting her vote for president at the polling place of Rochester's eighth ward, which was set up in a barber's shop on West Street, though the law forbade any woman to vote: a tall, spare woman with a strong jaw, a long straight nose, a firm straight mouth and steady gray-blue eyes, her graying brown hair parted in the middle and drawn smoothly back into a knot, as her photographs of the 1870s show her, in a plain black silk dress with a small white lace collar and a dark red shawl over her shoulders. She stands at the inspectors' high wooden counter, which comes up to her waist, and with her right hand at the height of her chest she pushes her folded paper ballot into the slot in the lid of a wooden ballot box that stands on the counter, her chin up and her gaze level and unafraid. The box is a plain wooden box about as long as her forearm, standing on the counter close in front of us, its slot just below the level of her shoulder. Behind the counter sit two election inspectors, each different: a clean-shaven young man of about twenty-four looking at her with his mouth open, unsure, and a stout older man with gray side whiskers frowning, his arms folded. Behind them, a barber's chair with a high leather back, a shelf of shaving mugs and a window with the striped pole of the barber's shop outside. Morning light from the window. Seen from low beside the counter, close: her face three fifths of the way across the picture and a fifth of the way down, her hand and the ballot at the slot only a third of the way down, the lid of the box a little lower; the top of her head is well below the top edge. Her face, her hand, the ballot and the lid of the box are all in the top two fifths of the picture; everything below that is only the box's front, the counter and her skirt. America in 1872: no banner, no sash, no placard, no glass ballot box, no crowd. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.art: Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god at Ur, about 2270 BC, composing a hymn at night, dressed as the carved stone disc that bears her own name shows her: a woman of about thirty-five with a strong profile, a large straight nose and long dark hair falling down her back from under a round cap with a thick rolled brim, in a long robe of tiered woollen flounces, row above row of hanging tufts, from her shoulders to her ankles. She sits on a low stool on the flat roof of the temple house under a thin crescent moon, a small cushion-shaped tablet of damp clay, about as big as her palm, lying in her left hand, and a cut reed as long as her hand in her right, its squared end pressed into the clay to make a small wedge-shaped dent; her lips are parted as she tries the line aloud. The marks on the clay are tiny wedge dents, texture only. A lamp of oil burns in a large sea shell beside her. Below lie the flat mud-brick roofs of the city and the palm groves along the river. The sky holds only the thin crescent moon and a few small stars: no second moon, no sun, no disc or circle of any kind. She is alone. Seen from the roof beside her, from the waist up, her face in three-quarter view right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Early Mesopotamia: no great stepped tower yet (that was built two centuries later), no winged bulls, no Egyptian dress, no pen, brush, ink or paper. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only night sky there.

links.homer>aeschylus: An ancient writer reports that Aeschylus called his own plays slices from the great banquet of Homer.

cards.tx: Steadfast: +2 Might when defending.
cards.fact: He gave Greek plays a second actor, so that for the first time two people could argue face to face on the stage. He had fought the Persians at Marathon, and his grave spoke of that and never mentioned his plays.
cards.art: Aeschylus in the spring of 472 BC, in the theater under the Acropolis of Athens, rehearsing his play The Persians: a broad, weathered man of fifty-three with a bald crown, a full gray beard and the scarred forearms of an old soldier, in a plain wool cloak that leaves his right arm free. He stands on the beaten earth of the round dancing floor, holding up in both hands a mask of stiffened painted linen, life-size and natural, a bearded man's face with a small open mouth and its own dark hair and beard attached, and is about to settle it over the head of an actor who wears a long patterned robe with sleeves in the Persian fashion. A second actor, younger and thinner, waits facing the first with his own mask in his hand: for the first time there are two actors to argue face to face. A piper sits on the ground tuning a double pipe, two separate slender pipes, one held in each hand, both in his mouth. The audience seats are plain wooden benches on the hillside, empty, and above them is the bare rock of the Acropolis with broken walls. Four people only. Seen from the dancing floor, from the waist up, the playwright's face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Athens in 472 BC: no stone theater, no raised stage, no columns, no great temple on the rock (the Parthenon was not begun until 447 BC), no grinning comedy masks, no tall-browed grimacing masks of later centuries. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only hillside and sky there.

cards.fact: He was the best-loved poet of Tang China and wandered most of his life; about a thousand of his poems of friends, mountains, the Moon and wine survive. Legend says he drowned embracing the Moon's reflection.
cards.art: Li Bai about 744, drinking alone under the Moon, as in the best known of his poems: a man of forty-three with a free, handsome face, a thin beard and bright eyes, in the loose robe of a Tang gentleman with wide sleeves, a black gauze cap pushed back on his head and a straight sword at his belt. He stands among blossoming trees on a terrace on a mountainside, his head tilted back, raising a small wine cup high in his right hand toward the full moon as if inviting it to drink, and his left arm is flung out. The moonlight throws his long shadow across the white stones behind him, so that he, the Moon and the shadow make a party of three. A stoneware wine jar stands on a rock. He is alone: one man, one moon, one shadow. Seen from below the terrace, from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture and the Moon high at the center. Tang China: no boat, no drowning, no Japanese dress. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only blossom branches there.
cards.check: The figure of about a thousand poems was not returned.

links.murasaki>seishonagon: Murasaki Shikibu and Sei Shōnagon served rival empresses, and Murasaki wrote in her diary that Sei was dreadfully conceited.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: A lady at the Japanese court, she filled a notebook with lists of things that delighted or annoyed her, and sharp sketches of the people around her. The Pillow Book has been read for a thousand years.
cards.art: Sei Shonagon about the year 995, on a snowy morning in the empress's rooms in Kyoto, in the best-known scene of her Pillow Book: a quick-witted court lady of about thirty with a pale oval face and loose black hair that falls straight down her back to the floor, in many layers of loose silk robes whose colored edges show at the neck and at the wide sleeves. The empress has asked what the snow looks like on a mountain in an old Chinese poem, and Sei, instead of answering, has gone to the outer wall and is rolling up a hanging blind of fine split bamboo with both hands raised, so that the white garden outside, a pine bough heavy with snow, suddenly floods the dim room with light. Behind her the young empress, eighteen, half hidden by a curtain stand of hanging silk panels, laughs, and two other ladies, one older, look up from a low charcoal brazier. Seen from inside the room, Sei from the knees up, her face turned back toward us right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Heian Japan: no writing desk in this picture, no later kimono with a wide sash, no pinned-up hair with combs, no fan held open, no paper sliding screens. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dark ceiling there.
cards.check: Some scholars think Sei had left court before Murasaki arrived; the link says only that they served rival empresses.

cards.fact: He spent thirty years on the Shahnameh, the Book of Kings: Persia's story from the creation, in some fifty thousand couplets, one of the longest poems by one person. It helped keep the Persian language alive.
cards.art: Ferdowsi about the year 1010, aged seventy, in the orchard of his house at Tus in eastern Persia, setting down the last lines of the Book of Kings: an old country gentleman with a long white beard and a tired, satisfied face, in a long quilted robe with a sash and a white turban, sitting cross-legged on a carpet under a mulberry tree with a sheet of paper on a small board propped on his raised knee. He has just lifted his reed pen, a plain cut reed with no feather, from the page and holds it in the air in his right hand. All around him on the carpet, in an open chest and stacked in a niche of the garden wall, are tied bundles of written pages, the work of thirty years, hundreds of them; the writing on every page is fine rows of marks, texture only, with no letter that can be read. Ferdowsi sits in the right half of the picture, with the trunk of the mulberry tree behind him at the right edge. Beside him on the same carpet, in the left half of the picture, at his right elbow and exactly as far from us as he is, kneels a boy of ten, pouring water from a ewer into a bowl. The boy is a real ten-year-old drawn at the same scale as the old man, not a tiny figure: his head is nearly as big as Ferdowsi's own head without the turban (about five sixths of it), his shoulders are two thirds as broad as the old man's, and kneeling upright the top of his cap comes up level with the seated old man's shoulder. The ewer is as tall as the boy's forearm is long and the bowl is as wide as his two hands side by side; both would look the right size in the old man's hands too. Two people only. Composed like a Persian manuscript painting, with flat bright color and a high horizon, but with the two people in true proportion to each other. Seen from the carpet, from the waist up: the old man's face is three fifths of the way across the picture from the left and a quarter of the way down, his whole turban is right of the middle of the picture, and the boy's head is lower, a third of the way across and two fifths of the way down. He wears a red quilted robe; the boy wears ochre. Persia about the year 1000: no printed or bound printed books, no quill, no heroes or monsters in the sky. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only leaves there.
cards.check: Sources give 30 to 33 years and 50,000 to 60,000 couplets.

cards.fact: A teacher of Islamic law in what is now Turkey, he poured out poems of longing for God after he met a wandering holy man, Shams. His followers, the Mevlevi, pray with a whirling dance.
cards.art: Rumi about 1250 in the goldbeaters' street of the market at Konya, in the story his followers told of how the turning dance began: a scholar of about forty-three with a brown beard and a rapt, lifted face, in a wide-sleeved robe and a large wound turban, who has stopped in the middle of the lane with his eyes closed, his right arm rising with the palm up and his left arm falling with the palm down, the skirts of his robe just beginning to swing out as he turns in time to the ringing of hammers. In the open-fronted shop beside him his friend the goldbeater, a grey-bearded man, and two apprentices, a youth and a boy, sit on the floor at low anvils; they have looked up but keep hammering, each with one short hammer raised, sheets of gold leaf shining on the bench. One passer-by, a woman with a basket on her head, has stopped. Five people only. Seen from down the lane, from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, the whole of his turban inside the picture. Seljuk Anatolia in the thirteenth century: no tall felt cap and white skirt of the later dervishes, no Ottoman dress, no minaret crowding the top corners. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only shop awning and shadow there.
cards.check: The goldsmiths' hammers are tied to his ecstasy and to Salah al-Din Zarkub in the sources; that the turning began there is the order's own story (picture brief only).

cards.fact: A soldier who lost the use of his left hand in a sea battle, he was later held by pirates for five years in Algiers. In his late fifties he published Don Quixote, about an old gentleman who reads too many tales of knights and sets out to be one.
cards.art: Miguel de Cervantes about 1600, in his early fifties, a tax collector who has spent years on the roads of the south, writing at an inn on the plain of La Mancha, with the face he described himself: an oval face with a hooked but well-proportioned nose, chestnut hair, a smooth open forehead, lively eyes, a beard gone silver and large moustaches, a little stooped in the shoulders. He wears a worn black doublet with a small plain white collar. He sits at a rough table by the inn's open door, a goose-feather quill in his right hand above a sheet of paper, and his left hand, which lies on the paper to hold it still, is stiff and half closed, crippled by an old wound. He has looked up from the page and out of the door, amused, to where a thin old farmer on a bony horse and a stout man on a donkey are passing along the road in the heat, small and far off, carrying nothing in their hands, with two white tower windmills on the ridge behind them, each a round white tower with a cone roof and four lattice sails. A jug, bread, his saddlebags; the writing on the page is rows of marks, texture only. Seen from inside the dark room, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Spain about 1600: no wide cartwheel ruff, no knight in full armor, no lance. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dark rafters there.

links.galileo>gentileschi: Artemisia Gentileschi came to know Galileo in Florence, and the two wrote to each other for years afterwards.

cards.tx: +2 Might when attacking a Figure whose card shows more Might.
cards.fact: She was painting like a master at seventeen, and was the first woman admitted to the academy of art in Florence. Her pictures show strong women from old stories in the middle of the action.
cards.art: Artemisia Gentileschi about 1638, at work, in the pose of her own self-portrait as the art of painting: a strong-armed woman of forty-five with a round face flushed with effort and dark hair coming loose from its knot, in a green silk dress with the sleeves pushed up above the elbow and a brown apron, a thin gold chain around her neck from which a tiny mask hangs. A tall canvas stands on its easel at the far left edge of the picture, turned almost edge-on to us, so that all we see of it is a narrow upright strip: its tacked side edge. Its painted face is turned away from us, toward her. She stands to the right of it, seen from her left side in three-quarter view as in her self-portrait, leaning steeply in toward it, her right arm stretched up and across with a long thin brush held near its end between thumb and fingers, the bristle tip touching the hidden painted face of the canvas (never its back or its wooden frame), her left hand low, its thumb through the hole of a small wooden palette, with three more brushes held in the same hand, her eyes on the point where her brush touches. Hard light from a high window falls on her forehead, forearm and bare neck against a plain brown wall. She is alone. Seen from close beside the easel, from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Nothing of the painted picture is shown. Italy in the 1630s: no beret, no smock of a later age, no paint tubes. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only shadowed wall there.
cards.check: Her death is given as 1653 or about 1656.

links.libai>basho: Bashō opens his travel diary by echoing Li Bai's line that the passing days and months are travelers too.

cards.tx: Voyager: can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: In 1689 he sold his house and set off on foot through the wild north of Japan, some 2,400 kilometers, writing as he went. His diary, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, is full of the three-line poems we call haiku.
cards.art: Matsuo Bashō in the summer of 1689, aged forty-five, shooting the rapids of the Mogami River in the far north of Japan, swollen with the early summer rains, as his travel diary tells: a slight, weathered man with a shaved head, in the black robe of a lay monk hitched up at the knees, straw sandals and a wide round hat of woven sedge tied under his chin. He kneels in the middle of a long, narrow flat-bottomed rice boat that is racing bow-down between green cliffs, one hand gripping the side and the other clamping his hat to his head, his mouth open in something between terror and delight. Behind him his companion, a younger man with a shaved head in the same dark robe, clings to their bundles, and a boatman in a straw rain cape stands in the stern leaning his whole weight on a long pole. Three people only. White water, a thread of waterfall down the cliff, rain. It is early summer: the leaves are full and green, drawn in black and ochre, with no red autumn maple leaves anywhere. Seen from the bank just ahead of the boat, Bashō from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Edo Japan: no sword, no samurai topknot. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wet cliff and leaves there.
cards.check: The journey of 1689, its length and the echo of Li Bai in the opening were confirmed.

cards.fact: At twenty he walked some 400 kilometers to hear a famous organist, and stayed three months longer than his employers allowed. He wrote over a thousand pieces of music, and four of his sons became composers too.
cards.art: Johann Sebastian Bach in the late autumn of 1705, aged twenty, on his long walk across Germany to hear the old organist of Lubeck: a sturdy young man with the face of his later portrait made young: broad, square and full in the cheeks, with heavy dark brows drawn together, a strong nose with a broad tip, a wide firm mouth and a heavy jaw, not a handsome hero's face, and his own brown hair tied back, in a long traveling coat, muddy boots and a broad-brimmed hat, a leather satchel of music across his back and a stout stick in his right hand. He has come over the last rise of a flat, wet road at sunset and stopped dead: the road bends away to the left in front of him, and there, far off across the marshes, small in the lower left of the picture, stand the brick walls of the city and, above them, the two tall slender spires, side by side, of the great church he has walked three weeks to reach. He stares at them, breathing hard, with the beginning of a grin. He is alone on the road. Seen from the roadside a little ahead of him and from the height of his shoulder, so that the flat horizon lies two fifths of the way down the picture, level with his chest, and the two spires stand up from it at the left, clear against the sky, at the height of his shoulder. He stands at the right in profile, facing left toward the city, from the knees up, his face right of center, a quarter of the way down the picture, with plain sky above his hat. Germany in 1705: no white wig, no organ, no sheet music in his hand, no cart or horse. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only evening sky there.
cards.check: The count of his works and his sons were not returned.

links.homer>wheatley: The first poem in Phillis Wheatley's book praises Homer by name.
links.virgil>wheatley: Phillis Wheatley learned Latin in her teens, and in the first poem of her book she wishes she could sing as Virgil did.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: Sold in Boston at about seven, she read the Bible within sixteen months. In 1773 she became the first African American to publish poems, once eighteen Boston men swore she had written them.
cards.art: Phillis Wheatley about 1772, aged about nineteen, writing late at night in the house in Boston where she was held as a slave, in the pose of the portrait printed in her own book: a slight young Black woman with a thoughtful, delicate face, in a plain dark dress with a white kerchief crossed at the neck, a white apron and a frilled white cap. She sits at a small round table with a sheet of paper before her, a goose-feather quill in her right hand held just above the page, her left hand raised with one finger against her cheek, looking up and away as the next line comes to her. On the table are an inkstand, one candle and a small thick book lying closed. She is alone. Any writing on the paper is fine rows of marks, texture only. The room is dark and bare behind her. She sits at the right of the picture, turned in profile toward the left, as in that portrait, the table and the candle at the left. Seen from beside the table, from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Boston in the 1770s: no chains, no headwrap of a later period, no fine silk gown. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only darkness there.
cards.check: Checked at the merge against the 1773 book itself (archive.org, poemsonvarioussu00whea_1): John Wheatley's letter gives the sixteen months, the Bible and her Latin; To Maecenas is the first poem and names Homer and Virgil ("O could I rival thine and Virgil's page").

cards.fact: By his own account he was kidnapped as a boy from what is now Nigeria. Enslaved as a sailor, he traded on the side until he could buy his freedom, and his life story of 1789 helped to turn Britain against the slave trade.
cards.art: Olaudah Equiano on 11 July 1766, aged about twenty-one, on the Caribbean island of Montserrat, at the moment he becomes a free man: a young Black sailor with a broad, open face, wide-set eyes and short hair, in his best clothes, a short blue sailor's jacket, a checked shirt, a neckcloth and wide trousers, standing in a merchant's counting room with a single sheet of paper, his freedom, held in both hands close to his chest. His whole head is well inside the picture: the top of his hair is a fifth of the way down the picture, with a wide band of plain wooden wall above it. His master has this moment signed it and handed it back; Equiano's eyes are shut and his head is tilted back, and he is drawing an enormous breath, tears on his cheeks. Behind the desk the man who owned him until a minute ago, a Quaker merchant of middle age in a plain brown coat and a broad plain hat, is still holding the quill, looking up at him. Through the open door, the harbor and a small single-masted sloop at anchor. Two people only. The paper carries rows of marks and a wax seal, texture only, nothing that can be read. Seen from beside the desk, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. No chains or whips in the picture, no bare-chested figure, no coins. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wooden wall there.
cards.check: Some scholars doubt his African birth; the card says it is his own account.

cards.fact: She wrote her six novels of love, money and family on small sheets at a little table in the sitting room, and published them without her name; the title page of the first said only “By a Lady”. They have never been out of print.
cards.art: Jane Austen on the evening of 28 January 1813, aged thirty-seven, at her cottage at Chawton, the day the first copy of Pride and Prejudice came to her from London, which she called her own darling child: by the fire she is reading the new novel aloud to her mother and their neighbor Miss Benn, who did not know who had written it. Jane, as her nephew remembered her: a grown woman of thirty-seven, not a girl, rather tall and slender, with full round cheeks, a small well-formed nose and mouth, bright hazel eyes, a clear brown complexion with a rich color and brown curls close round her face at the front of a white muslin cap, in a plain high-waisted dress with long sleeves and a shawl. She stands at the side of the fireplace with one small volume bound in plain boards open in her left hand, a book no bigger than her hand, and reads with relish, acting the part, one eyebrow up and the corner of her mouth lifting in a dry, knowing smile, her right hand raised in a small gesture as she speaks a line. The fire lights her strongly from below and from the side, gold on her face and black shadow behind, and her one shadow is thrown large up the wall behind her. In the lower left, seated in the shadow and nearer to us, the two listeners, each a real, dignified person and not a caricature: her mother, a fine-boned, upright gentlewoman of seventy-three with a long straight aristocratic nose, a thin face and a frilled white cap, listening with quiet pride; and Miss Benn, a plain, poor woman of about fifty in a worn shawl, leaning forward, delighted. One candle on the mantelpiece; a low ceiling with a beam. Seen from low down beside the hearth, Jane from the waist up, her face three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down; her face, the book and her raised hand are in the upper half of the picture. England in 1813: no bonnet indoors, no wide Victorian skirts, no gas light, no large desk, no writing anywhere that can be read. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: He could not read any language, yet over about twelve years he worked out 86 signs, one for each syllable of Cherokee. Within a few years most of his people could read and write, and they had their own newspaper.
cards.art: Sequoyah in 1821, showing the leading men of the Cherokee Nation that his signs can carry speech, with the help of his young daughter Ayoka: a man of about fifty with a calm, deep-lined face, dressed as the portrait painted of him in 1828 shows him, in a blue striped coat over a white shirt with a red neckcloth, a red patterned cloth wound around his head as a turban, a thin long-stemmed pipe in his right hand, sitting on a bench with his lame left leg stretched stiffly out in front of him, in ordinary cloth leggings and a moccasin, not bandaged. He watches without a word as his daughter, a girl of six in a calico dress, who was sent out of the house while the men told him what to write, stands in the foreground with her back half turned to us and reads their message aloud from a sheet of paper she holds up in both hands; the sheet is turned toward her, so that we see only its blank back, and no writing shows anywhere in the picture. Three headmen, each different in age and build, in cloth turbans, hunting coats and trade-cloth shirts, lean toward her, one with his hand over his mouth. A log house, a low fire. Five people only. Seen from beside the girl, so that Sequoyah faces us from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. No feathered headdress, no tipi, no buckskin fringe costume, no medal, no letters or signs on anything. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only log wall there.

links.hokusai>hiroshige: Hiroshige turned to landscape after Hokusai's views of Mount Fuji had made such prints the fashion in Edo.

cards.fact: The son of a fire warden, he kept his own post in the Edo fire brigade for years while he learned to draw. His prints of travelers caught in rain, snow and mist on the road to Kyoto sold in the thousands.
cards.art: Hiroshige in 1832, aged thirty-five, sketching on the great road from Edo to Kyoto as a sudden summer storm breaks: a round-faced, mild-looking man with a shaved crown and a small topknot, in a traveling kimono tucked up at the knees with leggings and straw sandals, sitting on the bench of a roadside tea stall under its dripping thatched eave. A small sketchbook of soft paper is open on his knee and his brush, a thin bamboo brush held upright between thumb and two fingers, is moving fast, a little case of ink at his side, but his eyes are on the road, where two bearers with a covered litter and a man hunched under a paper umbrella are running bent double up a hill into slanting gray rain, while a grove of bamboo behind them bows in the wind in three fading bands of gray. The tea woman, an older woman in an apron, holds out a cup he has not noticed. The sketch on the page is a few loose strokes, with no writing. Seen from the road, looking in under the eave, Hiroshige from the waist up, his head in the upper third of the picture, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down. Edo Japan: no great wave, no Mount Fuji, no samurai armor. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only thatch and rain there.

links.moliere>goethe: Goethe said that Molière was so great that he was astonished afresh each time he read him.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: Poet, playwright, minister of a small German state and student of plants and color, he worked for some sixty years on Faust, about a scholar who bargains with the devil, and finished it months before he died.
cards.art: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe in April 1787, aged thirty-seven, in the public garden by the sea at Palermo in Sicily, where the idea came to him that all plants are variations on one plan: a tall, handsome man with large dark eyes, a strong long nose, a high forehead and his brown hair tied back unpowdered, in a pale traveling coat with a wide collar, his broad-brimmed gray hat lying on the path beside him. He has gone down on one knee in front of a bed of strange southern plants and holds a single large leaf flat on his left palm, running the forefinger of his right hand along its ribs, his eyes going from the leaf to the plant it came from, while a pocket volume of Homer, which he brought out to read, lies forgotten face down in the grass. Lemon trees, a fan palm and tall flowering stems surround him, and the sea is blue beyond a low wall. He is alone. Seen from the flower bed, low, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Italy in 1787: no powdered wig, no devil or scholar's study, no reclining pose among ruins, no writing on the book. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only palm fronds there.
cards.check: The sixty years on Faust, finished in 1831, were confirmed. The search did not return his words about Shakespeare (the speech Zum Shakespeares-Tag, 1771). At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

cards.tx: Enemies can't clash with this Figure.
cards.fact: She seldom left her family's house, and in later years spoke to visitors from behind a half-open door. Only about ten of her poems were printed in her life; after she died her sister found nearly eighteen hundred, many sewn into little books.
cards.art: Emily Dickinson about 1875, in her middle forties, at the upstairs window of her family's brick house in Amherst, lowering a treat to the children of the neighbourhood, as one of them remembered all his life: a small, slight woman with auburn hair parted in the middle and drawn back smooth over her ears, large dark eyes, a full mouth and a quick, laughing look, in a plain white cotton dress with a flat collar and a row of small buttons down the front. She leans out over the sill with both hands paying out a much-knotted cord, at the end of which a little basket of gingerbread, long oval cakes, crisp and brown (not gingerbread men), has just begun to jerk its way down: the basket hangs only a little below the window sill, two fifths of the way down the picture, with a long drop of bare brick wall still under it, and at the very bottom edge of the picture are the stretched-up hands and the tops of the heads of three children who stand in the garden far below. She is a woman in her forties, with fine lines at her eyes, not a girl. Behind her in the room is a small square writing table with a lamp. Summer leaves frame the window. Seen from outside and a little below, Emily from the waist up in the window, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. New England in the 1870s: no black dress, no veil, no gravestones, no bonnet. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only brick wall and leaves there.
cards.check: The half-open door and the basket of gingerbread were not returned.

cards.fact: A count who had fought as an army officer, he wrote War and Peace, a novel with more than five hundred characters. In old age he dressed as a peasant, worked in the fields and taught that nobody should answer violence with violence.
cards.art: Leo Tolstoy about 1890, aged sixty-two, mowing hay with the peasants on his own estate: a big, strong old man with a long grey-white beard, a broad nose, shaggy brows and small piercing eyes, in a loose white Russian peasant shirt worn outside his trousers and belted at the waist, rough trousers tucked into boots and a soft pale cap. He stands with his legs wide apart in a meadow at sunrise, in the middle of a stroke with a Russian scythe: a straight wooden shaft about as long as he is tall, his left hand gripping its upper end near his left hip and his right hand on a short peg handle half way down, the long, narrow, gently curved steel blade, about as long as his arm, fixed at a right angle to the foot of the shaft and sweeping flat just above the ground, its point toward his left, the cut grass falling in a curved swath at his feet. Sweat darkens his shirt; his face is set and content. One other mower, a fair, broad young peasant a few paces behind him and to the side, holding his scythe the same way, glances at him to see whether the old count can keep the pace, and far back one woman in a headscarf turns the hay with a wooden rake. Three people only; a white manor house shows through birch trees far off. Seen from in front, low, Tolstoy from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Russia in the 1890s: no officer's uniform, no writing desk, no fur coat, no line of mowers. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dawn sky there.
cards.check: Not searched for his own facts (the Gandhi letters and Tolstoy Farm were confirmed under Gandhi). At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

links.mozart>tchaikovsky: Tchaikovsky loved Mozart above all other composers, and built his suite Mozartiana from Mozart's tunes.

cards.fact: He trained as a law clerk before he gave himself to music. His ballets Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker are danced all over the world, though Swan Lake was coldly received at first.
cards.art: Pyotr Tchaikovsky in the autumn of 1892, aged fifty-two, on the solitary two-hour walk he took every afternoon, wet or fine, in the country round his house at Klin, north of Moscow, composing in his head as he went: as the photographs of his last years show him, a neat, slight man who looks older than his age, with white hair cropped short, a trim white beard and moustache, a high forehead, dark brows and gentle, anxious eyes, in a long dark overcoat buttoned to the neck and a soft dark felt hat pushed back off his forehead. He has stopped dead on a path through a wood of white birches with the last yellow leaves coming down around him, a walking stick hooked over his left forearm, and is writing fast with a short pencil in a little paper-covered exercise book that lies open on his left palm, his head tilted and his lips pursed as he hums the tune he is catching. The page carries a few quick strokes, texture only. Beyond the trunks, far off and small, are a field and the roof of a wooden country house. He is quite alone: no person or animal anywhere. Seen from the path a few steps ahead of him, low, from the knees up, his face in three-quarter view right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Russia in 1892: no stage, no dancers, no orchestra, no piano, no conductor's stick, no dark-haired young man. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only birch twigs and sky there.
cards.check: The law school, the clerk's post and the cold reception of Swan Lake in 1877 were confirmed. The search did not return Mozartiana. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

cards.fact: Samuel Clemens took his pen name from the riverboat men's cry for safe water two fathoms deep. Born in a year Halley's Comet passed, he said he would go out with it, and died the day after it next came closest to the Sun.
cards.art: Samuel Clemens, later Mark Twain, in 1859, aged twenty-three, a newly licensed pilot on a Mississippi steamboat: a slim young man with a thick mop of reddish-brown curls, bushy brows over sharp grey-green eyes, a hawk nose and side whiskers, with no moustache, in his shirtsleeves, a dark waistcoat and a loosely tied neckcloth, his coat hung on a hook: river pilots of his day wore no uniform. He stands high in the glass-sided pilot house at an enormous wooden steering wheel with turned spokes, taller than he is and half sunk through a slot in the floor, so that its rim rises in front of him to the height of his head; both his hands are on its spokes and his whole body leans into the turn, his eyes narrowed on the brown river ahead. Two bell ropes with brass knobs hang from the roof beside him, and through the wide front opening of the pilot house the two tall black smokestacks of the boat rise side by side ahead of him, with the bend of the river and a line of ripples that marks a sandbar beyond. Dawn mist on the water. He is alone. Seen from inside the pilot house at his right side and a little behind him: he stands at the right of the picture in profile, facing left, which is forward; the great wheel is in front of him, seen at a slant as a tall oval; and beyond the wheel, through the open front of the pilot house at the left, the two smokestacks stand ahead of the pilot house with the river beyond them. He never faces away from the smokestacks. From the knees up, his face in profile right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. No white suit, no white hair or moustache, no cigar, no peaked cap, no brass-buttoned jacket. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only window frame and mist there.

links.hiroshige>vangogh: Van Gogh collected Japanese prints, and in 1887 he copied two of Hiroshige's in oil paint to learn from them.

cards.fact: He took up painting at twenty-seven and made nearly nine hundred paintings in the ten years he had left, at times one a day. He sold very few, and never knew that they would be among the best loved in the world.
cards.art: Vincent van Gogh in April 1888, aged thirty-five, painting a fruit orchard in blossom outside Arles while the mistral blows, as he wrote to his brother that he did, with his easel tied down to iron pegs driven into the ground so that the wind could not throw it over: a wiry man of middle height, thin, with close-cropped red-orange hair, a short rough red beard, hollow cheeks, a bony brow and pale green-blue eyes narrowed in concentration, as his own self-portraits of 1887 and 1888 show him, both of his ears whole and unbandaged, in a battered straw hat with a wide brim pulled down hard, a loose workman's jacket and rough trousers. He leans into the wind, his right hand reaching to the canvas with a loaded brush and a wooden palette thick with paint hooked on his left thumb. The easel is one wooden field easel with three legs standing in the grass; one cord runs from its top to an iron peg driven into the ground on the left, and another from its top to a peg on the right, each tied at both ends. The canvas is turned away from us so that we see only its back and its stretcher bars; the painting itself is not shown. Around him one peach tree in pink blossom and two white plum trees, each a different shape, their branches bent by the wind, loose petals streaming past across a hard, clear sky with long thin streaks of cloud blown out flat; a low fence of dry reeds behind. Seen from low in the grass, in front of him and a little to his left, from the knees up, the easel at the left of the picture and he at the right of it, his face three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, lit by bright sun. His head, hat, hands, the top of the easel and the blossom are in the upper half of the picture. No sunflowers, no bandaged ear, no swirling sky copied from his later painting, no pipe, no stars, no sun drawn in the sky. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: His age when he began and the count of paintings were not returned.

cards.fact: His Maple Leaf Rag of 1899 sold hundreds of thousands of copies as sheet music and paid him a penny on each. The King of Ragtime had a hit all over again more than seventy years later, when The Entertainer came back.
cards.art: Scott Joplin in the late summer of 1899, aged about thirty-one, in a music shop in Sedalia, Missouri, on the day his Maple Leaf Rag is first in print: a slight, quiet, serious young Black man with close-cut hair, a round forehead and a clean-shaven face, as the photograph of him a few years later shows him, in a neat dark three-piece suit with a high white collar and a tie, standing at the shop counter. He has taken the top copy from a fresh stack of sheet music and holds it open in both hands, reading down the page, his lips pressed together and the fingers of his right hand, without his knowing it, tapping the rhythm on the edge of the paper. We see the copy from behind and below: its cover is a plain panel of printer's ornament with no words, and every printed sheet in the shop carries only bands of pattern, texture only, nothing that can be read. The white-bearded shop owner, a man of fifty-eight, watches him over his spectacles from behind the counter. Two violins and one banjo hang on the wall, and an upright piano stands closed in the corner. Two people only. Seen from the shop door, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Missouri in 1899: nobody is playing, no straw boater and striped jacket, no saloon, no signs or lettering anywhere. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only shelves in shadow there.
cards.check: Sources say the rag sold more than a million copies in the end.

cards.fact: He became pharaoh at about nine and died at about nineteen. His small tomb lay hidden for over three thousand years, and in 1922 it was found holding five thousand objects, among them a mask of solid gold.
cards.art: Tutankhamun about 1325 BC, aged about seventeen, in a palace garden with his young queen, drawn after the scenes on the furniture from his own tomb: a slender youth with a narrow face, large almond eyes rimmed with black, full lips, a slightly receding chin and long pierced ears, as his portraits show him, in a long pleated kilt of fine white linen with a wide sash, a broad collar of colored beads on his bare chest, sandals, and the blue crown of the pharaohs: a close-fitting helmet-shaped cap of blue leather studded all over with small gold rings, swelling a little toward the back, no taller above his brow than his face is long, with a gold cobra at the front. He leans with both hands on a tall straight walking stick, one foot set a little behind the other, as scenes from his tomb show him, and bends his head toward the queen, who stands facing him, a girl of about nineteen, nearly as tall as he is, in a clinging pleated white dress and a heavy black wig, and holds up to him two bunches of lotus and papyrus flowers, one in each hand. Behind them are a pool with two ducks, fruit trees and a painted pavilion. They are drawn as real, solid people in a real garden, with depth, strong evening light and black cast shadows, in the same graphic-novel style as the rest of the set, not as a flat Egyptian wall painting. Seen from close by and a little below, in three-quarter view, both of them from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, the whole of his crown inside the picture with leaves and sky above it. No gold mask on his face, no striped headcloth, no mummy, no curse, no crook and flail. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only leaves and sky there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: His ages were not returned. Whether he was lame is disputed, so the brief shows the stick without saying why.

cards.fact: He ruled Egypt sixty-six years, fathered about a hundred children and built grander than any other pharaoh. At Abu Simbel his cliff temple lets the rising Sun reach the statues at its back twice a year.
cards.art: Ramesses II about 1250 BC, in his fifties, inside his rock temple at Abu Simbel at the moment of sunrise on one of the two days of the year when the light reaches its heart: a tall, lean pharaoh with a high-bridged, hooked nose, a long jaw and a long neck, as his statues show him, clean-shaven, in a pleated white linen robe with wide sleeves, a broad jewelled collar and the blue war crown of the pharaohs, a close-fitting helmet-shaped cap of blue leather studded all over with small gold rings, swelling a little toward the back, no taller above his brow than his face is long, with a gold cobra at the front, holding up a small bowl of burning incense in both hands. He stands at the right, near us, in the small dark inner chamber, turned toward us and toward the light, and a single level beam of gold light, come all the way down the long hall behind us, strikes his raised arms and his face. Against the back wall behind him four stone figures sit side by side on one stone bench cut from the rock, each about the size of a living man sitting down, their hands on their knees: the beam lights three of them, and the one at the left end stays in shadow. From left to right they are a figure in a plain close cap (in shadow), a figure in a crown of two tall straight plumes, a king in a rounded crown, and a figure with a falcon's head under a sun disc. The whole chamber is cut out of the solid rock of a cliff: its walls, floor, ceiling and bench are smooth unbroken rock, with no joints, no blocks and no bricks anywhere. On the side walls a few large carved and painted figures of the king and the gods glimmer, figures only: there are no bands of signs, no writing and no letters of any kind on any wall. Seen from the hall at the height of the king's own eyes (not from below), looking in along the beam: the king from the thighs up, standing just right of the middle of the picture, his face about three fifths of the way across and a quarter of the way down, the whole of his crown inside the picture and well clear of the top right corner. The four seated figures are close behind him at the center left, in the upper half of the picture: their heads come level with his shoulders and their knees level with his waist, so that all four are seen whole above the middle of the picture. No pyramids, no striped headcloth, no mummy, no false beard. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only darkness there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Counts of his children run from 88 to 103.

cards.cap: Samos and Croton, c. 570 to c. 495 BC
cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: He led a secretive brotherhood in southern Italy who lived by strict rules, ate no meat, and believed that number is the key to everything. They found that strings whose lengths stand as two to one, or three to two, sound sweet together.
cards.art: Pythagoras about 520 BC at Croton in southern Italy, showing his followers that music is number: a tall, grave man of about fifty with long hair and a full dark beard streaked with gray, in a long white linen robe with a cloak over one shoulder, standing in a courtyard at dusk. On a chest-high block of stone in front of him lies a plain long narrow sounding box of wood, about as long as his arm, with one single gut string stretched along its top from end to end over a low fixed bridge at each end. With his left hand he holds a small movable wooden bridge under the string exactly one third of the way along it, so that the string is divided into a short part and a part twice as long, and with the forefinger of his right hand he plucks the longer part; his head is bent to the sound. Three followers, all in plain white, sit on the ground in front of the block, listening in silence: a gray-haired woman with her eyes closed, a broad middle-aged man, and a young man who holds a knotted cord marked off in equal parts. The first stars are out above the courtyard wall. Seen from low down among the listeners, Pythagoras from the waist up, his face a little right of the center of the picture, about three fifths of the way across and a quarter of the way down, the top of his head well inside the picture with sky above it. The sounding box is level with his chest, above the middle of the picture, and the listeners' heads are low in the picture. Greek Italy in the sixth century BC: only one string, no triangle diagram held up like a sign, no telescope, no lyre, no harp, no guitar. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only dusk sky there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: He became king of the Maya city of Palenque at twelve and ruled for sixty-eight years, one of the longest reigns in history. In 1952 his tomb was found deep inside a pyramid, his face covered with a mask of jade.
cards.art: Pakal of Palenque on the day in the year 615 when he becomes king at twelve years old, drawn after the carved stone panel in his own palace that shows the scene: a slim boy of twelve, a child and not a grown man, with the long sloping forehead and high-bridged nose the Maya admired, his black hair cut in a stepped fringe over his brow and cheeks, long behind, and gathered up at the crown into a tuft that falls forward (no shaved sides), wearing a short kilt, a wide collar and wristbands of green jade beads, his chest bare. He sits cross-legged on a low stone throne carved as one jaguar with two heads: a single long spotted body that makes a level bench, with a jaguar's head at its left end looking left and a jaguar's head at its right end looking right, the two heads facing away from each other, and one short leg under each end. He is turned toward his mother, who sits on the floor before him, lower than he is, in a dress and short cape covered with a net of jade beads, and lifts up to him in both hands a tall crown shaped like a drum, a little wider at its flat top than at its base and about as tall as his head and neck, covered in even rows of small flat square plates of pale green jade and white shell, with one spray of long, soft, drooping green tail feathers of the quetzal bird falling back from its top (feathers with fine barbs, not stiff leaves). He reaches for it gravely with one hand. Behind them are the white plastered walls of a palace room painted with red bands, and through a doorway with a pointed stone vault two temples of Palenque stand above the forest in mist: each a low, broad platform of a few steps, and on it a small temple like a house with three doorways and a sloping roof, crowned along its ridge by a tall thin upright screen of pierced stone latticework (not steep towering pyramids). Seen from the side, Pakal from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. The Maya of the seventh century: no Aztec sun stone, no feather war bonnet, no sacrifice, no metal. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only plaster wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: An abbess on the Rhine, she wrote down the visions she had seen since childhood, and books on medicine and plants. More of her music survives than of any other composer of her time: some seventy songs, words and tunes.
cards.art: Hildegard of Bingen about 1150, aged fifty-two, receiving a vision and writing it down, drawn after the picture at the front of her own book: a woman with a pale, strong face lifted upward and wide gray eyes, in the black habit and black veil of a Benedictine nun with a white band around her face, seated on a wooden chair in a small arched cell. From a square opening in the roof above her exactly five long tongues of red and gold flame reach down, well apart from one another like the five fingers of a spread hand, each ending in its own point on her forehead: five flames, no more and no fewer, and she, without looking at her hands, is writing with a thin pointed metal stylus, held like a pen in her right hand, on a pair of wax tablets held on her knee with her left: two small wooden boards hinged together like an open book, their inner faces filled with dark wax. At the right edge a tonsured monk, her secretary, has put his head through a little window in the cell wall and stares up at the flames, a sheet of parchment forgotten in his hand. Composed with the flat color and gold ground of a twelfth-century manuscript painting. Seen from inside the cell, from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. No halo, no harp, no quill, no witch's herbs. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only painted arch there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: King of Ethiopia, he is remembered for eleven churches at his capital that were not built up from the ground but carved down into it, each cut from the solid rock. Pilgrims still come to pray in them, and the town now bears his name.
cards.art: Lalibela, king of Ethiopia, about the year 1200, at the rim of the pit in which one of his churches is being carved downward out of the living rock: a lean, dark, bearded man of middle age with a calm, absorbed face, in long white cotton robes with a colored border, a white cloth wound around his head beneath a plain gold band, holding in his right hand a tall staff topped with a cross. He stands at the right of the picture on the high edge of a deep square pit cut straight down into a hillside of red-brown stone, and looks down into it. The pit opens to the left of him and behind him, filling the middle of the picture: in the middle of the pit, cut free of the rock all round, stands the church, one solid block of the same red-brown rock in the shape of a cross with four equal arms, as tall as six men, its flat roof level with the ground where the king stands and carved with a cross inside a cross. Far down around its walls three tiny masons, each doing something different, are at work: one on a ladder hollowing out a window with an iron pick, one cutting a doorway, one carrying away a basket of chips. One old priest in white with a big drum hung from his neck stands a few paces behind the king. Seen from the hillside just above the rim, the king from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, the church in its pit at the center left, level with his waist. No angels shown, no European crown, no built stonework of blocks or bricks, no dome, no tower. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only dry hillside and sky there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Tradition gives all eleven churches to his reign; some scholars think the work ran longer.

links.elizabeth>grace: Grace O'Malley sailed to England in 1593 and put her case to Queen Elizabeth face to face.

cards.cap: Clew Bay, Ireland, c. 1530 to c. 1603
cards.tx: Voyager: can walk to any Place. Raider: +2 Might when attacking on the other player's side.
cards.fact: An Irish chieftain with her own fleet of galleys, she was called a pirate by the English. At about sixty-three she sailed to London, put her case to Queen Elizabeth, and won most of what she asked.
cards.art: Grace O'Malley, Gráinne Ní Mháille, about 1577, at her tower house on the shore of Clew Bay in the west of Ireland, sending her galleys to sea: a tall, weathered woman of forty-seven, not old, with grey-streaked dark hair blowing loose and a hard, humorous face, in the dress of a Gaelic noblewoman, a full-sleeved linen tunic dyed yellow under a heavy fringed wool mantle fastened at the breast, a long knife at her belt. She stands at the head of the sea steps under a plain square stone tower four stories high, one hand on the wet rock, the other pointing out to the mouth of the bay, calling an order down to the ship's boat that is pushing off from the foot of the steps to row out to her galley. The ship's boat is an open wooden rowing boat built of overlapping planks, about three times as long as a man is tall, seen from its side and a little from above, lying along the bottom of the picture with its stern at the left and its bow at the right, against the lowest step. Four of her crew are in it, each different. At the stern, the left end, sits a grey-bearded steersman with one hand on the tiller. In the middle sit the two rowers, side by side on one bench, with their backs to the bow and the steps and their faces toward the steersman, as rowers sit. The rower nearer to us, a broad dark-haired man in a purple tunic, pulls one oar with both hands: this oar is one straight shaft that goes from his hands out over the near edge of the boat, between two wooden pegs, and slants down into the water in front of the boat, where its narrow blade is half under water in a splash of foam. The rower beyond him, a red-haired young man in green, pulls the other oar, which goes out over the far edge of the boat, away from us, so that only its handle in his two hands and a short length of its shaft are seen. At the bow, the right end, a boy stands inside the boat with both hands on a short pole, no longer than he is tall, its far end set against the lowest step to push the boat off. Each oar and the pole is held by one person only; no shaft is shared by two people, no shaft ends inside the boat, and none passes through anybody. Further out her galley lies at anchor: a long, low, open wooden ship built of overlapping planks, about eight times as long as the men aboard it are tall, with a tall post at the bow and at the stern, a rudder hung on the stern post, one mast, shorter than the hull is long, with one square sail rolled up on its yard, and its long oars drawn in; only two men are aboard, one standing at the bow and one at the stern. A mooring rope runs from the galley's stern post, sagging to the water, up through a slit window of the tower above her. Islands, rain cloud and a gap of bright sea. Seen from the water below the steps, from the knees up, her face about three fifths of the way across the picture, no farther right than that, and a quarter of the way down, well clear of the top right corner, with tower wall above and behind her head. The galley at anchor is at the left in the upper half of the picture, level with her shoulders and her pointing arm, its whole mast in view; the boat with its four crew is along the bottom. Sixteenth-century Ireland: no eyepatch, no three-cornered hat, no skull flag, no cannon, no ship with three masts. Only tower wall and cloud are in the top left and the top right of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Accounts differ on whether she and the queen spoke in Latin or English; the card does not say.

cards.fact: When Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, he had twenty thousand workers build her the Taj Mahal. His own son kept him prisoner for his last eight years, in a fort that looked across the river at it.
cards.art: Shah Jahan about 1665, in his seventies, a prisoner in the fort at Agra, looking across the river at the tomb he built for his wife: a thin, upright old man with a full, neatly trimmed white beard, a fine straight nose and a sad face, as the portraits of his court painters show him, in a plain white muslin coat tied at the side and a small flat turban with one single pearl at its front, seated on a cushion in an eight-sided marble pavilion whose walls are inlaid with flowers of colored stone. He sits turned away from the room, one hand on the low carved marble railing of the balcony, gazing out. Beyond the railing the wide river bends away in the haze of early morning, and on its far bank, small and pale and perfect, stands the Taj Mahal: a white building on a high square platform, with one large bulb-shaped dome, a small domed kiosk at each side of it, and four slim round towers, one standing at each corner of the platform, all four to be seen. His eldest daughter, a woman of fifty in a plain veil, sits behind him with a book. Seen from inside the pavilion, a little to one side, the emperor from the waist up, his face in profile right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, the tomb in the distance at the center left. Mughal India: no jewelled throne, no courtiers, no sword. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only inlaid marble wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

links.wollstonecraft>shelley: Mary Shelley was Mary Wollstonecraft's daughter. Her mother died days after she was born, and she grew up reading her books.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: Kept indoors by storms on Lake Geneva in 1816, she and her friends each agreed to write a ghost story. Hers, written at eighteen, was Frankenstein, about a student who makes a living man and flees him.
cards.art: Mary Godwin, soon to be Mary Shelley, in June 1816, aged eighteen, on the stormy night at a villa above Lake Geneva when the idea of Frankenstein comes to her: a slight, pale girl of eighteen with a long oval face, a very high broad forehead, a long straight nose, thin lips, grave grey-hazel eyes and light brown hair parted in the middle and pinned up behind, plain and intense rather than pretty, in a plain high-waisted dress with a shawl. She stands alone at a tall window with her left hand pressed flat to the glass and a lit candle in a candlestick in her right, and she has gone rigid, staring not at the storm but at something in her own mind; a flash of lightning from over the lake behind us lights her face white and throws the shadow of the window bars across her dress. Behind her in the room three young men talk by the fire, careless shapes in firelight with books and wine glasses, each different, one with dark curls and an open collar, one tall and thin with wild fair hair, one stout and dark; none of them has noticed her. Rain runs down the panes between us and her. Her whole face shows clear in one large pane, with no window bar across it. The room has no other window, and neither the lake nor the lightning itself is drawn. Seen from outside the window looking in, Mary from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. 1816: no monster shown anywhere, no laboratory, no bolts, no castle. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only dark window frame and rain there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.fact: A poor shoemaker's son, he left home alone at fourteen for Copenhagen. He wrote over 150 fairy tales, The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling among them, and cut scenes from folded paper as he told them.
cards.art: Hans Christian Andersen about 1850, aged forty-five, telling a story to the children of a Danish country house and cutting it out of paper as he goes: a very tall, thin, awkward man with a long face, a large long nose, small deep-set eyes close together, a high forehead with wavy brown hair brushed up and back from it, clean-shaven, with a kind, mobile face, as his photographs show him, in a black frock coat with a high collar and a loose silk tie, perched on a chair too low for him with his knees up. In his big right hand he holds a pair of very large paper scissors, his thumb and fingers through its two rings, the blades pointing up and away from him; with his left hand he holds up by its top edge the sheet of white paper he has just unfolded, cut into one lacy picture that is the same on both sides of its middle fold, five paper figures in a row: at the far left a little man in a tall hat, then one swan, in the middle one dancer on one toe, then one swan, and at the far right a little man in a tall hat (two swans in all, each facing the dancer). There are exactly four children in the room, each different in age and dress: three sit on the floor around his knees looking up, and the fourth stands at the window holding an earlier cutting up to the glass so that the daylight shines through it. A tall tiled stove, a rag rug. Seen from behind the smallest child, Andersen from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Denmark about 1850: no beard, no mermaid or duckling drawn in the room, no wizard's robe. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: He wrote tales of dread and The Raven, and in 1841 invented the detective story, whose hero solves a murder by reasoning alone. He was found dying in Baltimore at forty, and nobody knows why.
cards.art: Edgar Allan Poe in the winter of 1846, aged thirty-seven, writing by night in his small cottage outside New York: a slight man with a very broad pale forehead, dark tumbled hair, a dark moustache, no beard, and large, shadowed gray eyes under uneven brows, as the photographs of his last years show him, in a worn black coat buttoned to the neck against the cold, with a black neckcloth. He sits at a bare table writing with a slender pen held in his right hand, its nib on the paper, on a long narrow strip of paper made of sheets pasted end to end, which trails off the table and curls on the floor. A large tortoiseshell cat, mottled black and orange, sits upright on his left shoulder, as she really did, watching the pen. One candle stands on the table; its light throws his shadow and the cat's, joined into a single strange tall shape, up the whitewashed wall behind him. The fireplace is cold, black and empty, with no fire and no glow in it, and a few books stand on a hanging shelf. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. No raven, no skull, no bottle. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only bare wall above the shadow there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The cat on his shoulder and the strips of pasted paper are in the picture brief only and were not returned.

links.poe>verne: Jules Verne admired Edgar Allan Poe's tales, and wrote a sequel to Poe's story of a voyage toward the South Pole.

cards.tx: Voyager: can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: Before any submarine crossed an ocean or aeroplane flew, he sent his heroes under the sea, around the Moon and around the world in eighty days, each trip worked out from real science. Few authors are translated more.
cards.art: Jules Verne about 1870, aged forty-two, writing in the tiny cabin of his own sailing boat on the coast of northern France, where he wrote much of his tale of a voyage under the sea: a broad-shouldered man with thick curly brown hair, a full curly brown beard and moustache, a broad forehead and lively pale eyes, the left eyelid drooping a little, as his photographs show him, in a seaman's knitted jersey and a pea jacket, sitting wedged on a narrow bunk at a fold-down table that slopes with the boat. He writes with a pencil in his right hand in a thick notebook that he holds flat with his left, and has just raised his head and turned it to stare at the small round brass-rimmed window in the planking beside him, at the right of the picture: his eyes are on the window, in which a green wave has just broken against the glass, so that for a moment the glass is full of water and light, as if the boat were under the sea, and the green light falls on his face. A sea chart pinned to the planking, an oil lamp swinging on its hook, a row of scientific journals behind a rail. Seen from the cabin door, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. France about 1870: no white hair, no submarine, no diving helmet, no balloon. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only dark deck beams there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: That he is among the most translated authors was not returned.

links.sittingbull>oakley: Sitting Bull saw Annie Oakley shoot in 1884, adopted her as a daughter, and gave her a name that means Little Sure Shot.

cards.tx: +2 Might when attacking a Figure whose card shows more Might.
cards.fact: She learned to shoot as a child to feed her family, and at fifteen she out-shot a traveling marksman, whom she later married. In Buffalo Bill's show she could hit the thin edge of a playing card at thirty paces.
