The lower oval holds nine signs, from left to right: a small triangle, a lion lying down, one reed leaf, a looped cord, a small square, an eagle standing in profile, an open hand, a mouth shaped like a lens, and a second eagle. Only three signs are in both ovals, the lion, the square and the looped cord, and three thin pencil lines slant across the paper to join each of them to its twin. The scholar's right hand, coming in from the lower right, holds a pencil with its point on the lower lion; his left hand, coming in from the lower left, pins down a printed engraving of a tall slim stone obelisk on a base. Around the sheet lie a candle burned low in a brass stick, a stack of worn books, an inkwell with a quill standing in it, and a cup. Only the two hands and their frayed shirt cuffs are in the picture; no face. Gray morning light from a small window. Historically accurate: true Egyptian hieroglyphs inside two ovals, no pyramids, no mummy, no sphinx, no writing in modern letters anywhere. The sheet with the two ovals is right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and window.
cards.check: The letter (read on 27 September, signed on the 22nd) and the twelve signs won from the ovals of Ptolemy and Cleopatra were confirmed; so was his reading of the name Ramesses from Abu Simbel on 14 September.

links.newton>halley: Edmond Halley used Newton's law of gravity to show that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one comet coming back.

cards.tx: One of your Figures that can't act right now can act this turn.
cards.fit: The comet came back when Halley had said it would.
cards.fact: Halley saw that one comet had come three times, 76 years apart, and said it would return around 1758. He died in 1742. On Christmas night of 1758 a Dresden farmer found it: the first comet return ever foretold.
cards.art: Christmas night of 1758 on a farm at Prohlis near Dresden, seen from the snowy yard: a broad-shouldered Saxon farmer of thirty-five, clean-shaven, in a heavy wool coat, a knitted cap and boots, stands at the left with one eye to the small eyepiece at the lower end of a long slim telescope of dark wood and brass, longer than he is tall, which rests on a wooden trestle stand and slants up to the right, pointed low over the snow-covered roof of a timber-framed barn. In the clear black sky just above the barn roof, among sharp winter stars, hangs a small soft round patch of light, dimmer than the bright stars around it, with only the faintest short wisp of a tail: the comet. The telescope is aimed straight at the comet. A square tin candle lantern with thin horn panes and a ring on top, a candle burning inside it, stands in the snow at his feet beside an open notebook, and his breath smokes. Nobody else; one warm lit window in the low farmhouse behind. Historically accurate: the comet is small and dim, not a blazing streak; no observatory dome, no wig, no tricorne hat, and no glass paraffin lamp or hurricane lantern, which had not been invented. The farmer's head is left of center, a third of the way down; the comet is right of center, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain black sky with a few stars.
cards.check: Johann Georg Palitzsch, farmer and amateur astronomer, 25 December 1758 (one source says Christmas Eve), and Halley's death in 1742 were confirmed.

links.magellan>naovictoria: The Victoria was the last of the five ships that Magellan led out of Spain in 1519.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: The Victoria's one cargo of cloves paid for the whole voyage.
cards.fact: On 6 September 1522 the small, leaking Victoria reached Spain with eighteen men, three years after sailing west, the first ship around the world. Her cloves were worth more than the whole fleet of five had cost.
cards.art: The ship Victoria coming into the mouth of the Guadalquivir at Sanlucar in Spain on 6 September 1522, the first ship to sail around the world, seen from a small empty rowing boat some way off her side, far enough that the whole ship is in view from stem to stern with water all round her: a short, round-bellied wooden carrack of the early 1500s. She is a real ship and her crew are tiny beside her: she is ten times as long as a man is tall, her side at the waist stands a man and a half high above the water, her mainsail alone is five men tall, and her mainmast rises eight times a man's height above the deck. She is built like a carrack: a raised forecastle at the bow, a low open waist amidships, and a raised half-deck and plain sterncastle at the stern. She has three masts, each standing upright in the hull, and each mast carries its own single yard: the foremast one level yard with one square sail; the tall mainmast in the middle one level yard, hung across it like the bar of a letter T, with one big square sail below it and a round basket top above it; and the small mast at the stern one slanting yard with one three-cornered lateen sail. Her paint is gone, her sails are patched and gray, green weed hangs along her waterline, and a thin stream of water runs from a wooden pump over her side. Standing on the deck of the waist, behind its solid wooden rail, are three of her crew, each different and all of them thin, bearded and in ragged shirts. They are very small figures, seen from far off: each man, head to foot, is no taller than one twentieth of the picture's height and one tenth of the ship's length, and his head is no bigger than one of the cloves in the foreground. The rail hides each of them from the waist down, so no legs or feet show: one shades his eyes toward the shore, one is bent over the pump handle, one is slumped with his arms and chin on the rail, too weak to stand. Nobody stands or sits on the rail and no legs hang over the side. In the near foreground, in the small boat, an open sack spills dark brown cloves, each like a small nail with a round head, across a plank; nobody is in the small boat. Low sandy shore, a small white town with one church tower, hard afternoon light. Historically accurate: no gun smoke, no crowd on the shore, no flags, no later galleon's high carved stern, no rows of gun ports, not a Viking ship or an open boat. The ship's hull and masts are right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: 6 September 1522 at Sanlúcar and the eighteen men were confirmed (some lists count seventeen Europeans and the men taken on in Asia). Sources say the cloves, about 26 tons, covered the cost of the expedition or were worth twice as much.

links.archimedes>syracuse: Archimedes designed the machines on the walls of Syracuse, his own city, when the Romans attacked it from the sea.

cards.tx: Quick. When an enemy Figure would win a clash it started at your Gate or your Outpost, the Defense of Syracuse plays itself for 1 Spark you kept. The enemy Figure goes back to its own Gate instead, if there is room, and nobody is knocked out.
cards.fit: Archimedes's machines saved the wall at the moment the attack came.
cards.fact: When Rome attacked Syracuse by sea in 213 BC, Polybius says, beams swung out over the walls to drop weights on the ships, and iron claws stood others on end. The city held out for over a year.
cards.art: The sea wall of Syracuse in 213 BC in the first gray light after a night attack, seen from the water below and to one side: one single high, flat, sheer wall of pale stone blocks rising straight from the sea along the right of the picture, seen at a slant, its courses of blocks level and its top edge one straight line; no second wall, no tower, no ledge. Over its top a great wooden beam, as long as the wall is tall, is swung out on a pivot like the arm of a crane. From the beam's end one heavy chain runs straight down to an iron grapple shaped like a hand with three hooked fingers, which has caught the bow of one Roman warship and is hauling it up out of the water, so that the ship hangs steeply tilted with its bow high and its stern still in the sea, water pouring off it. The ship is a big war galley, long and slim, and its men are tiny on it: it is fifteen times as long as a man is tall and eight times as long as its hull is deep, and its hull is as deep from rail to keel as two men standing one on the other. The claw grips the upcurved stem post at the bow, the high end; just below the claw the bronze ram, a blunt three-bladed beak sheathed in bronze, juts forward from the foot of the bow. The curved sternpost and two steering oars are at the low end, in the sea. One whole flank of the hull faces us: along that flank, from a single row of oar ports, hang about twelve long oars, loose and drooping at different angles, some crossed, some fallen away into the sea below; the blades of a few oars of the other flank show past the keel. Three Roman soldiers, each different, in plain round bronze helmets with a small knob on top and no crest or plume, each with a long oval shield as tall as from his shoulder to his knee, cling to the ship's rail far apart from one another. They are very small figures: each soldier, head to foot, is no taller than one twentieth of the picture's height and one fifteenth of the ship's length. On the wall top, smaller still because they are farther away, two Greek defenders steady the beam with two ropes, each rope tied to the beam at its upper end and held in a defender's hands at its lower end. A second ship is backing away at the lower left, small in the distance. Historically accurate, after Polybius: one ship lifted by its bow, no burning mirrors, no fire, no cannon, no rows of identical soldiers. The beam, the claw and the lifted bow are right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Polybius (Histories 8.6) was confirmed for the weights and the claws; the siege ran from spring 213 to the autumn of 212. Whether a claw could lift a large warship is still argued about, so the fact gives it as his account.
cards.power: 2026-11-12: a Quick power of its own in place of Phalanx's (Tim was 'not a fan' of three cards with one power). Archimedes's engines kept the Romans off the walls of Syracuse: an enemy Figure that would win a clash it started at your Gate or your Outpost is driven back to its own Gate.

links.press>folio: About 750 copies were printed in London, and some 230 of them still exist.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: About half his plays came down to us through this one book.
cards.fact: In 1623 two of Shakespeare's fellow actors printed 36 of his plays in one book. About half, Macbeth, Twelfth Night and The Tempest among them, had never been printed and might have been lost.
cards.art: A printer's workshop in London in 1623, seen close across a table: a tall stack of large printed sheets, folded once and gathered but not yet bound, the top sheet showing a page of two columns of small print inside ruled borders, the print only fine gray lines too small to read; and beside the stack one finished copy bound in plain brown calfskin, as tall as a forearm, lying shut. Two men stand behind the table, and a row of freshly printed sheets, each folded over a wooden rail near the ceiling like washing over a bar, with no pegs or clips, each showing two columns of fine gray print, crosses the top of the picture and hides both of them from the shoulders up, so that we see hands and clothes and no faces: one older man in an actor's good black doublet with white cuffs, laying a bundle of worn handwritten playbooks tied with string on the table; the other a printer in a leather apron black with ink, his sleeves rolled, lifting a fresh damp sheet by its two top corners. Behind them the heavy wooden frame and screw of a hand printing press with its long pull bar, and two round leather ink balls on a shelf. Candle and window light. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no portrait on any page, no quill being used, no modern machinery. Composition: the table top is in the upper half of the picture, the top of the stack of sheets a third of the way down and right of center, the bound book beside it; the lower half is only the front of the heavy table and the floor. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain hanging paper and dark beams.
cards.check: Heminges and Condell, the 36 plays, about 750 copies and 230 to 235 survivors were confirmed. That eighteen of the plays were first printed here is standard and was not returned, so the fact says about half. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

links.michelangelo>david: Michelangelo was twenty-nine when his David was unveiled in Florence.

cards.tx: Add +4 Might to your total at a Place where you have a Figure, until the round ends.
cards.fit: A giant came to stand at the city's door.
cards.fact: Michelangelo's David is seventeen feet tall. Forty men took four days to move it half a mile to Florence's main square, upright in a wooden cage rolled on greased beams, and it was unveiled there on 8 September 1504.
cards.art: The moving of Michelangelo's David through a street of Florence in May 1504, seen close from the street, from among the workmen and a little below. The statue stands in a tall cage of heavy timbers and is completely wrapped for the journey in a heavy pale canvas drape: the cloth covers the whole figure from the top of its head down to the timbers, with no marble showing anywhere, no face, no hair and no hands. The drape is bound tight with several turns of rope, at the neck, across the chest and at the waist, each tied in a knot, so the cloth pulls close and the shape underneath still reads as a giant standing man: the round of the head turned to its left, the broad shoulders, one arm bent up to the shoulder and the other hanging at the side. Thick ropes run up from under its arms to a beam across the top of the cage, because the statue hangs in the cage and does not stand. The statue is about three times the height of the men, so its head is far above them. In front of the cage, three workmen, each different in age, build and dress, in caps, shirts and hose of 1504: one leans his whole weight on a long wooden lever, one carries a short beam on his shoulder, one kneels and pours grease from a clay pot onto a wooden beam lying on the paving stones under the cage. A narrow street of plain stone houses; at its far end, small, the battlemented stone tower of the Palazzo della Signoria, where the statue is going. Morning light on the marble. Historically accurate: the statue is whole and unbroken, no pedestal, no rows of identical workers. The top of the cage is below the top edge of the picture, with sky above it; the statue's head is a little right of center, a fifth of the way down the picture, well clear of the top edge. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky between the roofs.
cards.check: The height (5.17 meters), the forty men, four days, the cage on greased beams and 8 September 1504 were confirmed. Sources give the arrival in the square as 18 May or 8 June.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: The uproar in the hall stopped everything else.
cards.fact: At the 1913 Paris premiere of Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, the audience shouted and argued until the dancers could not hear the orchestra. Most accounts say Nijinsky, who made the dance, called the counts from the wings.
cards.art: The wings of the stage at the Theatre des Champs-Elysees in Paris on 29 May 1913, the first night of The Rite of Spring, seen from deep in the wings looking across the stage, side on: in the near shadow, among hanging ropes and the wooden back of a canvas flat, a slight young man of twenty-four with slanting eyes, high cheekbones and dark hair, in a black evening tailcoat and white shirt front, stands on a plain wooden chair, leaning forward, one hand gripping a rope, the other beating the air, his mouth wide open, shouting the counts to the dancers; from the left edge two hands in dark sleeves hold him back by the tails of his coat. Beyond him, out in the hard stage light, three dancers, each different, are caught in the middle of a heavy, flat-footed jump with their knees bent and their feet turned in: two young women with long braids and headbands and one man in a pointed cap with a false beard, all in long loose cream smocks painted with bands of red patterns at the hem, cuffs and neck, belted, with soft boots bound with cross-straps up the shin. Behind the dancers is the painted backcloth of the ballet: green hills, gray boulders and a great streaked sky. The audience and the front of the stage are out of sight; nothing of the hall is in the picture. Historically accurate: no tutus, no pointe shoes, no tights, no footlights, no rows of identical dancers. The standing man's head is right of center, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark curtain.
cards.check: The date, the theater and the noise were confirmed. Stravinsky said Nijinsky shouted the counts from a chair in the wings; the company's stage manager remembered him standing silent, so the fact says most accounts.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: A franc a seat, and before long the seats were full all day.
cards.fact: On 28 December 1895, in a basement room of a café in Paris, the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten films, each less than a minute long, to people who had paid one franc. Fewer than forty came that first evening.
cards.art: The first paid film show of the Lumiere brothers, in a low basement room under a cafe in Paris on 28 December 1895, seen from behind and to one side of the projector: in the near foreground, on a tall wooden stand, the Cinematographe, a polished walnut box no bigger than a hat box with a small crank handle on its side, turned by one hand that comes in from the left edge in a dark sleeve; a short brass lens sticks out of the far face of the box, pointing away from us at the screen, and from that lens a cone of light widens across the dark room to the screen. Close behind the box, nearer to us, stands a separate black metal lamp house with a little chimney, shining forward into the back of the box. On a white cloth screen at the far end is a gray, black-and-white picture of a factory gate with workers walking out toward us: women in long skirts, pale blouses and wide hats, and one man pushing a bicycle. Between the projector and the screen sit only four spectators on cane chairs, seen from behind, each different: a man in a top hat leaning forward, a woman in a feathered hat with her hand to her mouth, an old man with a cane, a young woman turning to her neighbor. Historically accurate: the picture on the screen is black and white and silent, no train rushing at the audience, no electric projector, no reels above the box, no lens facing us, no rows of identical heads. The screen is right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark wall.
cards.check: The date, the Salon Indien of the Grand Café, the ten films and the one franc were confirmed; the audience is given as 33, 35 or about 40. A paid show in Berlin by the Skladanowsky brothers was eight weeks earlier, so the card does not call this the first.

links.caesar>rubicon: In January of 49 BC Caesar led the Thirteenth Legion across the Rubicon, the small river that marked the edge of Italy.

cards.tx: Jump one of your Figures to any Place. It can't act again this turn.
cards.fit: Caesar was over the line and far down the road before anyone could stop him.
cards.fact: A Roman general had to give up his army before entering Italy. In January 49 BC Caesar crossed the little border river Rubicon with a legion behind him. There was no going back, and civil war began.
cards.art: The river Rubicon at first light on a January morning in 49 BC, seen from the Italian bank, low at the water's edge: a stream so narrow and shallow that a man can wade it in ten strides, running between low banks of wet brown reeds. Three soldiers of the late Roman Republic are wading across toward us, each different in age and build, bare-legged, in mail shirts and plain bronze helmets with a small knob on top, with long oval shields slung on their backs: the first, a gray veteran, is already stepping out onto this bank with water streaming from his hobnailed sandal-boots; the second carries a pole topped with a silver eagle; and the third, a young recruit of eighteen, looks back over his shoulder at the bank they have left. On this side, in the mud at the lower left, are the fresh footprints of one man who has gone on ahead, already filling with water. A little upstream at the right, small, a plank footbridge on two trestles crosses the stream, with nobody on it. One torch burns on the far bank. Mist, a leafless willow, a few last stars in a paling sky. Historically accurate: the general himself is not in the picture, no horses, no laurel wreaths, no rectangular shields, no armor of metal strips, no red crests in rows, no rows of identical soldiers. The silver eagle is right of center, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark sky.
cards.check: The Thirteenth Legion, January of 49 BC and the law were confirmed. The day is usually given as 10 January, but neither the date nor the exact stream is certain.

links.menelik>adwa: Menelik II led the armies of Ethiopia at Adwa on 1 March 1896.

cards.tx: Add +4 Might to your total at a Place where you have a Figure, until the round ends.
cards.fit: The whole country came to stand in one place.
cards.fact: Lords from all over Ethiopia brought their soldiers to Adwa for the emperor Menelik and the empress Taytu. Three Italian columns crept up by night on 1 March 1896, and the waiting Ethiopians beat them.
cards.art: The hills east of Adwa in Ethiopia at first light on 1 March 1896, seen from an Ethiopian position looking down a rocky slope: in the foreground three Ethiopians, each different, wait behind boulders: a grey-bearded nobleman wearing on his head a tall band of long tawny lion's-mane hair that stands up round his brow like a crown of fur (only the hair of the mane: no lion's face, no ears, no muzzle, no whole lion skin), and on his shoulders a cape of embroidered velvet edged with lion's mane over a white robe, with a long curved sword at his side and a round hide shield covered with silver bosses and filigree; a young rifleman in a white cotton wrap with a cartridge belt round his waist, aiming a single-shot breech-loading rifle with a wooden stock down the slope: the rifle is a long infantry rifle, as long as he is from his feet to his chest and five times as long as his head, with the butt against his shoulder and a long thin barrel reaching far out past his forward hand; and a woman in a white cotton dress bringing a water gourd. On the next ridge, small and far off, two red royal umbrellas with gold fringe mark where the emperor and the empress stand. Down in the valley, small, a short broken line of soldiers in pale uniforms, some in tropical helmets and some in red caps, is coming out of the mist. Behind rise the steep jagged peaks and sugar-loaf rocks of Adwa. Dignified and exact. Historically accurate: rifles as well as swords and shields, no close view of wounds, no bare-chested warriors, no animal-skin loincloths, no rows of identical soldiers. The nobleman's head is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The night march of three brigades by separate tracks, the Ethiopians already in position, Taytu's part beside Menelik and the defeat by the end of the day were confirmed. The dress in the picture brief is from memory and needs a check against photographs and paintings of the time.

links.ramesses>kadesh: Ramesses II made this peace with the Hittite king Hattusili III in the twenty-first year of his reign.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: Two armies that had fought for years put their weapons down.
cards.fact: About 1259 BC Egypt and the Hittites swore to end their long war. Their treaty is the oldest whose words survive, and both copies exist: carved on Egyptian temple walls and on clay tablets found in Turkey.
cards.art: The peace treaty between Egypt and the Hittites as the Hittite king sent it to Egypt about 1259 BC, seen close over a table of dark wood: a flat tablet of bright silver about the size of a large book, covered with fine straight rows of tiny wedge-shaped marks pressed like bird tracks, and in the middle of it a round seal as wide as a palm, showing a tall god with a pointed cap embracing a smaller king. Two people hold the tablet upright between them from opposite sides of the table, and we see only their hands and forearms: from the left a brown Egyptian hand with a broad gold bracelet and a sleeve of fine pleated white linen; from the right a paler hand with a seal ring on one finger, in the long fringed woollen sleeve of a Hittite envoy. On the table below lie a clay tablet with the same wedge marks and a roll of papyrus. No faces. Sunlight through a doorway, one painted column with a lotus-bud top behind. Historically accurate: wedge-shaped cuneiform marks on the silver and no Egyptian picture signs on it, no weapons on the table, no coins, no writing that can be read. The silver tablet is right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall.
cards.check: The date (1259 or 1258 BC), both versions and the United Nations' own words, the earliest peace treaty whose text is known to have survived, were confirmed. That the treaty was first sent on a silver tablet (picture brief only) is from memory.

links.kublai>typhoon: Kublai Khan sent the fleet against Japan in 1281, seven years after his first one had turned back.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: The storm stopped a whole fleet where it lay.
cards.fact: In 1281 Kublai Khan's great fleet lay off Japan for weeks, held back by a twelve-mile wall around Hakata Bay and by night raids in small boats. In mid-August a typhoon wrecked most of the ships at their moorings.
cards.art: The typhoon of mid-August 1281 wrecking the fleet of Kublai Khan off Takashima on the coast of Kyushu, seen from a rocky headland above the bay: in the foreground, among wind-bent pines, two samurai, each different, crouch against the wind on the rocks: one older, in dark laced armor of small plates with big square shoulder guards, holding his helmet on with one hand; one young and bareheaded with a very tall bow, gripped below its middle, and a quiver at his hip; both look out to sea. Out in the bay, under a black sky and flying spray, three big wooden Chinese ships with high square sterns, flat bows and sails of ribbed matting on two masts have been driven together; one is rolling over, its mast gone; broken planks and a great wooden anchor with a stone bar across it wash in the surf below the rocks. Rain in sheets, one break of livid light on the horizon. Historically accurate: only three ships and two men, no stone castle, no lightning dragon, no cannon, no rows of identical ships or soldiers. The ships are right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain storm cloud.
cards.check: The wall of about twelve miles, the mid-August storm and the loss of most of the fleet were confirmed. The fleet was moored off Takashima, west of Hakata Bay, when the storm came. Historians differ on how much the storm, and how much the defenders, decided it.

links.tutankhamun>tomb: The tomb was Tutankhamun's own, sealed some 3,250 years before and still full.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: A king's treasure came up into the light.
cards.fact: On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter's workmen found a stone step in the Valley of the Kings; by one account a water boy found it. The steps led to a sealed door, and the last of what lay behind it came out only in 1932.
cards.art: The first look into Tutankhamun's tomb on 26 November 1922, seen from inside the dark room looking back at the blocked doorway: a wall of rough plastered stones with a small ragged hole broken through its upper corner, and through the hole a bare hand holding a lit candle and, behind it, part of a man's face peering in: one wide eye, a dark eyebrow, a neat dark moustache and a clean-shaven chin; bareheaded, no hat, no beard. The hole is small, only just big enough to show the hand, the candle and half of the face, and the face is small in the picture. The man is an ordinary man, the same height as the statue, and the wall he looks through is farther from us than the statue is, so his face is drawn a little smaller than the statue's face, and his hand a little smaller than the statue's hand: from his eyebrow to his chin is no more than one sixteenth of the picture's height. The candle's flickering light falls into the room on three things only. First, standing in front of the wall in the lower left, nearer to us than the wall, one life-size wooden statue of a king standing guard, seen in profile and facing right: its skin is painted shining black, and it wears a gold headcloth, a broad gold collar, a stiff gold kilt and gold sandals, and holds a tall gold staff upright in one hand and a short gold mace in the other; it is the height of a man, and its head is the largest head in the picture. Second, in the lower right, the side of a painted wooden chest with a rounded lid, as high as the statue's knee. Third, on the floor between them, a heap of white egg-shaped boxes, each the size of a loaf. Everything else is black. Dust wavers in the candlelight. Historically accurate: a candle, not an electric torch; only one statue; no golden mask, no mummy, no coffin, no writing that can be read. The hole and the candle are right of center in the upper half of the picture and the statue's head is below them, left of center, in the upper half too. Only darkness is in the top left and the top right of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: 4 November, the first look on 26 November and the last objects sent to Cairo in 1932 were confirmed; the water boy is given by some accounts only.

links.hatshepsut>thutmose: Hatshepsut, his stepmother, ruled as pharaoh beside the young Thutmose III for about twenty years, and he ruled alone after she died.

cards.tx: Raider: +2 Might when attacking on the other player's side.
cards.fact: His generals feared the narrow pass to Megiddo, but he led his army through it single file and came out where no enemy was waiting: they were guarding the easier roads. He went on to lead some seventeen campaigns.
cards.art: Thutmose III, pharaoh of Egypt, about 1457 BC, leading his army through the narrow Aruna pass on the way to Megiddo, the road his generals had begged him not to take: a slim, wiry man of about thirty-five with the face his statues give him, a narrow face with a strong, slightly hooked nose, large almond-shaped eyes and a small, firm mouth, clean-shaven, wearing the blue war crown (a close-fitting cap of blue leather dotted with small gold rings, with a gold cobra at the brow, no taller above his brow than his face is long), a pleated white linen kilt, a short linen shirt and a broad collar of colored beads, with a bow and a quiver slung on his back. He walks on foot at the head of the column, toward us down the stony floor of the pass, leading one chariot horse by its bridle in his right hand: a small, slender horse whose back is level with the king's chest, with a red and white plume on its head and no saddle. Behind him, in single file, come only three men, each different: a gray-haired officer in a linen kilt and a padded cap, looking up at the cliffs, and two young soldiers carrying between them on their shoulders a light chariot body, an open frame of bent wood and leather with its wheels taken off, as the chariots were carried through the pass. The walls of the pass are steep, dry brown rock on both sides, close together, with only a narrow strip of pale sky above. Seen from low on the path in front of him, from the knees up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down; the horse's head is beside him at the left, a little above his shoulder. Egypt of the New Kingdom: nobody rides on horseback, no saddles, no stirrups, no iron, no camels, no pyramids, no Greek or Roman armor, no sword held up in the air. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting Wikipedia, National Geographic and the Fordham translation of the Annals at Karnak confirmed the council of war, the generals' fear of the Aruna pass, the march through it single file with the chariots taken apart and carried, and the enemy waiting on the two easier roads; his reign (c. 1479 to 1425 BC), the shared rule with Hatshepsut, his stepmother and aunt, for about twenty years, and the seventeen campaigns (sources give 16 to 20) were confirmed the same way. The Annals are the king's own account. The picture's dress is from his statues and New Kingdom reliefs, not checked against one source.

links.leonidas>themistocles: In 480 BC Themistocles's ships held the strait of Artemisium while Leonidas held the pass of Thermopylae, and when the pass fell the fleet fell back to Salamis.

cards.tx: +2 Might when attacking a Figure whose card shows more Might.
cards.fact: In 483 BC he talked Athens into spending a new strike of silver on warships, not sharing it out. Three years later his false message lured the bigger Persian fleet into the narrows of Salamis, and he beat it there.
cards.art: Themistocles of Athens on the morning of the battle of Salamis in September 480 BC, aged about forty-five, standing on the raised steering deck at the stern of a big Athenian warship, a trireme about thirty-five meters long: a broad-shouldered, thick-necked man with a heavy, square, determined face, a broad nose, a short full beard and short curly hair, as the portrait bust of him found at Ostia shows him, bare-headed, in a white linen tunic belted at the waist and a red cloak fastened on one shoulder, his right arm stretched out to the right, pointing ahead toward the enemy, his hand no higher than his own eyes and well below the top right corner of the picture. Beside him and a step behind, at the left, the helmsman, a lean grey-bearded sailor, grips the long steering oar that slants down over the ship's side into the water. Behind the two men the ship's stern rises and curls forward over their heads, ending in a fan of several thin curved wooden slats like the tail feathers of a bird; it is one solid piece of the hull, painted black with pitch. In front of Themistocles, nearer to us, the ship's long, narrow, flat deck runs toward us and out of the picture at the bottom; the deck is wide enough only for two men to pass. The ship has no mast and no sail, for in battle the masts were left ashore. Beyond the stern, small and far off across the calm water of a narrow strait, only the steep rocky shore of the island of Salamis: no other ships anywhere in the picture. Seen from low on the deck in front of him, from the waist up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Greece in 480 BC: no Viking ships, no dragon or curled prows, no small rowing boat, no sails, no cannon, no Roman armor, no helmet on his head, no rows of oars. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting Britannica, Plutarch (Themistocles 4) and other pages confirmed the silver strike at Laurion in 483 BC, his proposal to spend it on warships instead of sharing it out (most sources say 200 triremes; Plutarch says 100, so the card gives no number), the false message carried by Sicinnus that drew the Persian fleet into the narrows, and the battle of Salamis in 480 BC. That the sea fight at Artemisium was fought in the same days as Thermopylae, and that the fleet withdrew to Salamis when news of Thermopylae came, was confirmed the same way. The face in the picture brief is from the Ostia herm, a Roman copy of a portrait of his own time.

links.alexander>mehmed: Arrian's life of Alexander was among the Greek books at Mehmed II's court, and his Greek historian Kritoboulos set Mehmed's deeds beside Alexander's.

cards.tx: When you play this Figure, the weakest enemy Figure here is pushed one step toward its Gate.
cards.fact: At twenty-one he besieged Constantinople with giant cannon. When a chain across the harbor barred his ships, he had some seventy of them dragged overland on greased logs, and the city fell on 29 May 1453.
cards.art: Mehmed II, the Ottoman sultan, on 22 April 1453, aged twenty-one, on the hill above the harbor of Constantinople, watching his galleys hauled overland: a lean young man with a hooked, aquiline nose, a thin face, dark eyes under strong brows and a short, sparse dark beard and moustache, wearing a large white turban wound round a tall red cap whose top shows above it, and a long kaftan of red and gold patterned silk over a plain inner robe, a sash at his waist, standing still with his left hand on the hilt of a sheathed sword. Behind him to the left, coming up the slope toward the crest of the hill, one long, narrow wooden galley with its oars drawn in and its mast lowered slides up a track of logs laid side by side across the ground, greased and shining. Two thick ropes run from its bow up the hill, each tied fast at the bow, and each is hauled on by three men, every man different in age and dress, leaning hard on the rope, and by one pair of oxen. The galley is about twenty paces long, and its hull is taller than the men pulling it. Far below, the water of the Golden Horn, and beyond it the long land walls and domes of the city. Seen from low on the hillside in front of him, from the waist up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. The Ottoman court of 1453: no fez, no muskets, no flags, no crescent emblems, no cannon in this picture, no rows of men. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search confirmed his age (twenty-one) and the fall of the city on 29 May 1453, Orban's giant bombards, and the ships hauled overland on greased logs into the Golden Horn on 22 April to get round the chain across its mouth; sources give 70 to 80 ships, so the card says some seventy. The Legacy Line: a Byzantina Symmeikta article (2020) citing Raby, Mehmed the Conqueror's Greek Scriptorium (Dumbarton Oaks Papers 37, 1983) lists Arrian's Anabasis among the Greek texts at his court, and Kritoboulos's preface, dedicated to him, sets his deeds beside those of Alexander and his generals. The face in the brief follows Bellini's portrait of 1480 made younger; no portrait of him at twenty-one exists.

links.ibnsina>khayyam: Omar Khayyam called Ibn Sina his teacher, though Ibn Sina died before he was born, and he translated one of Ibn Sina's discourses.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: He solved cubic equations by finding where two curves cross, and led the astronomers who measured the year for a new calendar in 1079. The four-line poems told under his name are read all over the world.
cards.art: Omar Khayyam, mathematician and astronomer, about 1079, aged about thirty, working late at night on a flat roof in Isfahan: a lean man with a short dark beard and a thoughtful, intent face, in a long robe with wide sleeves and a modest white turban. He sits cross-legged on a woven carpet at a low wooden writing board laid across his knees, and holds a pair of brass dividers in his right hand, its two legs open, one point resting on the board; with a reed pen in his left hand he is just finishing a drawing on a large sheet of paper on the board: one big circle, and one long open curve that sweeps in from the edge of the sheet and crosses the circle, with a dot at the place where the curve and the circle cross. He has lifted his eyes from the drawing and gazes up at the night sky, where one bright star stands out among many. Beside him an oil lamp burns in a small pottery dish on the carpet and lights his face and the sheet from below, and a few closed books lie stacked. Behind him, below the low parapet of the roof, the dark flat roofs of the city, one plain brick dome and a few tall cypress trees in moonlight. Seen from low in front of him, from the waist up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, with starry sky above him; the drawing board and the drawing are in the upper half of the picture, below his face, tilted toward us so that the circle and the curve can be seen. Persia in the eleventh century: no telescope, no globe, no quadrant or other instrument besides the dividers, no wine cups or jugs, no roses, no tiled turquoise domes, no European dress, no writing that can be read. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Muslim Heritage and the Dictionary of Scientific Biography confirmed his dates (1048 to 1131, Nishapur; some give a few years earlier for his death), his geometric solutions of cubic equations by intersecting conic sections, and his part in the calendar reform for Malik-Shah completed in 1079. The Legacy Line: the Stanford entry quotes him calling Ibn Sina "my teacher" and lists his translation of Ibn Sina's Lucid Discourse (al-Khutba al-gharra'); Ibn Sina died in 1037. Left out because they could not be confirmed: the story that he died reading Ibn Sina, and the claim that his calendar was more accurate than the Gregorian. Which quatrains are really his is disputed, so the card says poems "told under his name". No likeness of him exists.

cards.tx: Can't be moved. +1 Might for each round this Figure stays, up to +2.
cards.fact: He spent much of his long reign rebuilding Babylon. Its Ishtar Gate was faced with bricks glazed deep blue, with rows of bulls and dragons standing out on them, and a gate rebuilt from its bricks now stands in a museum in Berlin.
cards.art: Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon, about 575 BC, aged about sixty, looking at the newly set glazed bricks of a lion on the wall of the Processional Way in Babylon: a powerfully built man of ordinary height with a long, full, square-cut beard in rows of tight curls and curled hair to his shoulders, wearing the tall cap of a Babylonian king, which narrows upward from his brow to a rounded, domed top like an egg standing on end (not flat-topped, not a cylinder), with a narrow band round its base, and a long robe with short sleeves with a fringed shawl wrapped round it and over one shoulder, holding a long staff. He stands at the right, turned three-quarters toward the wall and toward us, one hand raised toward the lion. The wall, which fills the left of the picture, is one flat wall faced with bricks glazed a deep blue, and on it, standing out in low relief and glazed white and yellow, strides one lion, about as long as a man is tall and a half again, with an open roaring mouth and a mane of yellow curls; a narrow band of white and yellow rosettes runs along the wall below it. One craftsman on a short wooden ladder, a short wiry man with a cloth round his head, presses the last glazed brick of the lion's head into place, and another, an older man, kneels at the foot of the ladder by a basket of glazed bricks. The kneeling craftsman is as near to us as the king is, so his head is the same size as the king's head: the king is a man among men, not a giant. The street is paved with large flat stone slabs. Seen from low in front of him, from the knees up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, with clear sky above his cap, the lion's head about level with his. Babylon in the sixth century BC: not the Ishtar Gate, no hanging gardens, no pyramids, no captives or chains, no camels, no writing that can be read. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting Wikipedia, World History Encyclopedia and the Institute for the Study of the Ancient World confirmed his reign (605 to 562 BC), his rebuilding of Babylon, the Ishtar Gate of blue-glazed brick with rows of bulls and mušḫuššu dragons in relief (lions lined the Processional Way), and its reconstruction in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin from the excavated bricks. No Legacy Line: none of the cards in the set has a true link to him. The picture shows the lions of the Processional Way, not the gate, because Cyrus the Great's picture already shows the gate. No likeness of him exists; the cap and robe follow Neo-Babylonian royal stelae and are not checked against one source.

cards.tx: Can't be moved. +1 Might for each round this Figure stays, up to +2.
cards.fact: Brass instruments gave him readings that disagreed, so he built his own in stone, too big to bend or wear. He raised five observatories in northern India, and at Jaipur, the city he founded, his great sundial stands about ninety feet tall.
cards.art: Sawai Jai Singh II, Maharaja of Amber, about 1734, aged about forty-five, at his new observatory in Jaipur, reading the time from his great sundial: a strongly built man with a full face, a dark moustache and a short dark beard, wearing a long white muslin jama tied at the side and gathered at the waist, a patterned sash, a tightly wound turban with a jewelled ornament at the front, a string of pearls and a sheathed sword at his side. He stands at the right on a stone platform at the foot of the great sundial and points to a curved stone scale beside him: a wall that sweeps down and round in a quarter circle, its rim inlaid with white marble marked with fine lines, on which the sharp, straight edge of a shadow falls across the marks. Behind him to the left rises the sundial's pointer: one huge wall of pale plastered stone shaped as a long right-angled triangle, its sloping top edge a straight flight of steps climbing steeply away to a small open pavilion with a domed roof at the very top, about fifteen times the height of a man. Beside the king an old astronomer in a white dhoti and shawl kneels with a slate and a piece of chalk, looking where the king points. Hard morning light, a clear deep sky. Seen from low in front of him, from the knees up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, the top of the great triangle and its little pavilion in the upper left of the picture, below and clear of the corner. Rajasthan in the 1730s: no telescope, no brass armillary sphere, no modern railings or visitors, no elephants. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting Wikipedia, BBC Sky at Night, Live History India and a review in the Indian Journal of History of Science confirmed his five observatories (Delhi, Jaipur, Varanasi, Ujjain, Mathura), his founding of Jaipur (1727), the Jaipur observatory (about 1728 to 1734), that he built in stone because brass instruments gave readings that disagreed, and the great sundial (Vrihat Samrat Yantra) about 27 m, some 88 feet, high. Left out: its accuracy, which sources give as anything from two to ninety seconds. No Legacy Line: he drew on Ulugh Beg's star tables, but Ulugh Beg is not a card. His face in the brief follows the general look of Rajput court portraits and is not checked against one portrait.

cards.tx: Scholar: draw a card when this Figure is played.
cards.fact: Taught by Portuguese priests, he studied so hard that one of them wrote that the king knew their faith better than he did. In 1526 he wrote to the king of Portugal demanding that his traders stop seizing Kongo's people.
cards.art: Afonso I, king of Kongo, in 1526, aged about seventy, dictating his letter to the king of Portugal in his palace at Mbanza Kongo: a lean, upright old man with close-cropped gray hair and a stern, intelligent face, wearing a close-fitting cap of finely knotted raffia fiber, the cap of a Kongo king, a long robe of fine raffia cloth woven in a pattern of small interlocking diamonds, a cape of imported red cloth over it, and a small cross on a chain on his chest, holding a closed book in his left hand. He stands at the right, leaning forward over a table with his right hand flat on it, speaking urgently. At the table his secretary, a young Kongo man in a raffia-cloth tunic and a cloth cap, writes with a quill on a large sheet of paper beside an inkpot. On the wall behind them hangs a large woven mat with a pattern of interlocking lines; through a doorway, palm trees and the woven walls of the royal enclosure. Both men are drawn at one scale. Seen from low in front of the king, from the knees up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Kongo in the 1520s: no chains, no captives, no spears, no feathered headdress, no animal skins, no European crown, nothing written that can be read. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting Wikipedia, World History Commons, the Cambridge History of Africa extract and Panorama's source book confirmed his reign (1509 to 1542) and his letters of 1526 to King João III of Portugal complaining that Portuguese traders were seizing free people and nobles' children. That the royal chaplain Rui de Aguiar wrote in 1516 that Afonso knew the Church's teaching better than he did came through Wikipedia, which cites Monumenta Missionaria Africana; the letter itself could not be read. Left out: his son Henrique made a bishop in 1518 (true, but there was no room). No Legacy Line: no card in the set has a true link to him. No likeness of him exists; the raffia cap and cloth follow later descriptions of the Kongo court and are not checked against a source of his own time.

links.amundsen>shackleton: Shackleton wrote that once Amundsen had reached the South Pole, one great aim was left in the Antarctic: to cross the whole continent from sea to sea.

cards.tx: Voyager: can walk to any Place. Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: When the ice crushed his ship Endurance in 1915, he sailed a small open boat 800 miles to South Georgia, crossed its mountains on foot and went back for his men. Every one of them was alive.
cards.art: Ernest Shackleton on 30 August 1916, aged forty-two, standing in the bow of a small rowing boat as it comes in toward the stony beach of Elephant Island to take off the men he had left there four months before: a broad-shouldered, solid man with a square jaw, a strong straight nose, heavy brows and dark hair parted in the middle, clean-shaven, his face weathered and urgent, in a thick wool sweater with a roll collar under a windproof jacket of pale gabardine, his right hand cupped beside his mouth as he calls out to the shore and his left hand gripping the boat's bow. Behind him sit two sailors in heavy coats and woollen caps, one behind the other, each pulling one oar: the nearer sailor's oar goes out over the boat's left side and the farther sailor's oar over its right side, as men row a boat. The boat is a plain wooden open boat about four times as long as a man is tall, big enough for the three men: Shackleton standing in it is a man of ordinary size, not a giant. Far beyond, out on dark water among floating lumps of ice, lies one small steamer with one funnel. Seen from low on the beach in front of the boat, looking out to sea, so that the boat comes toward us and Shackleton faces us, from the waist up, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, with gray sky above his head. Behind the boat, steep black cliffs and a glacier at one side, a gray sky with low cloud. 1916: no motorboat, no flags, no penguins, no fur-trimmed hood. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The Legacy Line is in Shackleton's own preface to South (1919), read in full on archive.org: "After the conquest of the South Pole by Amundsen ... there remained but one great main object of Antarctic journeyings, the crossing of the South Polar continent from sea to sea." The same book was searched for the rescue ("Are you all well?" "We are all well, boss"). A web search quoting the James Caird Society, the Royal Geographical Society and others confirmed the Endurance crushed in the ice in 1915, the 800-mile voyage of the James Caird to South Georgia (16 or 17 days), the crossing of the island and the rescue of every man on Elephant Island. Three men of the expedition's other party, on the far side of the continent, died; the card is about the Endurance's men. The face follows the photographs of him.

links.kublai>paiza: Marco Polo says Kublai Khan gave his father and uncle a tablet of gold, and that it got them horses and escorts everywhere on their three-year journey west.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It can't act again this turn.
cards.fit: A rider with the Great Khan's tablet changed to a fresh horse at every station, and could be at the other end of the empire within days.
cards.fact: A paiza was a tablet bearing the Great Khan's orders. Marco Polo says the Khan's riders found fresh horses at a station every twenty-five miles, and those with urgent news covered two hundred miles a day.
cards.art: A Mongol paiza, the Great Khan's tablet of authority, about 1270, seen very close, held up in a messenger's hand at a post station on the open steppe at dusk: a long, flat plate of gold, about as long as a man's forearm and as wide as his palm, with rounded ends, a round hole near its upper end through which a plaited leather cord runs, and down the middle of its face one single column of raised vertical script in the old Mongol way of writing, written from top to bottom like a hanging thread with small strokes on one side, worn smooth and impossible to read, with no Latin letters. The gloved right hand that holds it up belongs to a messenger in a belted, padded Mongol coat that wraps over to his right side and a fur-edged hat, his weathered, travel-worn face just above and to the right of the tablet, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. The tablet is in the upper half of the picture, right of center, catching the low light, and does not hide his face. A station keeper, an old man in a felt coat, walks a fresh saddled horse toward him on a lead rope held in his hand, from a round white felt tent: a small, stocky Mongolian horse with a thick mane, its back no higher than the old man's shoulder, with a high wooden saddle and two stirrups. A thin line of smoke rises from the open round smoke hole at the very top of the tent's roof; there is no chimney pipe. Low golden light, wide grass, distant hills, one tent only. Thirteenth-century Mongolia: no guns, no flags, no stove pipes, no Chinese or European writing, no letters that can be read, no rows of tents or horses. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Read in full in Yule and Cordier's translation of Marco Polo (1903, volume 1, archive.org): the Prologue's chapter VIII, "How the Great Kaan gave them a Tablet of Gold", with horses and escorts in every land and the three years to Layas; Book II on the tablets of authority; and the chapter on the post stations ("at every twenty-five miles ... a station which they call Yamb") and the riders who "travel a good two hundred or two hundred and fifty miles in the day". The Metropolitan Museum's paiza (1993.256, iron inlaid with silver, Phags-pa script) was confirmed through a web search. The gold tablet in the brief follows surviving gold paizas in general, not one object.

links.cyrus>cyruscylinder: The Cylinder is Cyrus's own account of how he entered Babylon in 539 BC without a battle.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: Cyrus says he let the peoples and the gods carried off to Babylon go home.
cards.fact: After Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, his account of it was written on this clay barrel. It says he sent the gods of many cities back to their temples and their people back home. It was dug up in Babylon in 1879.
cards.art: The Cyrus Cylinder being written in Babylon in 539 BC: a Babylonian scribe, an older man with a long curled beard, a plain round cap and a fringed shawl over one shoulder, sits cross-legged on a reed mat in a plain mud-brick room, seen from a little way off and from low in front of him, his whole figure from the head to the knees in the picture, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, with plain wall above his cap, so that his head is well inside the picture and nowhere near its top edge. He holds across his left palm a fresh clay cylinder shaped like a small barrel, swelling in the middle and narrower toward its two flat ends, of damp, pale buff clay, a little longer than his hand and as thick as his wrist, and with his right hand he presses the end of a reed stylus, cut off square like the end of a little stick, into it, leaving tiny wedge-shaped marks in neat rows that run round the cylinder from one end to the other; most of its surface is already covered. He looks down at his work. The cylinder and his two hands are in the middle of the picture, in its upper half, just below his beard. Beside his knee are a basket of reeds, a small pot of water and a lump of clay. A small square window in the wall behind him shows only a strip of evening sky. Historically accurate: clay and reed only, no paper, no ink, no pen or pointed stylus, no metal tools, nothing written that can be read, no winged emblem, no gate, no animals on the walls. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: The translation in R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (1912), read in full on archive.org: line 17, Marduk let him enter Babylon "without battle", and lines 32 to 34, "the gods, who dwelt in them, I brought them back to their places ... All their inhabitants I collected and restored them to their dwelling places." A web search quoting Wikipedia and the British Museum confirmed its discovery in Babylon by Hormuzd Rassam in 1879, its size (22.9 cm, about nine inches, long) and the date (after 539 BC). It is not a charter of human rights, and the card does not call it one.

links.victoria>exhibition: Queen Victoria opened the Great Exhibition on 1 May 1851, and her husband, Prince Albert, had led the work of bringing it about.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: Its profit paid for the land on which three great museums stand.
cards.fact: In 1851 some six million visits were made to the Crystal Palace, a hall of iron and glass in Hyde Park. The profit bought the land where the Science Museum, the Natural History Museum and the V&A stand.
cards.art: The Great Exhibition inside the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park in the summer of 1851, seen in the great transept: one single semicircular vault of glass panes on slender iron ribs curving high overhead, with two full-grown elm trees, living trees of the park, standing under it inside the hall, and at the center the Crystal Fountain, a tall tiered fountain of clear glass about four and a half times a man's height, water falling from its tiers and sparkling. In front, near us, a family who have come up from the country on a cheap excursion train, each different: a father of forty in a worn brown coat and a low-crowned hat, holding on his shoulders a girl of six in a plain blue dress who points up at the glass roof with her mouth open, and beside them the mother in a shawl and a bonnet. The girl's head is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Farther off and smaller, only a few other visitors, each a particular person: an old lady with an ear trumpet, two soldiers in red coats, a sailor. Light pours down through the glass. Historically accurate: the dress of 1851, no hooped crinolines, no electric light, no flags or banners with writing, no rows of identical people. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting Historic UK, History Hit, the Royal Collection Trust and others confirmed the opening by Queen Victoria and Prince Albert on 1 May 1851, Prince Albert's part in bringing it about, Paxton's hall of iron and glass in Hyde Park, a profit of about £186,000 that bought land in South Kensington for the Science Museum, the Natural History Museum and the V&A, and about six million visitors (the least firmly sourced figure; the count is of visits, so the card says visits). The elms inside the transept and the Crystal Fountain in the brief are from memory and were not searched.

links.franklin>declaration: Benjamin Franklin sat on the committee of five chosen to draft the Declaration, and he read over Thomas Jefferson's draft before it went to Congress.

cards.tx: Add +4 Might to your total at a Place where you have a Figure, until the round ends.
cards.fit: Thirteen colonies stood together in one place.
cards.fact: On 4 July 1776 the Continental Congress declared thirteen colonies free of Britain. Congress cut a quarter of Thomas Jefferson's draft, but it kept the words “all men are created equal.”
cards.art: The first public reading of the Declaration of Independence, at noon on 8 July 1776, in the yard behind the State House in Philadelphia: Colonel John Nixon, a man of about forty in a dark blue coat, a buff waistcoat and a black three-cornered hat, stands on a plain wooden platform a little above the crowd and reads aloud from one large printed sheet held in both hands, his voice carrying. Seen from low among the listeners, so that he stands above them at the right, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, with clear sky above him. In the foreground, nearer to us and lower in the picture, only four listeners, each a particular person turned toward him: a cooper in a leather apron with his sleeves rolled up; a young woman in a linen cap and a shawl holding a market basket; an elderly Black craftsman in a brown coat, listening hard with his hat in his hand; and a boy of ten standing on a barrel. Behind the platform rise the red brick and white trim of the State House and its tall wooden tower; summer trees. Historically accurate: nothing on the sheet can be read, no flags, no bell, no stars and stripes, no muskets, no rows of people. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting the National Archives' Founders Online, Monticello, the American Philosophical Society and others confirmed the Committee of Five (Jefferson, Adams, Franklin, Sherman, Livingston), that Jefferson's draft went first to Adams and then to Franklin, the approval on 4 July 1776, and that Congress made 86 changes and cut the draft by more than a quarter. The National Park Service confirmed John Nixon's first public reading in the State House Yard at noon on 8 July 1776, which the picture shows. The platform is drawn plainly because the search did not confirm what it was.

links.khayyam>rubaiyat: Edward FitzGerald made his poem from Persian quatrains told under Omar Khayyam's name, and called him the Astronomer-Poet of Persia.

cards.tx: One of your Figures that can't act right now can act this turn.
cards.fit: A poet seven hundred years dead was given a second life.
cards.fact: Edward FitzGerald's Rubáiyát hardly sold when it came out in 1859. Two years later, at a penny a copy, it reached Dante Gabriel Rossetti and his friends, and it became one of the best-loved poems in English.
cards.art: A rainy afternoon in London in 1861, outside a bookseller's shop: a box of cheap books on a trestle under the shop window, full of thin pamphlets in plain brown paper covers, and a young man of thirty in a dark frock coat, with a short dark beard and moustache and thick dark hair, who has stopped there under his umbrella and is reading one of the pamphlets where he stands, utterly absorbed, the umbrella tilting forgotten so that the rain wets his shoulder. His face is lit with delight, three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down; the open pamphlet, held up in front of his chest, is in the upper half of the picture, and its pages show only a few short blocks of four lines of print each, too small to read. Behind the window glass, shelves of leather-bound books and the bookseller, an older man in spectacles, glancing out at him. Wet cobbles, one lamp post, one hansom cab far off. Victorian London: no writing that can be read anywhere, no signs, no prices, no modern clothes. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: A web search quoting Wikisource's first edition, the Morgan Library, Sotheby's, the Rosenbach and others confirmed the 250 copies printed for Quaritch in 1859 with the title Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, the Astronomer-Poet of Persia, the poor sales, the remaindered copies in Quaritch's penny box, and their reaching Rossetti and his circle in 1861. Who found it first (Whitley Stokes, who passed it to Rossetti, or Swinburne) is told differently, so the card says only that it reached Rossetti and his friends. FitzGerald's poem is a free version, not a translation line for line. The man in the picture is not named and is not drawn as anyone in particular.

links.caesar>triumph: Caesar held four triumphs in one month of 46 BC, for his wars in Gaul, Alexandria, Pontus and Africa.
links.augustus>triumph: Augustus held three triumphs in Rome, for his victories in Dalmatia, at Actium and at Alexandria.

cards.tx: Choose a Domain where you have a Figure. If you hold it when this round ends, it scores you double Renown.
cards.fit: A Roman general's triumph made one victory the city's to remember.
cards.fact: Rome gave a victorious general a parade called a triumph. In 46 BC Caesar held four. At one, forty elephants carried torches beside him up the Capitol, and at another a sign read: I came, I saw, I conquered.
cards.art: Julius Caesar's triumph for Gaul in Rome in 46 BC, at nightfall, as Suetonius tells it: Caesar, aged fifty-four, rides up the steep road to the Capitol standing in a tall, round-fronted two-wheeled chariot drawn by four white horses abreast, between elephants that carry burning torches. He has the face of the portrait bust from Tusculum: a thin, lined, clean-shaven face with high cheekbones, a long neck and a high, receding hairline, and he wears a laurel wreath and a purple toga embroidered with gold, one hand raised to the crowd. His head is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down, and he and the horses' heads are in the upper half of the picture. On the left of the road, one elephant, seen side-on and close to us, with a tall iron stand of burning torches strapped upright on its back and its mahout sitting on its neck; its shoulder is one and a half times as high as a man. Beyond the chariot on the right, the tail of a second elephant going up the road ahead. In front of the horses three soldiers of his legions in mail shirts, each different, singing as they march, one older and gray, one young, one with a bandaged arm; behind, the temple roof of the Capitol against a deep blue sky. Late Roman Republic: no stirrups, no saddles on the horses, no crowns, no rows of soldiers, no banners with letters, no writing anywhere. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Suetonius, Divus Julius 37, read in full in the Gutenberg translation on archive.org: five triumphs, four of them in one month after the defeat of Scipio, the first for Gaul, then Alexandria, Pontus and Africa; at the Gallic triumph he went up the Capitol by torchlight with forty elephants carrying torches on his right and left; in the Pontic triumph a tablet I CAME, I SAW, I CONQUERED was carried before him. Augustus 22: three curule triumphs, for Dalmatia, Actium and Alexandria. The year 46 BC, Caesar's age and that a triumph was the parade of a general who had won a war are from memory, not in the text read. The picture's four horses and gold-embroidered purple toga are the usual account of a triumph (memory); the Tusculum bust for his face (memory).

links.michelangelo>medici: Lorenzo de' Medici took the young Michelangelo into his own house, where the boy ate at Lorenzo's table with his children until Lorenzo died in 1492.

cards.tx: When this round ends, every Culture Domain you hold scores double Renown for you.
cards.fit: A banker's money let a boy of fifteen become Michelangelo.
cards.fact: Lorenzo de' Medici, head of Florence's great banking family, kept a garden full of ancient statues where young artists came to study, and he paid them an allowance. One of them was Michelangelo, aged about fifteen.
cards.art: The sculpture garden of Lorenzo de' Medici by San Marco in Florence, about 1490, on a summer afternoon: Lorenzo, aged about forty, of ordinary height and build, stands beside a block-topped stone bench and laughs as he points at the mouth of a small marble head of an old laughing faun that a boy has just carved. Lorenzo has the face of his portraits: a strong jutting jaw, a flattened, pushed-in nose, heavy brows and straight dark hair to his shoulders, in a long dark red gown of good wool with a plain belt and a dark cap. His head is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. The boy, the young Michelangelo, fifteen, small and wiry with short curly dark hair, in a plain smock with marble dust on it, holds a mallet and a small chisel the right size for his hand and looks up at Lorenzo; he and Lorenzo stand side by side at the same distance from us, so their heads are the same size, and the top of the boy's head comes up to Lorenzo's chin; the man is not a giant. The faun's head, no bigger than a man's head, stands on the bench between them in the upper half of the picture. Behind them, under cypress and laurel trees, two ancient marble statues on plinths, one a draped standing figure and one a seated man, both whole, and a low garden wall of plastered brick. Renaissance Florence: no writing anywhere, no other people. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Vasari, Life of Michelagnolo (de Vere's translation, vol. IX, the Gutenberg text on archive.org), read: Lorenzo de' Medici's garden full of antiques and pictures gathered for study; all the young men in the garden were salaried; Lorenzo took Michelangelo into his own house, where he ate at Lorenzo's table with his own children, at about fifteen or sixteen, for four years until Lorenzo died in 1492; the faun's head whose tooth he knocked out (the picture). That the Medici were Florence's great banking family, and Lorenzo's looks (jutting jaw, flattened nose) from his portraits, are from memory. The year 1490 is Vasari's 'the year after he had been placed with Domenico', taken as about 1490.

cards.tx: When this round ends, every Commerce Domain you hold scores double Renown for you.
cards.fit: Merchant towns that traded together grew strong enough to beat a king.
cards.fact: The Hansa, a league of merchant towns led by Lübeck, traded from London to Novgorod. King Waldemar of Denmark mocked its seventy-seven towns as geese. They beat him, and the Treaty of Stralsund of 1370 gave them his forts in Scania for fifteen years.
cards.art: The harbor of Lübeck about 1370, on a gray, windy morning: one Hanseatic cog moored side-on to a timber quay, seen from the quay a little above it. The cog is one solid ship: a broad, deep, round-bellied hull of overlapping planks, a straight sloping stem and a straight sternpost with a rudder hung on it, one mast with one big square sail of plain canvas furled on its yard, and a boxy wooden castle at the stern. It is about twenty-five paces long, and its side stands twice a man's height above the water. On the quay in front of it a merchant in his forties, in a long fur-lined coat and a hood, checks barrels as they come off by cutting notches in a wooden tally stick; his head is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Two dockers, each different, one young and one old, roll a barrel down a single plank from the ship's side. Behind the ship, across the water, a row of tall brick merchants' houses with stepped gables, each house different in width and height, and the twin spires of a great brick church. The fourteenth century: no cannon on the ship, no flags with letters, no writing anywhere, no round portholes. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Helen Zimmern, The Hansa Towns (1889), the Gutenberg text on archive.org, read: the seventy-seven cities whom Waldemar had derided as geese dictated the peace; the Treaty of Stralsund (1370) gave the League two-thirds of the revenues of Scania and its strongholds for fifteen years; the Steelyard in London and St Peter's Court at Novgorod; the emperor's envoys addressed Lübeck as the head of the Hansa. The look of a cog and of Lübeck's brick houses with stepped gables in the brief are from memory.

links.dante>holyyear: Dante compared the sinners in Hell to the Jubilee crowds on the bridge in Rome, kept in two streams, one going to St Peter's and the other coming back.

cards.tx: When this round ends, every Domain you hold scores double Renown for you.
cards.fit: When all the world came to one city for a year, whoever held it grew rich.
cards.fact: In 1300 Pope Boniface VIII pardoned every pilgrim who visited the churches of St Peter and St Paul in Rome. Giovanni Villani, who went, saw 200,000 pilgrims in the city all year, and every Roman grew rich on the trade.
cards.art: The bridge of Sant'Angelo in Rome in the spring of 1300, the Jubilee year, seen from the river bank a little below the bridge: a stone bridge of round arches over the Tiber, and at its far end the huge round drum of the castle of Sant'Angelo, the old tomb of Hadrian made into a fortress, with a squat tower on top. On the bridge, as Dante describes it, the pilgrims keep to two streams: those on the near side walk toward St Peter's and those on the far side walk back toward the city. Only seven pilgrims are drawn, each a particular person, each different in age, build, dress and pose: an old woman leaning on a staff, a young father carrying a small child on his shoulders, a tired friar in a gray habit, a broad-shouldered merchant with a pack, a girl holding her mother's hand, and an old man with a broad-brimmed hat and a pilgrim's staff and a small cloth bag. The young father and child, nearest to us, are in the upper half of the picture, the father's head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Below the bridge the green river and a moored boat. The Middle Ages: no crowds, no rows or columns of repeated people, no statues of angels on the bridge (they came later), no dome of St Peter's (it came later), no writing anywhere. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Giovanni Villani's Chronicle, Book VIII ch. 36 (Selfe and Wicksteed's selections, the Gutenberg text on archive.org), read: Boniface VIII's indulgence of 1300 to those who visited the churches of St Peter and St Paul (thirty days for Romans, fifteen for others); 200,000 pilgrims in Rome all year besides the inhabitants; all the Romans enriched by the trade; Villani himself was there. Dante, Inferno XVIII 28-33 (Longfellow): the Romans' way of passing the Jubilee crowds over the bridge, one side facing the Castle going to St Peter's, the other going toward the Mount. The bridge's arches and the castle's look in 1300 are from memory; the brief leaves out the later angels and dome.

cards.tx: Quick. When the other player plays a Deed that doubles Renown, or that moves one of your Figures, makes it miss a turn or clashes with it, the Tribune's Veto plays itself for 1 Spark you kept, and their Deed does nothing.
cards.fit: One word from the people's tribune could stop the most powerful men in Rome.
cards.fact: Any one tribune of the people could stop a law by himself: veto is Latin for I forbid. In 133 BC Marcus Octavius used it against his friend and fellow tribune Tiberius Gracchus's law to share out public land, and Tiberius had the people vote him out of office.
