cards.art: The Roman Forum in 133 BC, on the speakers' platform, the Rostra, a high stone platform whose front is decked with the bronze beaks cut from the prows of captured warships: each beak a heavy pointed bronze casting about as long as a man's arm, like a blunt spearhead with three flat horizontal fins, fixed point-outward along the platform's front; no animals, no animal heads, no rams' horns anywhere: the young tribune Marcus Octavius, about thirty, clean-shaven with short dark hair and a calm, stubborn face, in a plain white toga, stands with his right arm out and his open palm raised flat toward the man beside him, saying the one word that stops a law. His head is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Beside him, a step away and turned to him, his friend Tiberius Gracchus, also about thirty, in a plain white toga, holds against his chest a small pair of wooden writing tablets hinged together, no bigger than his hand, with his law written in the wax inside, his face caught between hurt and anger. Below the platform, at the bottom of the picture, the heads and raised hands of four citizens, each different, one bald and old, one young, one woman with her hair covered, one with a beard. Behind, the columns and pediment of one temple against a hot white sky. The Roman Republic: no armor, no soldiers, no purple, no crowns, no writing that can be read, no rows of repeated people. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus (Dryden's translation as revised by Clough, the Gutenberg text on archive.org), read: Marcus Octavius, his fellow tribune and intimate friend, hindered the passing of the land law, 'it being the rule that any tribune has a power to hinder an act, and that all the rest can effect nothing, if only one of them dissents'; Tiberius put Octavius's deposition to the vote of the tribes and he was deprived of his tribuneship; Tiberius spoke from the rostra. The year 133 BC, that veto is Latin for I forbid, and the bronze rams on the Rostra are from memory.

cards.tx: Ward: the other player's Deeds have no effect on your Figures here, and Seneca Falls, Himeji Castle, Nan Madol and Nineveh can't work against them.
cards.fit: A bishop who faced Attila and turned him back keeps what stands with him from harm.
cards.fact: In 452 Attila's Huns had come into northern Italy. Leo went with two of Rome's leading men to Attila's camp on the river Mincio, and Attila turned back. Three years later Leo met the Vandal king at the gates of Rome and won his promise not to burn the city.
cards.art: Pope Leo I in 452, about fifty years old, on the bank of the river Mincio in northern Italy, on his way to meet Attila: a broad, strong, grey-bearded man with short gray hair and a firm, unafraid face, in the plain dress of a bishop of his time, a long white tunic with wide sleeves under a heavy cream mantle, and over his shoulders a narrow white woollen band, the pallium, marked with small dark crosses; he is bareheaded and carries nothing. He stands on the near bank seen from a little below, from the knees up, one hand raised, palm out, in a calm gesture of greeting and of stopping. His head is three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Behind him on the left, two Roman senators, each different, one stout and one thin, in togas over long tunics, waiting. Across the shallow river, small and far off, three Hun horsemen, each different, in long belted coats and fur-trimmed caps with short recurved bows in cases at their hips, sitting their small horses without stirrups and looking toward him; behind them a low hill with a few round felt tents, each a different size. Late Roman Italy: no mitre, no papal crown, no crosier, no halo, no apostles in the sky, no horned helmets, no stirrups, no caricature of the Huns, no writing anywhere. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Gibbon, Decline and Fall, ch. 35 (the Gutenberg text on archive.org), read: Leo, bishop of Rome, went with Avienus (a consular senator) and Trigetius (a former praetorian prefect) to Attila's tent where the Mincius flows into Lake Benacus, and Attila left Italy; Gibbon gives the apparition of Peter and Paul as legend, so the card and the brief leave it out. Ch. 36: Leo met Genseric at the gates of Rome, who promised to protect the buildings from fire. The years 452, 455 and 440 to 461 are from memory. The brief's dress (no mitre or tiara, which are later) and the Huns' dress (no stirrups, recurved bows) are from memory.

links.@constantinople>walls: The walls ran across the land side of Constantinople, from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn.

cards.tx: Mend one of your broken Seals, or if none is broken, add a fourth Seal. You can't have more than 4 Seals.
cards.fit: Walls that held for a thousand years kept the city's Gate whole.
cards.fact: The walls were built across the land side of Constantinople for the boy emperor Theodosius II. In 447, with Attila's Huns near, an earthquake brought down fifty-eight towers. They were rebuilt at once, and held until 1453.
cards.art: The land walls of Constantinople in 447, a few weeks after the earthquake, seen side-on from outside the city across the dry moat, in clear morning light: two walls, one behind the other, both running from left to right and away into the distance. Nearest us, beyond the dry moat, the outer wall: a low wall about twice a man's height with small square towers. Behind it, across a narrow terrace, the inner wall, twice as high as the outer wall, with great square towers that stand up well above the outer wall. Both are built of pale limestone blocks banded every few courses with five rows of thin red brick. In the middle of the picture one great square tower of the inner wall is being rebuilt: its top has fallen and lies as a heap of rubble at its foot, and wooden scaffolding of poles lashed with rope stands against it, each rope tied at both ends. On the scaffold, three masons, each different in age and build, one lifting a squared stone block the right size for one man to carry, one spreading mortar with a trowel, one setting a line of red bricks; on the ground the overseer, a lean grey-bearded engineer in a long tunic and cloak, holding a plain wooden measuring rod and standing on the near edge of the moat, looking up at the tower, his head three fifths of the way across the picture and a quarter of the way down. Each tower is one solid object in one perspective, the towers spaced evenly and each a little different in its stones, the walls straight and standing, nothing mirrored. Late Roman: no cannon, no flags with crescents or eagles, no writing anywhere, no rows of repeated workers. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Gibbon, Decline and Fall, ch. 32 (vol. 3, the Gutenberg text on archive.org), read: under the prefect Anthemius, in the young Theodosius II's minority, Constantinople was protected by new and more extensive walls; ch. 34: while the Huns ravaged the East, the walls had been shaken by an earthquake and the fall of fifty-eight towers opened a breach, which was speedily repaired; ch. 68 (vol. 6): the land side between the two waters was a double wall with a deep ditch, which Mehmed II's cannon attacked in 1453. The years 413 and 447, and the bands of brick in the limestone, are from memory.

heldForGuides.tx: Scholar. Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
heldForGuides.fact: She found two new elements, polonium and radium, boiling down tons of ore in a leaky shed to win a speck of radium. She is still the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
heldForGuides.art: Marie Curie about 1900 in the old shed in Paris where she refined radium, late in the evening: a slight woman of thirty-three with a high forehead, gray eyes and fair hair pinned up loosely, in a plain dark dress under a stained work smock. She has paused in the doorway on her way out and looks back over her shoulder into the dark room, one hand on the frame, her tired face lit faintly blue-green. On rough shelves and a deal table stand rows of small glass tubes and dishes, each glowing softly with the same pale light. In the shadows are an iron stove, a big cast-iron basin and the heavy iron rod, nearly as tall as she is, with which she stirred the boiling ore. Seen from inside the shed, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. Paris about 1900: no white laboratory coat, no protective gloves or mask, no electric lamps. Keep the top left corner dark roof glass.
heldForGuides.check: The two elements, 1898 and the Nobel Prizes were confirmed; the shed and the tons of ore were not returned.

links.douglass>lincoln: Frederick Douglass went to the White House in 1863 to press Lincoln for fair treatment of Black soldiers, and Lincoln sent for him again the next year to ask his advice.

heldForGuides.tx: He has +1 Might for each of your other Figures here.
heldForGuides.fact: Born in a one-room log cabin, with less than a year of school in all, he taught himself law and became president as the United States broke in two. He held the Union together through four years of civil war and signed the order that began the end of slavery.
heldForGuides.art: Abraham Lincoln in the summer of 1862, in the telegraph office of the War Department, where he went to read the news from the armies and where he began to write the order of emancipation: a very tall, gaunt man of fifty-three with a deeply lined face, a dark beard without a moustache and untidy black hair, in a black frock coat with a gray wool shawl around his shoulders. He sits hunched at a borrowed desk by the window, his long legs folded under it, writing a line slowly on a sheet of foolscap and then gazing out at the street; his tall hat stands upside down on the desk with papers in it. Behind him two young operators bend over clicking brass telegraph keys. Seen from across the desk, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Washington in 1862: no monument, no flag draped behind, no log cabin. Keep the top left corner window light and wall.

links.thoreau>gandhi: Gandhi read Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience in South Africa and printed parts of it in his own newspaper.
links.tolstoy>gandhi: Gandhi exchanged letters with Tolstoy in the last year of the old writer's life, and named his community in South Africa Tolstoy Farm.

heldForGuides.tx: Legacy of Henry David Thoreau or Leo Tolstoy. Law: enemy Figures here can't clash.
heldForGuides.fact: He led India toward independence without weapons, by refusing to obey unjust laws and accepting the punishment. In 1930 he walked 240 miles to the sea with a growing crowd and picked up a handful of salt, breaking a law that taxed it.
heldForGuides.art: Mohandas Gandhi about 1930, aged sixty, at his daily spinning in the community where he lived in western India: a small, thin, brown man with a shaved head, large ears, round wire spectacles and a gray moustache, wearing only a short white homespun cloth wrapped at the waist and a white shawl over one shoulder. He sits cross-legged on the bare floor of an open verandah at a small wooden spinning wheel that folds flat into a box, turning the wheel with his right hand and drawing out a long fine thread of cotton with his left, raised high, his eyes on the thread. Beside him are a little pile of cotton slivers, a pocket watch on a string and a stack of letters held down by a stone. Whitewashed wall, a neem tree, morning light. Seen from the floor in front of him, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. No crowd, no flag, no walking staff in this picture. Keep the top left corner plain white wall.
heldForGuides.check: Accounts of the Salt March give 78 to 80 companions and 200 to 240 miles.

links.gandhi>mandela: The campaign of peaceful law-breaking that Mandela helped lead in 1952 followed the method Gandhi had first tried in South Africa.

heldForGuides.tx: Legacy of Gandhi. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
heldForGuides.fact: He spent twenty-seven years in prison for fighting laws that set South Africans apart by the color of their skin. Four years after he walked free he was elected president, and he asked the country to forgive and not to take revenge.
heldForGuides.art: Nelson Mandela about 1965, aged forty-seven, a prisoner in the lime quarry on Robben Island: a tall, broad-shouldered man with close-cropped hair, a strong jaw and a steady look, in the prison dress given to Black prisoners there, a khaki shirt, short trousers and sandals without socks. He stands in the white glare of the quarry floor with a pick resting head-down on the ground under his folded hands, and has turned to speak to a half circle of other prisoners who sit on blocks of lime in the mouth of a shallow cave cut in the quarry face, one of them drawing in the dust with a finger as if at a lesson. A warder with a rifle stands far off on the rim. Everything is bleached white and the men squint against it. Seen from the cave mouth, Mandela from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No bars, no raised fist, no gray-haired elder statesman. Keep the top left corner pale quarry wall.
heldForGuides.check: The 27 years, the release in 1990, the election of 1994 and the lime quarry were confirmed. The search did not return that the 1952 campaign followed Gandhi's method.

heldForGuides.tx: Swift. Raider: he has +2 Might when he attacks on the other player's side.
heldForGuides.fact: Born Temüjin, he was left fatherless and hunted as a boy. In 1206 he joined the warring peoples of the steppe into one nation, and his riders went on to build the largest land empire in history, tied together by relays of mounted messengers.
heldForGuides.art: Temüjin in the spring of 1206 by the Onon River in Mongolia, at the great gathering where he is named Genghis Khan: a tall, strongly built man in his forties with a broad forehead, a long beard and watchful, cat-like eyes, as a Persian writer who spoke to those who had seen him described him, in a plain belted robe of blue wool that crosses over the chest, felt boots and a fur-edged cap, his hair in a braid behind each ear. He stands on a spread of white felt before a tall pole from which hang nine white horse tails, the standard of the new nation, and looks out over our heads. In front of him, at the bottom of the picture, the chiefs of the steppe peoples have taken off their caps and hung their belts around their necks, and are kneeling. Round felt tents and horse herds stretch to the hills. Seen from among the chiefs, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No portrait of him from life exists: no horned helmet, no fur barbarian costume, no throne. Keep the top left corner open sky.

heldForGuides.tx: When you play her, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
heldForGuides.fact: She rose from a junior place among the emperor's women to rule China, and in 690 took the throne in her own name. In all of China's history she is the only woman who reigned as emperor.
heldForGuides.art: Wu Zetian in the year 690, aged sixty-six, on the day she takes the throne of China as emperor: a stately woman with a full, strong face, short broad painted brows and a small red flower mark between them, her black hair piled high and set with gold phoenix pins, in layered court robes of deep yellow and red, a wide-sleeved robe crossed at the chest over a long high-waisted skirt, with a long trailing sash. She stands at the top of a broad flight of palace steps with her hands folded inside her sleeves, looking down without expression. Below her on the steps three officials, one old and thin, one stout and one young, in black gauze caps with two short tails at the back and round-collared robes belted at the waist, are pressing their foreheads to the stone, and the young one, who has looked up too soon, is caught in her gaze. The courtyard beyond them is empty paving: no rows of kneeling figures. Red pillars rise behind her under a broad roof of dark gray tile with a gently curving ridge, in the Tang manner. Seen from the steps below, from the knees up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Tang dynasty China: no Manchu headdress, no long nail guards, no dragon throne and no yellow glazed roofs of later dynasties. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only roof eaves and sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
heldForGuides.why: Became a Guide in the roster of twelve (2026-11-12): a Guide is not also a card.

heldForGuides.tx: He has +2 Might while you have more Figures here than the other player.
heldForGuides.fact: Emperor of most of India, he could not read, yet he kept a library of 24,000 books and had them read aloud to him every day. He called scholars of many faiths to his court to argue their beliefs in front of him.
heldForGuides.art: Akbar, Mughal emperor of India, about 1580, listening to a night debate between the faiths in the hall he built for it at Fatehpur Sikri, drawn after the paintings of his own court: a sturdy, broad-chested man of thirty-eight with a moustache and no beard, his long hair gathered up under a small, tight, flat turban, in a plain white muslin coat tied at the side, seated on a low platform with one knee drawn up and his chin on his hand, listening hard. In a ring on the carpet below him sit five speakers, each in his own dress: a Muslim jurist in a large turban with a book open on a folding stand, a Hindu scholar bare to the waist with a sacred thread and a mark on his brow, a Jain monk in plain white with a shaven head, a Zoroastrian priest in white with a white cap, and a Jesuit father in a black gown and black cap, who has risen to his knees and is making his point with both hands. Oil lamps in niches of carved red sandstone. Seen from the edge of the ring, the emperor from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Sixteenth-century Mughal India: no Taj Mahal, no later jewelled turbans with plumes. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only carved red stone there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

merge: Relics and Deeds: engine.js names each Relic and Deed by its key ('compass', 'press', 'antikythera', 'eureka', 'caravan', 'decree', 'eclipse', 'encore', 'fairwinds', 'ambush', 'trojan', 'rift', 'phalanx'). Every new Relic and Deed here has `as`: the existing card whose effect, cost and rules text it takes. To play them, the engine (and the EV handlers in ui.js that name those keys) must look up `CARDS[key].as || key` where it now compares the key. Two Relics with the same `as` do the same thing, so a player should not be able to have both in play (hasRelic should compare `as`). The engine has three Relic effects, so the 20 Relics here are seven that work as the Compass, nine as the Printing Press and four as the Antikythera Mechanism.
Relics have no faction in the game (f is 'N'), and that is kept, so any deck can play any of them. Deeds have a faction, and there are six in each of the five.

Mailed to Freedom takes the Trojan Horse's effect. If the Trojan Horse has left cards.js by the time of the merge, the engine has to keep that effect under this card's key (or another name) for the card to work.

Eras: cards.js has six eras and the last, The Age of Steam, ends in 1900. Eight Figures here have a year after 1900 (Einstein, Turing, Martin Luther King Jr., Jim Thorpe, Jesse Owens, Frida Kahlo, Houdini and Amelia Earhart), and so do the Wright Flyer and nine Deeds (Christmas Truce, Salt March, Penicillin, The Rite of Spring, The Lincoln Memorial Concert, Bridge of Spies, The Summit of Everest, Tutankhamun's Tomb Opened and Lascaux Found). The Figures are given era 6, the only value cards.js knows, and the Library would file them under 1800 to 1900. A seventh era is needed before they go in, for example { n: 'The Modern Age', to: 2000 }.

tx is written from k, arr and insp with the wording existing cards use; boldKeys and GLOSS in ui.js need no change. `links` goes into LINKS in text.js as it stands, `say` into SAY. No card here has a focus setting (FY): that is set when each picture is checked on the card.
Pronunciations (say) are given only where a reader might stumble, as in text.js.

Picture briefs: the 50 Relics and Deeds follow the notes of 2026-11-11 (the thing itself large, a few particular people at most, no rows of copies, both top corners plain). The 100 Figures' briefs were written before those notes: each keeps its top left corner clear but does not yet ask for the top right corner or for the head a fifth of the way down, and a few show more people than the notes allow. They need that pass before art is made.

Balance: node scripts/anoria/sim-set-150.js 12000 plays robot games with the new Figures added in memory and compares each with the Figures its faction already has. The Relics and Deeds cannot be played until the engine reads `as`; each is exactly as strong as the card it copies, but 50 more of them in the pool has not been tested. After the merge: node scripts/anoria/run.js cards 6000, then pacing.js (241 cards in all).

heldForLater.why: Tim, 2026-11-11: "Martin Luther King and Nelson Mandela are too contemporary. Maybe I can get them into a later set, but like we said originally, nothing within the past hundred years." Every card whose own moment (its year, `y`) is after 1926 left the set. Their pictures are in scripts/anoria/held/art/ and their briefs are here, for a later set. Also held (Tim, the same day: "any figures like Frida Kahlo that you think are aggressively protected, you can hold them back as well"): Albert Einstein (the Hebrew University of Jerusalem licenses and enforces his name and likeness) and Jim Thorpe (his name and likeness are licensed for his family by an agency). The named line Standing on the Shoulders of Giants keeps Newton, Faraday and Tesla.

links.ada>turing: In 1950 Turing answered what he called Lady Lovelace's Objection, her remark that a machine can do only what we know how to order it to do.

cards.tx: Legacy of Ada Lovelace. When you play him, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: At twenty-four he described, on paper, a single machine that could carry out any calculation, the idea behind every computer since. In the Second World War he designed machines that broke Germany's Enigma code day after day.
cards.art: Alan Turing in 1940, on a night shift in a wooden hut at Bletchley Park: a young man of twenty-eight with dark hair parted at the side and falling over his forehead, deep-set blue eyes and a clean-shaven face, in a tweed jacket with a pullover and a carelessly knotted tie, half standing at a long trestle table with a dark top. Two long strips of stiff paper, each as tall as a hand is long and longer than his arm, lie one on top of the other on the table, each printed with close columns of tiny marks and punched with many small round holes; with the fingertips of his left hand he slides the upper strip along the lower one, watching for the places where two holes line up and the dark table shows through, and his right hand holds a pencil over a notepad. A shaded desk lamp lights the strips and his face from below. Also on the table are stacks of message slips, and a cipher machine like a small typewriter in an open wooden box, with round keys, a panel of small round windows above the keys, and three small toothed wheels showing at the top. Behind him his tea mug is fastened to the radiator pipe by a small chain and padlock. Blackout curtains at the window. Seen from across the table, low, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his hair. He died within living memory, so this is a respectful, recognisable portrait taken from the photographs of him at this age, at his documented work, with nothing invented. Britain in 1940: no computer screens, no modern keyboards, no uniform, no readable letters, no clocks, dials or plates on the wall. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with his head, the lamp, both hands, the two punched strips where his fingers slide them, the cipher machine and the chained mug all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the near end of the table with the strips running off toward us. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only board wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

links.thoreau>king: As a student at Morehouse College in Atlanta, Martin Luther King read Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience and went back to it again and again.

cards.tx: Legacy of Henry David Thoreau. When you play him, enemy Figures here miss their next turn.
cards.fact: A Baptist minister, he led marches, boycotts and sit-ins against laws that kept Black and white Americans apart, and was jailed for it about thirty times. In 1963 he told a quarter of a million people in Washington of his dream that children would be judged by their character, not their color.
cards.art: Martin Luther King Jr. at twenty-seven, on the night of 30 January 1956 in Montgomery, Alabama, on the porch of his own house an hour after it was bombed: a compact young Black man with a round, serious face, close-cut hair and a thin moustache, in a dark overcoat over a suit and tie, hatless, standing at the top of the porch steps of a white wooden house with one hand raised, palm out, speaking quietly. The front windows behind him are blown in, a porch column is cracked and the porch boards are splintered. Below him in the yard, in the light from the house, stand four of his neighbors, each a particular person of a different age, build and dress, two men and two women, angry, one man holding a stick and one a bottle, and as he speaks those two are lowering what they hold. Behind them is only darkness. Two white policemen in dark uniforms and peaked caps stand uneasily at the edge of the light. Seen from the yard, looking up, King from the knees up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. He died within living memory, so this is a respectful, recognisable portrait taken from the photographs of him at this age, at this documented moment, with nothing invented. Alabama in 1956: no podium, no microphones, no monument. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only night sky and porch roof there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: Counts of his arrests are 29 or 30.

cards.tx: Swift: he can walk on the turn you play him.
cards.fact: At the 1936 Olympics in Berlin, where Germany's rulers meant to show that their own race was the best, he won four gold medals. A German long jumper, Luz Long, made friends with him in front of the whole crowd.
cards.art: Jesse Owens in August 1936 at the Olympic Games in Berlin, in the air above the long-jump pit: a slim, long-legged young Black man of twenty-two with a calm, open face, in the white vest of the American team with a red and blue stripe slanting across the chest and white shorts, caught at the top of his leap with both legs flung forward, his arms reaching past his knees and his eyes fixed on the sand far ahead. A measuring board runs along the pit, and an official in a white jacket crouches with a marker. On the grass beside the runway a tall fair-haired German jumper in a tracksuit is watching him. The huge stone stadium behind is only a soft band of color, with no faces and no rows of heads drawn. Seen from beside the pit, low, his whole figure in the upper half of the picture, his head right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. He died within living memory, so this is a respectful, recognisable portrait taken from the photographs of him at these Games, at this documented moment, with nothing invented. No flags or party emblems of any kind are shown. Correct anatomy, two arms, two legs. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only stadium rim and sky there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.tx: Steadfast: she has +2 Might when she defends.
cards.fact: A bus crash at eighteen broke her spine and left her in pain for the rest of her life. She began to paint lying in bed, with a mirror fixed above her, and about a third of all her pictures are portraits of herself.
cards.art: Frida Kahlo in 1926, aged nineteen, a year after the accident, painting in bed at her family's house in Coyoacan: a young woman with strong dark brows that almost meet, black hair parted in the middle and drawn back tight into a knot, a firm mouth and a level, unflinching gaze, propped on pillows in a wooden four-poster bed. Her body is held rigid from hips to armpits in a white plaster corset, over which a plain white blouse hangs open. A small wooden easel made for her stands across her lap with a canvas on it, its back to us, and she holds a fine brush in her right hand and a little palette in her left, but she is not looking at the canvas: her eyes are raised to a mirror fixed flat to the underside of the bed's canopy above her, a long rectangle of glass in a wooden frame, seen from below at a steep angle so that it shows only a slanting gleam and the dark top of her head. Paint tubes on the blanket, a window on a courtyard with leaves. She is alone. Seen from the foot of the bed, from the waist up, her face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. She died within living memory, so this is a respectful, recognisable portrait taken from the photographs of her at this age, at this documented moment, with nothing invented. No monkey, no flower crown, no skeletons, no embroidered folk costume, no painting of hers shown. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only canopy cloth there.
cards.check: The count of 55 self-portraits among 143 paintings was found in one weak source only.

cards.tx: Voyager: he can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: A Sherpa who herded yaks as a boy in sight of Mount Everest, he first went to the mountain as a young porter in 1935 and went back six more times. In 1952 he climbed higher on it than anyone had before, and the year after that he stood on the top.
cards.art: Tenzing Norgay on 30 May 1953, aged thirty-nine, at the camp in the high valley below Mount Everest, the day after he stood on its summit, as the photographs taken that day show him: a lean, strong Sherpa with a wide, brilliant smile showing his teeth, high cheekbones, deep creases at the corners of his eyes, a sun-darkened face with a band of paler skin around his eyes where his goggles sat, and thick black hair blown about, in a quilted down jacket open at the neck over a wool jersey, with a knotted scarf. He sits on a wooden ration box of plain bare planks, with nothing painted, stencilled, stamped or written on it, holding an enamel mug of tea in both bare hands, laughing at someone out of the picture. His ice axe is stuck upright in the snow at the left of him, between him and the tent, the whole of it inside the picture and none of it cut by the edge: a straight wooden shaft about as long as his leg, its spike in the snow, and at its top a steel head set crosswise, with two different ends: on one side a long, narrow, slightly down-curved pick that tapers to a point, and on the other side a short, wide, flat blade like the blade of a small hoe, its square cutting edge as wide as three fingers (the two ends are not alike: it is not a pickaxe with two points). His snow goggles hang at his chest. Behind him are one small orange tent, a coil of rope, and a wall of blue-white ice and snow rising out of the picture. He is the only person shown. Seen from close in front, from the waist up, his head right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. He died within living memory, so this is a respectful, recognisable portrait taken from the photographs of him in 1953, at this documented moment, with nothing invented. 1953 clothing and gear: no modern bright climbing suit, no helmet, no flags in this picture, no oxygen mask on his face. Leave the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain, with only snow slope and deep blue sky there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
cards.check: Added at the merge in place of Amelia Earhart, who is already a card. Written from memory and not searched: seven expeditions to Everest between 1935 and 1953 and the height record of 1952 with Raymond Lambert are standard. His birth date is not certain (he took 29 May 1914), and he was born either in Khumbu or in Tibet and brought up in Khumbu; the caption gives Khumbu as his home.

links.thoreau>saltmarch: Gandhi printed parts of Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience in his own newspaper in 1907, twenty-three years before he walked to the sea.

cards.tx: You count 4 more Might at a Place where you have a Figure, until the end of the round.
cards.fit: By the time it reached the sea, a walk of 79 people had become a crowd two miles long.
cards.fact: The march began with Gandhi and 78 companions and took 24 days. By the time they reached the sea the line of walkers was about two miles long, and within the year some sixty thousand people had gone to jail for making or selling salt.
cards.art: The shore at Dandi in western India on the morning of 6 April 1930, seen very close and low: an old man's thin, sinewy brown hand and forearm reaching down to lift a small lump of gray mud crusted white with natural salt from the wet sand at the edge of the sea. The arm comes from a short white homespun wrap; a tall bamboo staff is planted in the sand beside it, and a pair of worn leather sandals lies there. Behind, small and out of focus, stand only three companions in white homespun, each different: a tall old man with a long white beard and a white cap, a young man in a white cap, and a woman in a plain homespun sari with her hands pressed together; beyond them flat mud, small waves and pale early light. No face in close view, no soldiers, no police, no flags, no rows or columns of repeated figures. The hand and the lump of salt are right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain morning sky.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: A spoiled dish turned out to be a find.
cards.fact: In September 1928 Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to his laboratory in London and found that mold had got into one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mold the bacteria had gone. The medicine made from that mold, penicillin, was ready for patients in the 1940s.
cards.art: A round glass culture dish held up to a window in a hospital laboratory in London in September 1928, seen very close: a shallow flat dish about as wide as a hand is long, its floor covered with a thin layer of clear amber jelly dotted all over with small round cream-gold spots, and near one edge a single large fluffy white patch of mold with a pale blue-green heart. All around that patch there is a clear ring where the spots have faded to ghosts and vanished; only farther away is the dish crowded with them. A thumb and two fingers hold the dish upright by its edge; a white coat cuff shows. Behind, out of focus, a crowded wooden bench of other glass dishes in stacks, a brass microscope, a rack of glass tubes plugged with cotton wool, a gas burner, and a sash window with brick chimney pots beyond. No face. Historically accurate: glass, not plastic; bare fingers, no rubber gloves, no printed labels, no writing. The dish is right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and window.
cards.check: 3 September 1928 and the dish were confirmed. Where he had been on holiday differs between sources, and one writer doubts the usual story because his first notebook entry is dated 30 October.

cards.tx: Make one of your Figures ready, so it can act again.
cards.fit: Shut out of the hall, Marian Anderson sang all the same.
cards.fact: In 1939 the great singer Marian Anderson was refused the biggest concert hall in Washington because she was Black. So on Easter Sunday she sang from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial instead, in the open air, to 75,000 people and to millions more by radio.
cards.art: Marian Anderson singing from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington on Easter Sunday, 9 April 1939, seen from the side and a little below: a tall, composed Black woman of forty-two with a calm oval face, her eyes closed, her head lifted a little and her mouth open in song, standing very straight with her hands clasped in front of her, in a long dark mink fur coat worn open at the throat over a bright scarf, and a small dark close-fitting hat. In front of her stands a cluster of six old-fashioned radio microphones on thin stands at the height of her chin. Behind her rise two of the great fluted white marble columns of the memorial, and between them, in deep shadow, the seated marble figure can just be made out. At the left edge a black grand piano with its lid raised and its player, an older white-haired man in a dark overcoat, seated on a bench. The listeners are not shown except as a soft band of color far below at the bottom edge. Cold bright afternoon. Dignified and still. Historically accurate: no banner, no flags, no modern loudspeakers, no rows of faces. Her head is right of center, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain pale sky and stone.
cards.check: Easter Sunday 9 April 1939, the 75,000 and the refusal of Constitution Hall by the Daughters of the American Revolution were confirmed; the society itself said the hall was already booked that day. Her coat and the microphones in the picture brief are from the photographs and need a check against them.

cards.tx: Swap two Figures at different Places. At least one must be yours.
cards.fit: Two men changed places across a line.
cards.fact: On the morning of 10 February 1962 two prisoners walked past each other on a bridge at the edge of Berlin, between East and West: Francis Gary Powers, an American pilot shot down over the Soviet Union, and Rudolf Abel, a Soviet spy caught in New York. Each went home.
cards.art: The Glienicke Bridge between Potsdam and West Berlin on the cold gray morning of 10 February 1962, seen from the roadway near one end, looking along it: a long steel road bridge painted pale green, its two side girders riveted lattice trusses whose top edge sweeps up to a peak over each of two river piers and sags low between them, like the chains of a suspension bridge; the roadway empty and wet, with a white line painted across it at the middle. At the line two prisoners are passing each other, walking in opposite directions, a few steps apart, each alone: one tall and young in a heavy dark overcoat and a Russian fur hat, carrying a small case, walking toward us; the other thin, stooped and older, bald and hatless, with spectacles, in a dark overcoat, carrying a bundle, walking away. They do not look at each other. Well behind each of them, small, stand two officials in overcoats and hats. Bare winter trees on the banks, mist on the water. Historically accurate: morning, not night; no searchlights, no soldiers in rows, no barbed wire on the bridge, no flags. The two men are right of center in the upper half, small against the bridge. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain gray sky.
cards.check: The date, the bridge, the two men and the morning hour were confirmed. A third man, the American student Frederic Pryor, was freed at Checkpoint Charlie as part of the same bargain.

links.tenzing>everest: Tenzing Norgay reached the summit with Edmund Hillary on 29 May 1953, on his seventh expedition to the mountain.

cards.tx: Jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: Two climbers reached the one place nobody had, and had nothing left for more that day.
cards.fact: At half past eleven on the morning of 29 May 1953 the Sherpa climber Tenzing Norgay and the New Zealander Edmund Hillary became the first people known to stand on the highest point on Earth. They stayed about fifteen minutes, because their oxygen was running low.
cards.art: The top of Mount Everest at half past eleven on the morning of 29 May 1953, seen from a few steps below the summit: a small rounded cone of snow against a sky so dark it is almost black, and on it one man standing, Tenzing Norgay, in a bulky dark windproof smock and trousers with the hood up, big pale knee-high boots with metal spikes strapped under them, thick mittens, his face entirely hidden by an oxygen mask with a ribbed hose and by dark snow goggles, an open frame with one oxygen cylinder on his back, a rope tied round his waist. He holds his ice axe up in his right hand above his head, and a string of four small flags blows out sideways from its shaft. The rope runs from his waist down to the lower left corner, where the mittened hand of his partner comes into the picture holding a small folding camera. Below and behind them the white ridges of other great mountains fall away under a floor of cloud. Only these two people, and only one of them seen whole. Historically accurate: 1953 clothing and oxygen set, a wooden-shafted ice axe, no fixed ropes, no ladders, no tents, no other climbers, no readable designs on the flags. His head is right of center, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark sky.
cards.check: The time, the fifteen minutes, the oxygen and the photograph of Tenzing with the flags of Britain, Nepal, the United Nations and India on his axe were confirmed.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: Behind a hole in the ground was a whole lost gallery.
cards.fact: In September 1940 Marcel Ravidat, who was eighteen, and three friends widened a hole left by a fallen tree near the village of Montignac in France and climbed down with a lamp. On the walls were horses, bulls and deer larger than life, painted by people who lived some 17,000 to 20,000 years before.
cards.art: The painted cave of Lascaux on 12 September 1940, seen from the floor looking up: a French country boy of eighteen in a patched jacket, shorts and heavy boots stands at the lower left with his back half to us, holding up a small home-made oil lamp, and its yellow light spreads over a curving wall and ceiling of pale chalky rock covered with animals painted in black, red and ochre exactly in the cave's own Stone Age style, flat and simple, not modern drawing: one great wild bull drawn only in thick black outline, with exactly two long horns curving forward and a muzzle marked with black dots, three times as long as the boy is tall, facing a line of four small horses painted the cave's way, with small heads, fat round bellies, short thin legs, stiff upright black manes like a brush and ochre flanks, no flowing manes or tails; above them one red cow with two short curved horns and no antlers; and between them two small red stags with branching antlers. A second boy, younger and smaller, is only a pair of legs sliding down a slope of loose stones from a dark opening at the left edge. Nobody else. Historically accurate: the animals are aurochs, horses and deer in the true style of the cave, no painted people, no handprints, no mammoths, no electric torch. The bull's head is right of center in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark rock.
cards.check: 12 September 1940, Ravidat and his three friends (Jacques Marsal, Georges Agnel, Simon Coencas) were confirmed. Accounts differ on the dog and on whether he first found the hole four days earlier, so the fact leaves both out. The age is given as about 17,000 or nearly 20,000 years.

links.newton>einstein: Einstein kept a picture of Newton on the wall of his study, and his own theory of gravity took the place of Newton's.
links.faraday>einstein: Einstein's first paper on relativity begins with Faraday's magnet and coil of wire.

cards.tx: Legacy of Isaac Newton or Michael Faraday. He has +1 Might for each Legacy line on your side, up to +2.
cards.fact: In 1905, while he worked as a clerk in the Swiss patent office, he published four papers that changed physics, one of them on relativity. He was twenty-six.
cards.art: Albert Einstein in 1905, aged twenty-six, at his desk in the patent office in Bern: a sturdy young man with thick dark wavy hair brushed back from a broad forehead, a dark moustache and large brown eyes, in a checked wool suit with a waistcoat, a stiff white collar and a tie, standing at a high sloping clerk's desk on which a patent drawing of some electrical machine is pinned, drawn in fine lines with no words. He stands as the photograph taken of him at that desk shows him, one hand resting on the desk and a pen in the other, and he has looked up from the drawing, lost in a thought. A tall window behind him shows the roofs of the old town. Seen from inside the office, from the waist up, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture, with clear space above his hair. He died within living memory, so this is a respectful, recognisable portrait taken from the photographs of him in 1905, at this documented place, with nothing invented. He is a young man: no white hair, no rumpled sweater, no blackboard, no formula written anywhere. The card shows only the upper half of this picture, so compose it with his head, both hands, the pen and the drawing on the sloping desk top, and the window all in the upper half; the lower half of the picture shows only the front of the desk and his legs. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner of the picture plain and empty, with only wall there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.

cards.tx: Swift: he can walk on the turn you play him.
cards.fact: A member of the Sac and Fox Nation, he won both the pentathlon and the decathlon at the 1912 Olympics. Before one event his shoes went missing, and he competed in two odd ones, one of them picked out of a rubbish bin.
cards.art: Jim Thorpe in July 1912 at the Olympic Games in Stockholm, winning the last race of the decathlon: a powerfully built young man of twenty-five with thick black hair and a broad, determined face, in the white vest of the American team with a shield on the chest and white shorts, driving for the finish tape on a cinder track with his chest thrown forward. On his feet are two shoes that do not match, one larger than the other and worn over extra socks. Two other runners, each different, are well behind him. A brick stadium with a clock tower (the clock's face is small and far off, with two hands and plain dots for the hours, no numerals), its wooden stands only a soft blur of color with no faces drawn, and two officials in straw hats beside the track. Seen from just past the finish line, low, his whole figure from head to feet so that both shoes can be seen, his face right of center, about a fifth of the way down the picture. He died within living memory, so this is a respectful, recognisable portrait taken from the photographs of him at these Games, at this documented moment, with nothing invented. 1912: no starting blocks, no modern running shoes, no feathers or costume of any kind. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only stadium tower and sky there: the card's own labels cover those two corners. Nothing round hangs or stands in those corners: no plates, dishes, bowls or medallions.
